#8438. Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

#8437. My Ice Fishing Buddies and I Got Trapped on the Water. One of Us Didn’t Make It

Published Oct 25, 2026 12:01 PM EDT

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

When dawn came on February 26, 1971, the sky was clear over Michigan’s Keweenaw Bay. The thermometer read 26°, and no wind stirred. Nicer winter days don’t come to Michigan’s Upper Peninsula.

Ralph Gianelli died that day after the weather suddenly turned fiendish. He drowned in storm-tossed waters of Lake Superior, probably close to where four of us had been ice-fishing only hours before. Carson Hodges and I barely missed the same fate. If luck had been worse, seven men could have been killed in the worst blizzard I’ve ever experienced.

My three partners and I were all experienced ice fishermen. We’d gone after lake trout on Lake Superior’s ice many times without serious trouble. As far as I could learn, Ralph was the first ice-fisherman to lose his life on Keweenaw Bay.

Ralph was a 55-year-old driver of heavy construction equipment. Joe Watson at 48 was the youngest member of our group. He’s a retail merchant. I work for the post office. Carson Hodges is a carpenter. He and I are in our mid 50’s. When we left our homes in Hancock that morning we were sure we’d finish the day with a fine catch of lake trout.

The trout waters of Keweenaw Bay are about two miles from shore in depths of 90 to 180 feet. The large triangular bay is about 175 miles northeast of Duluth. The Keweenaw Peninsula protects the bay on the northwest. A smaller peninsula juts out on the east side of the bay. This fairly protected water freezes over with hard, blue ice in winter.

The main waters of Lake Superior, however, seldom freeze, because they’re deep and storm-tossed. Ice on Keweenaw Bay usually ends in open water somewhere out on the vast expanse of Superior. This fact is foremost in the minds of the bay’s ice-fishermen. It rarely happens, but an outside section of the bay’s ice can crack off and float out. A fisherman caught on a drifting floe would be in serious trouble.

The area’s anglers stay off the ice in bad weather. Most use snowmobiles to get to the fishing. If bad weather develops, a snow machine can make it to shore in minutes. Some experienced anglers tow boats on sleighs behind their machines so that they’ll be ready for any emergency.

Still, nature can be violent, especially in the North Country winter. Blizzards and high winds can come as suddenly as an explosion. We left Hancock before dawn in two pickup trucks, each loaded with a snowmobile, sleighs, and ice-fishing gear. After 25 miles we pulled in at Makinen’s Landing, three miles north of Portage Entry. As the sun was topping the horizon we hooked the sleighs to the snowmobiles and headed southeast toward the trout grounds off Section Eight Point.

Joe and I shared the seat on one machine; Ralph and Carson rode the other. It didn’t take long to travel two miles to our fishing area. Minutes later we had our tents up and were fishing. The tents offer some protection against the bitter cold. They’re canvas and tepee-shaped, with struts hinged at the top to permit folding into compact rolls. A zipper opening serves as a door.

Joe and I soon decided to try a new spot. We snowmobiled a half-mile south and drilled holes 75 yards apart. About 10 a.m. I really got into the trout. I had three on the ice and had lost several others when I felt a sudden shudder across the ice. I jumped outside the tent and couldn’t believe how much the weather had changed. The sky was a mass of ugly clouds. But what surprised me most was the sudden increase in wind.

The wind was blowing southwest toward the open water of Lake Superior. Such a wind is dangerous because it can crack the ice and push the floes into the open water. I knew we should get off the bay in a hurry, so I took off to warn Joe. What I saw stopped me in my tracks. A ribbon of black water ran in a jagged line between me and the shore as far as I could see.

I was adrift on a huge ice floe. But I figured it would take a long time for the floe to begin moving. The crack didn’t look more than six inches wide. Joe was on the other side of the crack, so I ran toward him, yelling.

When I got close to the crack, I saw I’d badly misjudged its width. The black water was about six feet wide and looked wider. My blood ran cold as I saw I had no chance of jumping to safety.

I couldn’t believe that a huge floe could drift so fast. I guessed the mass of loose ice was about 14 miles wide and four miles across (our fishing area was four miles from open water, and the crack probably ran clear across the 14-mile-wide bay).

Joe was 20 yards from me. We discussed the situation in shouts for a moment. Then he began walking toward shore to organize a rescue. That’s when a heavy snowfall loomed like an onrushing wall of white. I saw Joe vanish in the blizzard.

My partner’s snowmobile was only a few yards away. I rushed to the machine, started the engine, drove to my fishing site, and grabbed my gear. Then I roared off to warn Ralph and Carson. They were on my side of the crack, still in their tents and unaware of what was happening. Now the crack was 20 feet wide. As I got close to my partners I jumped off the machine.

“It’s cracked off,” I hollered. “We’re adrift! Let’s get out of here!”

Ralph and Carson moved so fast that they hardly bothered looking at the widening channel of water. We loaded our gear and began snowmobiling north, staying about 50 feet from the edge of the ice. The only logical thing was to get as close as we could to Makinen’s Landing. Any rescue attempt would start there.

My two partners stayed 50 yards ahead of me because we wanted to spread the weight of the machines. We’d traveled about a mile when the eight-inch-thick ice cracked again. This split ran perpendicular to the first crack, and it shot between our two snowmobiles. Again I was amazed by how fast the gap widened. By the time I reached the crack it was four feet wide.

I had the throttle of Joe’s machine wide open. I wanted to jump the open water to the floe my partners were on. The machine made the hurdle, but when it landed its hood flew off. Then the engine stopped, and I couldn’t start it again.

Ralph and Carson saw my predicament, turned, and roared back. We abandoned Joe’s machine and traveled half a mile from the new crack. Then we stopped. There was no sense in going farther.

We were about 1½ miles east of Makinen’s Landing. We figured our only chance was to stay put and hope for rescue by boat. The blizzard was reaching full force. We couldn’t see 100 feet in the hard snow, and the wind was strengthening all the time. We knew that if we drifted far enough our floe would be smashed to bits by rough water. It seemed only a matter of time before we would meet death.

“Well, boys,” Ralph said, “we’re going for our last ride, and there’s nothing we can do about it.”

Though Ralph, Carson, and I didn’t know it, Joe had no chance of getting to the landing in time. He told me later what happened. Joe was worried about more ice cracking loose, so he headed for the closest shoreline, at Section Eight Point. In the blizzard he had to guess at directions. Several times he had to veer off course when he spotted open water ahead. Soon the snow was so deep that walking became difficult. Then water began flooding the ice and changing the snow to slush. Walking in that stuff was even tougher.

Joe finally made it to shore at 12:30, but he was still over a mile from Makinen’s Landing. He could have walked inland a half-mile to a road, but he stayed on the shoreline. He was hoping for a break in the blizzard so that he could see us. He could then direct rescuers to the proper area.

He had to make his way up and down cliffs, around huge rocks, and through snowdrifts. The shoreline there has practically no beach; it’s mostly a mountainlike jumble. So Joe didn’t reach the landing till midafternoon. He was completely exhausted.

“I just about killed myself on that trip,” he said later. “I kept bulling ahead because time seemed all-important. I didn’t dare stop to rest. I thought my heart was going to explode several times.”

Meanwhile another rescue effort was in the making.

Bruce Haataja and his brother Bob were also fishing that morning. They had set up about a mile north of us. If they had stayed on the ice, they would have been trapped too, but they quit fishing early. As soon as the weather changed they packed up and snowmobiled to Makinen’s Landing. They were on shore when the crack ripped across the bay.

They could have headed for home, but they didn’t. They knew we were still out on the ice, and they were worried. Harold Makinen was concerned too. The three men decided to wait for us to come in.

They couldn’t see us in the driving snow, but they eventually heard our snowmobile far out in the storm. When the engine suddenly stopped — and didn’t start again — the trio figured something was wrong.

That was when we stopped our snowmobile because we saw no sense in traveling farther. We were just about resigned to not being rescued. If we had known that the Haatajas were tying a 12-foot aluminum pram to their snowmobile and preparing to look for us, we would have had high hopes. The two brothers are veteran ice-fishermen from the Calumet, Michigan, area. Bob, 28, works with his father in a refrigeration business. Bruce is three years older and is a forestry technician.

With lots of luck, Bob and Bruce found us. They knew where we had been in relation to their own fishing area, so they followed the half-drifted over snowmobile track they’d made while traveling off the ice. They rode east to open water. The odds that they would end up almost directly across from us were slim, but that’s how it worked out.

Luck was with us in another way too. When the floe had first broken loose, the gap of open water probably had widened so fast because of a sudden change in water pressure near the crack. When that pressure eased off, the huge floe — it must have weighed thousands of tons — had become relatively immobile until the ever-stronger wind began pushing it. When Bob and Bruce found us, the gap was about 30 feet across. But it was again widening with ever-increasing speed.

Ralph, Carson, and I heard the Haatajas’ snowmobile coming long before we saw it. Then we saw the dim yellow glow of the machine’s headlight blinking in the blizzard. Bob and Bruce spotted us at about the same time.

Bob cut his boat loose, shoved it into the water, and rowed across the gap that now had widened to about 50 feet. The pram was small, so we decided that the safest procedure was to rescue one man at a time. I got in first. By the time we neared safe ice the wind was reaching gale force. A 12-foot pike pole was in the boat. As we came in stern first I shoved the pole out toward Bruce. He grabbed it and pulled the pram to the edge of the ice. I jumped from the stern as Bob got ready to row back across the gap.

Then Harold Makinen arrived, towing another boat with his snowmobile. When Bob saw the 10-foot aluminum pram, he waited till we shoved the smaller craft into the water. Then he tied it to his boat and rowed out.

The wind was blowing at least 40 miles an hour, and the floe was moving rapidly. By the time Bob reached it, the open water was 300 feet wide and building whitecaps.

“There’s nothing more I can do out here,” Harold said. “Things don’t look good. I’m heading in to notify the Coast Guard.”

Bruce and I could just make out the activity on the floe. Through the veil of snow we saw two men in one boat and one in the other, but we couldn’t identify the figures. The men and boats disappeared in the blizzard. Moments later we saw the smaller pram with one man aboard coming on strong.

We started Bruce’s snowmobile and beamed the headlight at the approaching boat. Several times we saw the man glance over his shoulder at the light. Then the falling snow thickened so much that we couldn’t see 20 feet. For several minutes we yelled and raced the snowmobile engine, hoping to be heard by the man in the pram.

Then the snow cleared for a few seconds, and Bruce and I looked out on a grim scene. We saw no sign of boats, men, or the ice floe. We saw nothing but endless water that the gale was churning to a froth.

We felt sure that the icy waters had claimed the three men, but we decided to stay and hope for a miracle. The vicious wind seemed ready to tear our clothes off. About 10 minutes later Harold snowmobiled up.

“This storm is getting worse,” he said. “We aren’t doing anybody any good out here. This ice may crack loose any minute. Let’s head for land before three more of us go into the water.”

Soon after we reached shore a Coast Guard crew arrived from their North Canal Station 35 miles away. They had a 16-foot boat with an outboard motor. Ten men in wetsuits began patrolling the ice while others launched the boat in the open water. It didn’t seem they could do much, because four to five-foot waves were rolling over the ice.

Harold was just about crazy with fear for the lost men — especially for Ralph, one of his best friends. Three times during the afternoon he snowmobiled out, hoping to help. The last time, the ice had six inches of water on it, and his machine broke down just after he reached shore.

About 4 p.m. Bob Haataja and Carson walked into Harold’s camp. I couldn’t believe my eyes. They learned that Ralph was still missing. Then they told us how they escaped death by the narrowest margin.

“When I got back to the floe I shoved the small pram toward Ralph,” said Bob. “Carson jumped into my boat, and we all took off. We’d made only a few yards when one of my oarlocks broke. I ran a piece of nylon rope through the oarlock hole and tied it to the oar. The arrangement worked, but by the time we were under way again Ralph had pulled ahead of us. I thought sure he’d make it. He must have swamped out there.”

“We almost swamped too,” added Carson. “The waves were so high that we knew we’d go under if we kept heading directly into them. Our only chance was to quarter across the whitecaps. We realized then that we’d have to row all the way to land.

“It took us over an hour to reach slightly calmer water, and another hour before we sighted shore. We figured our ordeal was about over when we were thirty yards from the beach. Then one of Bob’s oars broke, and we lost the paddle end. It looked as if our luck had run out, because we were both really beat.”

“I grabbed the pike pole,” Bob told us. “I jabbed it straight down, and it just barely reached bottom. We had to work furiously because the wind was already blowing us back to sea. When you’re looking death in the face you call up physical reserves in a hurry. I pushed with the pole, and Carson paddled with the good oar till we made it to shore.

“We were a mile and a half from here. The snow’s hip-deep in the rocks and cliffs along that shore, except for deer runways that are packed down. We stayed on runways most of the way back. Thank God for deer.”

The storm didn’t let up, so the Coast Guard suspended the search for Ralph at dusk. Joe, Carson, and I left for home to spend the night, but the road was so full of snow that we made only a few miles to a tavern and restaurant. We were told that all roads out were blocked, so we put up in a cabin. The next morning we followed a county plow back to the landing.

The snow stopped during the night, but the wind was still raging. The gale had broken up the ice we’d been on the day before, and that part of the bay was open water. There was practically no chance that Ralph was alive. Even so, a Coast Guard helicopter and other aircraft searched far out over Lake Superior. The hope was that Ralph might be on a floe that hadn’t broken up. But the pilots found no trace of any ice. The search was abandoned.

Related: Frozen Terror, One of the Greatest Survival Stories of All Time

Ralph’s body was found on June 8, 1972, off Point Abbaye on the east side of the bay. No trace of the 10-foot pram used by Ralph has ever been found. Nor has there ever been any report of the tents, sleighs, ice-fishing gear, and other items we used that would float. The two snowmobiles are somewhere on the bottom of Keweenaw Bay.

Bob Haataja was the man most responsible for saving Carson and me. The Michigan State Police presented him with a citation for heroism. The award was given at a dinner of the Lions Club in Calumet, Mich.

This story, “Day of Terror,” appeared in the May 1973 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8433. Spanish Team Bags First Ascent of Jugal II

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

The main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

#8432. How to Skin a Deer Like a Pro

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:38 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

If you ask a dozen hunters how to skin a deer, you’ll find that every one of them does something slightly different. While that may be frustrating for newer hunters, it should also be reassuring: There’s no one right way or right order to skin a deer. As long as you follow the general techniques and handy tips outlined below, you’ll be able to skin a deer in no time.

Once you do get the hang of it, skinning a deer is quick and easy. Butchering and packaging a deer can take all afternoon but “if it takes me 10 minutes to skin a deer,” says Cheyne Matzenbacher, a one-time deer processor and current deer outreach specialist for the National Deer Association, “that’s a long time.”

Read through the whole article or click on a topic below to jump ahead.

Although there are lots of tools and setups that can make skinning a deer much easier, the only thing you really need is a sharp knife. The best skinning knives are typically handy enough for maneuvering but durable enough for joint work. There’s nothing wrong with using a small folding skinning knife in the backcountry or a longer filet knife. Just don’t use a dull knife — it’s dangerous and takes longer to finish the job.

Before you can skin your deer, you need to gut or field dress your deer, which involves removing the internal organs from the chest and abdominal cavities. Once your deer is gutted, you’ll ideally want to hang it. It’s certainly possible to skin your deer on the ground or the bed of your pickup (I’ve done both many times), and if you plan to do this, you should study up on the gutless method of skinning deer and other big game. This process is preferred by backcountry hunters who quarter their deer in the field, slip the meat into game bags, and pack it back to camp or their trucks.

But for most whitetail hunters and Western hunters who hunt close to home, it’s easier and faster to skin a deer that’s hanging. The meat will also stay cleaner if it’s hanging instead of touching dirt, bacteria, and deer hair on, say, your tailgate. There are a dozen methods for hanging a deer, and they all depend on your location and the tools available to you.

Deer hunters are divided on this question. You can skin a deer that’s hanging head up or head down, but there are advantages to each method. When Matzenbacher worked as a deer processor for a season, he and his coworkers would hang deer by the head or neck to skin the animal, then flip it to hang head-down for butchering.

“Think about how a deer jumps over a fence: His legs are folded up against his body. Let gravity help you, and let the natural way a deer is going to fold up help you skin it,” says Matzenbacher. “Don’t fight it.”

I skin all my deer head-down, so that’s how I’ll walk you through this example. If you want to try the head-up method, the principles are all the same. Just start at the neck and work your way down. If you are planning to shoulder mount your deer, don’t follow all of these instructions; you’ll need to make very careful cuts near the forelegs and chest. These traditional instructions are for does or for bucks you plan to skull cap or Euro mount. Finally, redneck ingenuity abounds when it comes to skinning deer, and if you’re interested in working smarter, not harder, consider the golf-ball trick or skinning your deer with your truck.

Make identical circular cuts near the knee joints, circling the thin bone of the lower leg on the side closer to the hoof. (This is the only time you should be cutting down on deer hair. For all the rest of the cuts, insert your knife under the hide and cut parallel to the meat or away from the meat.)

Slip the tip of your knife under the hide inside one hind leg. Applying even pressure, cut up and out in a single smooth motion as you run your blade toward the pelvis until you reach the cut you made while field dressing. Do this on the other hind leg, then start to skin the hide away from the tendons where you’re going to put the gambrel and expose the knees. The idea is to remove just enough hide that you don’t have to skin around the metal of the gambrel once you hang the deer.

Thread the gambrel through the natural holes you just exposed in the hind legs (between the bone and thick tendon) and hoist your deer. Tie it off at a comfortable height to work on the hindquarters

Note: You can perform this at almost any point in the process. Some hunters prefer to do this before hanging their deer, others do it as needed throughout the process (as pictured). You can also use loppers or a reciprocating saw for this and may want a saw for the hind legs; just take care not to cut the big tendon on the hind legs.

Slightly bend the front legs and cut through the joint. Wiggle the leg to find the weakest point and use your knife blade to cut perpendicularly through the tendons and between the bones until the joint is free. This may seem tricky at first, but it’s simpler than it looks.

Run your knife between the lower leg cuts and the cut along the abdomen you made while field dressing. Do this on both sides of the inner hindquarters. Combined with the lower leg cuts (or removal) these are the major cuts that will allow you to skin most of your deer.

Using your off hand to lift the hide and your knife hand to make cuts parallel to the meat, begin to peel away the hide. Work from the inside of the hind leg around to the outside. Do this on both sides.

Separate the hide at the tail by either running your knife under the hide and pulling it off the tail like yanking off a sock, or cutting the tail off altogether. Use your knife to work between the joints or simply saw it off.

Now you can begin the easiest part of skinning a deer: letting gravity help you pull the hide off. You may need to raise the deer a little for this part. Once you’ve used your knife to separate the hide from the tail and the inside of the hind legs, set it aside and grab fist-fulls of hide. Using your body weight, pull the hide toward the ground. If the hide doesn’t pull free in places, you can use your knife to help release the hide by slicing the delicate white crackly tissue that connects the skin to the meat. You’ll likely need to do this around the belly area and occasionally along the back

The hide will start to form a tube as you peel it away and it gets closer to the chest and neck.

Before the hide gets in your way too much and starts to drape over the forelegs, make cuts inside the forelegs similar to the ones you made on the hindlegs, starting near the knee joint and running the blade along the backs of the legs until they reach the body and chest. (If you didn’t remove the lower forelegs before, be sure to do this before you try to pull the hide over it.) You can also just pull the skin over the forelegs by pushing down on the hide between the brisket and front of the cut front legs (see video above). It’s similar to pulling off a sock.

Continue to work the hide down over the shoulders and forelegs like you’re peeling off a sweatshirt. The cuts you made on the legs will appear and you can use your knife to free the hide.

Once the hide is over the shoulders, use your knife to separate it from the neck. The freed hide will be heavy now and starting to get in your way. Use its weight to your advantage so it pulls the at the hide still connected to the deer.

When you reach the base of the neck, use a saw or your knife to sever the head from the vertebrae. You’ll have to cut through meat and tendons on all sides until you reach the spine. If you’re using a knife, work through the vertebrae like you did with the knee joints, turning the deer’s head a little bit to help free space between the vertebrae. You want to make your cut at the atlas joint, the connection between the head and the first vertebra of the neck and spinal column.

Once you cut through the neckbone the hide should be completely removed from your deer, though still attached to the head. If you need to get your deer tested for CWD or plan to make a European mount, just slice away all that extra hide hanging off the head.

This step is only necessary if you plan to make your own skull mount. Start at the neck and cut away the skin as you did on the rest of the deer, making cuts parallel to the meat and skull until you’ve removed most of the skin. A flathead screwdriver can help free the hide at the base of a buck’s pedicles, which can be the trickiest part to remove. This is a more time consuming process and should be done carefully to avoid injury or scoring the skull with your knife, which can cause cosmetic damage.

No, you don’t have to hang a deer to skin it. I’ve skinned plenty of deer in the back of a pickup, and sometimes that’s your only option if you’re hunting in areas without many trees or access to a barn or meat pole. It’s definitely easier to skin a deer if it’s hanging since gravity helps remove the hide. It’s also easier to keep the meat clean if your deer is hanging when you skin it; skinning a deer on a level surface like a tailgate or outdoor table makes it more likely that you’ll get deer hair and possibly dirt or bacteria on the meat.

The only tool you must have to skin a deer is a reasonably sharp knife. There are plenty of additional tools that make the job easier, and those will depend on where you’re skinning your deer. If you’re working in the field, consider a hitch hoist for your vehicle and a pair of loppers to quickly remove legs. If you have the luxury of a garage, shed, or barn to hang your deer, along with electricity, you might invest in an electric winch and a Sawzall.

How fast you need to skin a deer depends on a few factors, including the temperature outside and your state’s carcass transportation laws. As a general rule, in the right conditions (cool and dry), a deer can hang hide-on for several weeks. (See below for more details.) If it’s hot and humid, skin the deer as fast as you can to help cool the meat and prevent spoilage. If temperatures are near or below freezing, you should skin a deer while the carcass is still warm and the hide is pliable; skinning a frozen deer is both difficult and time consuming. Meanwhile, CWD laws in your state may require you to debone all deer meat before crossing county or state lines. If such regulations apply where you hunt or live, you’re going to need to skin your deer so you can debone it before you hit the road.

A skinned deer can hang for up to a few weeks if it’s stored in the proper conditions. The deer needs to stay cool and dry, such as sheltered outside during the winter or (preferably) inside a walk-in cooler set to a consistent temperature. Experts recommend hanging deer for 7 to 10 days at a temperature between 35 and 45 degrees to allow enzymes to age, or tenderize, the meat. A deer will not age properly if it’s frozen.

Yes, you can age deer meat with the skin on. Opinions on this vary about which method (aging venison with or without the hide) is better. Any meat that’s exposed to air as it ages will develop a dried crust, and the hide can help protect that meat from drying. I once hung a doe, hide-on, in a walk in-cooler with the temperature set to 38 degrees for two weeks. It was surprisingly easy to skin after aging and I lost less meat than when I age completely skinned quarters. But if you let your deer hang for much longer than that (three weeks or more) the meat may over-tenderize and start to come away with the hide, forcing you to work slowly and possibly wasting meat. Still, letting deer meat hang for at least a day or more can help keep it dry, tenderize the venison, and concentrate flavor before butchering.

The best deer skinning knife is a sharp one. The type of knife—skinning, caping, boning, or filet—matters less than its sharpness and the cuts you make. Many hunters and wild game processors prefer different types of knives for different stages of the skinning process: There are skinning knives (usually slim, handy knives with a sturdy blade), flexible filet knives for working around awkward angles or different muscle groups, caping knives for skinning the shoulders and head of a trophy deer, and stout boning knives for separating knee joints. Try several types of knives to find the best deer skinning knife for you.

Remember, there is no single perfect way to skin a deer. Every deer hunter and processor I’ve met does something slightly different, and most swear their way is the best way. Find which tools and techniques work for how you hunt and what kind of facilities you have access to (if any). The only way to truly learn how to skin a deer is, well, to skin a deer. So sharpen your knife and get after it.

Natalie Krebs is the Executive Editor of Outdoor Life, where she tackles everything from reporting digital features to producing podcast episodes. Originally from Missouri, she currently lives in northwest Arkansas with her bird dog, Hatchet.

#8429. Alpha Direct: Ultralight Miracle Material or Overhyped Fad?

I do a LOT of outdoor recreation, and I can’t be limited to just the bluebird summer days. Rain or shine, burning heat or ice-cube chill, I’m outside doing endurance sports 12 months a year. I am also chronically cold.

My solution? Layers on layers on layers. I keep gloves in the pockets of all my jackets and have nearly a dozen active-insulation midlayers at home. The last few years, Alpha Direct has been my go-to fabric for getting outside when the temps drop too low for a simple base layer.

When I first reported on Alpha Direct (AD) hiking layers nearly three years ago, the fabric was just becoming part of the thru-hiking zeitgeist. I didn’t realize then that its popularity was about to explode, nor that many would come to see AD as the go-to layering system for adventure sports.

A huge factor in its adoption has been the multiplying cottage brands working with Alpha, and, more recently, even big brands like REI and Big Agnes taking a stab at products for the masses.

A Trek gear reviewer testing the Sambob Alpha 120 hoodie in 2024. Photo: Kate Richard

With more products in circulation and more time to age, criticism of the technology has grown as well. I’ve been using this fabric for nearly four years, including several garments I made myself. While I still reach for it for personal use, I’ll be the first to admit that it has drawbacks, and these days I only recommend it to a very specific type of user.

All that being said, is Alpha Direct really the miracle performance fabric of outdoor sports, or is it just another overhyped ultralight fad?

With its nearly transparent, open knit structure and hydrophobic polyester fiber, Alpha Direct is one of the most breathable fabrics on the market. This is especially true in lower fabric weights (with 60gsm and 90gsm being the most popular), where the insulating “tufts” of fiber are widely spaced, leaving lots of open channels for body steam to escape.

Three-season garments made of Alpha Direct typically weigh between 5 and 10 ounces, roughly half of what a standard grid fleece might weigh. This difference matters in backpacking. Even hikers who don’t consider themselves ultralight have to be conscious of weight and packed volume.

This low weight translates to insulating efficiency; Alpha Direct has one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios for synthetic insulations.

A packed-size comparison of various Polartec fleeces. Left to right: Power Grid High Warmth (15oz), R1 Air (10oz w/o hood), and two Alpha Direct 90s (4.9oz each). Despite being half the weight, the Alpha Direct hoodies fare well against the R1 Air (when capped with a wind shell).

Aesthetics aside, I think part of AD’s appeal is that it feels comfortable as both a next-to-skin or midlayer, and it moves and stretches well. A nice touch of its non-absorbent nature is that it rarely feels clammy, even when wet or damp.

Rocking my classic wind shirt + Alpha Direct combo at 14,000ft. The route from camp was almost entirely 3rd- and 4th-class scrambling, which is exposed, slow, and high-output at the same time. I’m happy with my layering choice here.

Polartec’s go-to fiber is polyester, aka plastic. The world is increasingly skeptical of plastic use, especially for food-and-water containers and clothing. The former is a huge concern for microplastics in the body, while the latter is criticized for microplastics in the environment.

Alpha Direct has earned itself a bad rap as an exceptional microplastic polluter, and fairly so. Having made quite a few Alpha Direct hoodies myself, I can confirm that the fabric sheds enough fibers to fill my lint trap during the first few washes. At a more microscopic level, polyester is generally known to break down quickly with age.

When this fabric first hit the thru-hiking world, it was used almost exclusively by ultralight nerds who are used to their gear being as fragile as tissue paper. Once it became more mainstream, old heads and traditional backpackers were quick to balk at its transparency and tearability.

Alpha also has an obvious kryptonite: velcro. Even light contact will tear some loft out of the knit, if not rip the garment entirely. The open base structure and loose tufts are destined to snag and tear on anything pointy, including branches, gates, and even components of your other layers.

As much as I enjoy its breathability as an active layer, I’ve pretty much banished AD from my climbing wardrobe, where even a gentle graze on relatively smooth rock can create pulls in the material.

Fresh Alpha Direct yardage on the left, and 3 years well-loved on the right. It’s hard to tell by photos, but the fresh version has quite a bit more front-side loft and a visible pattern of ‘back side’ insulation. The older piece is matted from age and light on back-side loft (either from shedding or “light” batch variation).

This drawback is becoming increasingly visible as the product grows more popular. When you can easily pull an AD hoody off the rack at your favorite generic outdoor retailer, it will land in the hands of many uninformed and incautious users. I’m convinced a lot of these made-for-the-masses options are tried, torn, and trashed within six months of purchase.

What time in the wardrobe has taught me most is that Alpha Direct mats and pills extremely fast. I didn’t see this coming; I was worried about overt fiber loss and ripping, not compression of the little fiber fuzzes that make AD work.

I’m not the only one who’s noticed. Diving into online forums, you’ll find quiet but increasingly common acknowledgments of quicker-than-expected wear. I’ve read about some hopeful fixes like “combing” it out or washing with certain soaps, but I haven’t found much that works in real life.

In a memorable critique, Jan of Nunatak Gear called it “FKT stuff … Alpha sheds, thins and rips readily. Besides environmental impacts the degradation lowers the performance faster than any other base layer I’ve owned.”

I still have my first Alpha layers nearly four years later, but I can’t say any of them are in great shape. Each shows the signs of being well loved: cuff trims torn off, holes from overgrown trails, and a noticeable reduction in loft, both from matting on the outside and actual fiber loss on the inside.

Layered up on the Innsbruck Via Ferrata. Yes, dish gloves and sleeping bag fabric is peak performance in cold and windy conditions.

Perhaps this is a bit of insider baseball, but I’ll be damned if I don’t mention the significant batch variation of this particular Polartec product. Even new off the shelf, the actual loft of a “90gsm” Alpha Direct varies widely. In some of my Alpha Direct yardage, I can barely tell there is supposed to be loft on both sides of the web-like base, while others have a clear “line” of raised insulation running through.

I’ve seen several manufacturers who actively sell products with AD that criticize this online, with the cult-favorite Dan Timmerman writing, “Alpha Direct 60 and 90 has incredible variation from roll to roll. Some 60 is more like 90 and some 90 is more like 60. It’s pretty much all over the place … I think every roll of AD60 and 90 has its own levels and characteristics that don’t necessarily line up with the general product specs.”

This makes it pretty hard to tell how much your garment is actually going to weigh (boo-hoo for the gram weenies), and more importantly, how warm it is actually going to be. You should therefore always test a new Alpha Direct garment before you commit to using it on a thru-hike.

Just a few weeks ago, Polartec announced a generational update to the full Alpha Direct product line. They promise to keep the same lightweight, breathable performance while improving strength, integrity, and snag resistance. This hopefully means less microplastic shedding and more time out in the wilds before a major tear.

How much better could this next generation actually be? The answer remains elusive. Polartec hasn’t published any stats or tests showing how much improvement we might see. But products made with the new Alpha Direct are already hitting the market, so consumers will soon find out for themselves. You can expect cult-classic brands like Senchi and new-to-AD brands like Patagonia to put new layers out in the coming months.

A photo of the next-gen Alpha Direct. Similar appearance, but will those puff balls stay in place better than the previous gen? Time will tell.

Honestly, I will continue to use Alpha Direct for at least as long as my current stock of clothes and yardage lasts. I like its efficiency, breathability, and layerability with different shells. I’m also fairly gentle with gear.

I am much more hesitant to recommend it to others now, though. The combination of fragility and fickle use in a larger clothing ecosystem puts a huge burden on the user to be educated.

In contrast, classic options like microgrid just work without you having to know anything about the fabric ahead of time. I’m also hesitant to promote a fabric with a known microplastic problem (which I still justify to myself by the lack of empirical data to the standard options).

Is it right for you? Maybe, maybe not. If you are a gram weenie or sensitive to layering just right while active, it’s probably worth a shot. If you are going in skeptical or just want something that works without the fuss, I would point you elsewhere. There’s a nearly infinite number of layering options out there.

Octayarn is a similar fabric to Alpha Direct that is manufactured by Teijin. It functions similarly to the Polartec offering but has a stronger face fabric (e.g., snag protection and opacity) at the cost of warmth-to-weight efficiency. When people complain about fragile Alpha, Octayarn alternatives like the Mountain Hardwear Airmesh Hoody usually get a shout-out from disillusioned hikers.

Even brands that once staked their identity on Alpha, like Senchi, have broadened their horizons. They recently released a new hoody adorably called the TurboSheep that takes an Alpha-like construction but mixes in a healthy dose of merino wool. While standard Alpha Direct with Wool is heavier than straight-up AD, these new Senchi hoodies come in familiar low fabric weights (60, 90, and 120gsm compared to ADW’s 150gsm floor).

I’m generally skeptical of mixed-fiber fabrics (they can sometimes be “master of none” and create unrecyclable/uncompostable landfill trash), but I can at least hope that any fibers being shed have a chance of natural decay.

If the spider-web technology of Alpha feels a little too new-school-cool, going retro with a grid fleece or thin puffy is tried and true. I mix in my Melanza hoodie and R1 Air just as often as my AD layers, although I do live in Colorado where these options are standard streetwear.

#8428. An Old-School Snowshoe Hare Hunt With Hounds Is the Most Underrated Winter Adventure

Published Oct 26, 2026 11:21 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

One of the things I like about snowshoe hare hunting is hot raspberry pie. Few restaurants serve it, especially in the dead of winter in a northern Michigan small-town cafe. One morning last February, my three hunting partners watched with interest, chins resting on their palms, as I sank a fork into the delicacy.

“Do you always eat raspberry pie for breakfast?” wondered Ralph Holsinger, who had invited me to join their hunting group.

“Only when I find a restaurant sensible enough to serve it.”

Another thing I like about hunting snowshoe or varying hares is trying to figure where they will appear ahead of the bawling pack of hounds. It’s a game of constant adjustment—moving up, moving over, squatting low to see through thick cover. You have to take into account the lay of the land and its habitat types and be able to sort out the hound music from what’s hot and what’s not. Sometimes the elastic circles the hares and hounds run are wide, and sometimes they are deceptively narrow.

Playing your hunches is also important because, after all, hares rarely do what they are supposed to do. That’s what Holsinger says, anyway, and he should know: He has been chasing the all-white bunnies for 50 years.

After leaving the restaurant, the four of us took stands along a fire lane through young jack-pine woods that flanked a cedar swamp. In quick succession, two separate hares gave me the slip. The first time I heard the dogs mushing through the snow toward me, I sneaked 20 yards to my left for a better shooting position. But I should have moved 40 yards because when the bounding bigfoot suddenly appeared, it was too far away for a shot. Joe Covert, a member of our hunting party, ended that romp when he shot the hare as it tried to cross the opening. Then, during the second chase, I should have stayed put; this time the elusive hare practically ran over my earlier position, but I wasn’t quick enough for a shot. It slipped by the other hunters, too, and now the pack had driven the snowshoe deep into the swamp.

We waited, 100 yards apart, and shuffled our feet against the cold. Thirty minutes passed, and now it was 10:30. Then I could hear it—the faint squeal of Squeaky, Holsinger’s lead beagle. Soon, Rambo barked in with a coarse bawl. The stretched-to-the-limit circle was tightening once again. The other dogs—Shane, Twinkie, Candy and John—began to cut loose with assorted chops, yelps and squeals that were definitely growing louder. The gutsy pack of hounds was pushing this splayfoot right down my throat. For once, I wouldn’t have to move at all.

Sinking to haunches, I swept the woods slowly from left to right and waited for the hare to materialize. You never hear snowshoe hares, at least not with snow on the ground, and certainly not with the hounds chorus ringing through the woods and in your ears. No, like true ghosts, snowshoes take shape before your eyes. Suddenly, and with a rush of adrenalin, they are there. So where was this one? The dogs were closing in too fast. Already I could see their skinny tails whipping left and right, but no rabbit.

There comes a point when the hunter of hares knows he has failed, and usually that is when he sees the dogs. They filed by at 30 yards, eagerly punching their noses in and out of the loose snow and ignoring me altogether. How did they know I was no threat to any swamp ghosts today? Snow-choked cedars muffled a shotgun blast, which told me that one of the other hunters, probably Marty Anthony, had ended this nonsense. So much for my hunches.

Seven species of hares—which actually differ from rabbits because they are born fully furred and with eyes open—are native to North America. The snowshoe, or so-called varying hare, turns all white in the winter and is the smallest. At an average of 14 to 15 inches, hares are a little longer than cottontail rabbits. At an average weight of 3 1/2 to four pounds, they are a bit heavier, too. Range of the hare includes the northern tier of states and all of Canada and Alaska. They also live in mountainous regions of the Alleghenies, California and New Mexico. Besides Alaska, 20 states have hunting seasons.

In addition to mysterious population swings that affect both rabbits and hares every 10 years or so, snowshoe numbers rise and fall dramatically according to habitat availability. In areas of aggressive timber-cutting activities or where fire has destroyed a forest, hares thrive on the new growth for a few years. Then, when the forest begins to mature, the animals may all but disappear.

According to Ben Tullar, a wildlife biologist with the New York Department of Environmental Conservation, abandoned farms in northern New York first support red spruce, balsam fir and white cedar. These conifer species get a head start on hardwoods such as maples, beech, yellow birch, black cherry and white ash. “For example, after a period of only five to 15 years,” Tullar said, “an abandoned pasture can support a huntable hare population for another five to 15 years. But the hardwoods eventually overtake the conifers, and a hardwood/softwood mixed forest develops with little understory vegetation and, consequently, no food or shelter for hares.”

When the habitat is right, populations explode because few animals are as prolific as snowshoe hares.

Snowshoe hares are an important food source for hawks, owls, foxes and coyotes. Apparently, hunting by man has little impact on their populations, and that is why seasons in most states are long and bag limits are usually liberal. Wisconsin hunters, for example, have enjoyed no closed seasons and no bag limits since 1965. During peak years, though, they shoot only about 3 percent of the state’s hare population. In Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Oregon and Washington, hares go underharvested most years.

Hares rarely hole up, a habit that makes them available to hunters on all but the coldest days. In bad weather, they crouch under snow-laden branches and have been known to tunnel under snow, but they don’t usually go underground, even when pushed by a hound pack. Most jumped hares don’t seem to be afraid of the dogs anyway, and I suspect that is because they know they can’t be caught. Most of them amble along, taking their time a few yards ahead of the dogs that flounder in deep snow. Put a crust on that snow, though, and hares will pick up enough speed to keep just ahead of the pack. Generally hares run a wide circle, returning to the same vicinity where the dogs started them. But not always. I’ve seen hares lope through the woods for a mile on a course as straight as a Nebraska section road. Years ago, Holsinger was hunting a linear strip of woods, between a Michigan Upper Peninsula highway and Lake Superior, when his dogs jump-started a snowshoe. When the rabbit took his dogs out of hearing, Holsinger leaped into his truck and drove two miles to where the cover petered out. Ten minutes later he shot the animal when it came bounding through. Most hares would have crossed the highway at some point; Holsinger’s hunch that this one would not paid off.

On a warm, sunny afternoon you can post an area punctuated by the Y-shaped prints of snowshoes and sometimes get shots at animals sunning themselves. Stillhunting, tracking and stalking are effective ways to hunt them, too, if you remember to move slowly and bend down to rabbit-eye level now and then. Just as quietly moving deer hunters look for the flick of a tail or some other part of a buck’s anatomy, so, too, should hare hunters watch for telltale movements or black-tipped ears on the white-on-white bunnies.

It’s easy to find out if hares are using an area by keeping an eye out for their tracks, trails, droppings and eating signs. Saplings girdled near the ground are pretty good clues that a hungry hare stopped by. If food is plentiful, snowshoes will occupy a five to 10-acre area all winter. But if food is scarce, they will migrate several miles in search of something to eat.

Sometimes hares can be pushovers but not very often. One occasion is during years when their populations are cycling high and the animals don’t exhibit the same degree of caution they do during lean population years. The other time is when a fluke of nature puts all-white hares in snowless woods, a condition that can happen in the late fall or late winter. Then, the rabbits are as easy to see as the Blaze Orange clothing on your hunting partner. Nature always helps wild things to adapt, however, because in portions of Oregon, Washington and British Columbia, where snow is generally scarce, snowshoe hares don’t turn white at all.

No matter where you find the varying hare, the most exciting way to hunt them is with hounds. Best scenting days are when temperatures are near freezing or higher and the snow packs underfoot. Worst conditions are extreme cold and powdery snow because what scent there is gets easily covered by the first dog floundering on the track.

“Only the hounds seem to know if hunting will be good or not,” said Holsinger, who has owned and raised dozens of high-stamina beagles, which are most hare hunters’ dog of choice. For two years a couple of Holsinger’s friends kept careful records, noting such hunting-day conditions as temperature, humidity, wind and dog behavior. Their conclusion? Not only is every day different, but it is often unpredictable. On good-weather days the dogs sometimes had trouble getting a chase going, and then on certain days of poor conditions, they ran well.

“Just listen to those hounds,” Holsinger said as he and I hurried down a logging road next to a swamp where the dogs were puzzling out a fresh track. “We put a new dog in that pack, and the music is sweeter than ever.”

Holsinger was striding along in front of me in a place where the woods necked down. Bouncing from one side of his game bag was the white head of a hare. Sticking from the other side were the fuzzy feet of another snowshoe. “The dogs are turning this way,” he said, looking back at me. “Where do you want to set up?”

Read Next: A Christmas Hunt for the Black Hare of Halcott Mountain

“I’ll take a stand right here,” I said and waved him on. “I have a hunch the rabbit will cross at this bottleneck.”

It didn’t. Instead, the hare loped across the road in front of Holsinger, who bowled it over with a load of 12-gauge, No. 5 shot.

It just wasn’t my day for hunches, but all was not lost. I knew where to get another wedge of hot raspberry pie.

#8426. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Big List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the big list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

#8422. Does This Advanced Method of Scent Control Actually Work for Deer Hunting? Here’s What 5 Independent Testers Had to Say

Published Oct 26, 2026 1:06 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Many of the deer hunting strategies we rely on aren’t scientifically proven. For the most part, we go with the gear and tactics that have worked in the field, not necessarily in research studies. The most controversial example of this is probably scent control. Numerous products claim to minimize human scent, and some of them are gimmicks. In this world of scent-control, the most technologically-advanced strategy — as well as one of the most dubious — is to use ozone.

Ozonics is the company that first used ozone to minimize hunter’s scent in 2007. In the decades to follow, the company has sold hundreds of thousands of units, says Ozonics president Buddy Piland. The current topline Ozonics unit costs $456 (on sale), which is serious cash for most deer hunters. Piland admits that marketing Ozonics so it’s perceived as a legitimate product (and not a gimmick) has been a challenge over the years.

“I’m selling you an invisible molecule,” he says. “I’m saying ‘Hey, there’s something coming out of this box that will keep deer from smelling you.’”

So is the price of Ozonics worth it? Do these units actually work as advertised?

You can search around on the internet and find testimonials from a variety of deer hunting personalities promising that Ozonics is a “game changer.” But you can also find testimonials from hunting personalities and influencers promising that almost any gear item out there works, no matter how frivolous it might be.

Cynical deer hunters don’t believe the hype, and they might not even believe the anecdotes of outdoor writers and editors. As hard as we searched, we couldn’t find any scientific, peer-reviewed research on the effectiveness of using ozone to kill human scent in the field.

So we devised a totally anecdotal, but also totally unbiased, experiment of our own. We gave new Ozonics units to five diehard deer hunters who have no sponsorships, TV shows, or big social media followings, and had them test the units throughout their 2023 deer season.

They are all experienced and skilled hunters who have killed big bucks over the years, but they’re also regular dudes. Most of them work blue-collar jobs when they’re not hunting. They have no problem calling out bullshit. Most importantly, they spend a lot of time in the woods. Altogether, they had more than 400 deer encounters while running Ozonics units.

We sent each hunter a survey at the end of their season. We did not pay them for participating in the survey (and neither did Ozonics).

But before we can decide if Ozonics works, or doesn’t work, we need to understand ozone. As Piland puts it, ozone is a molecule made of three connected oxygen atoms (O3), which is unstable and wants to revert to its natural state. Ozone attaches to bacteria or scent molecules and oxidizes them. Ozone is used in a variety of industries (you can read all about it here) but the takeaway for deer hunters is that the ozone being created by an Ozonics unit is supposed to attach to our scent molecules and neutralize them, thus preventing deer from smelling us.

There are a variety of ozone-producing devices on the market that can be used to treat clothing (usually in a bag), but Ozonics is the only company that produces a device suitable for use in the field.

Explained very plainly, an Ozonics unit creates ozone by sending high-voltage electricity through a coil and then blowing air across that coil. Over the years, the company has experimented with different levels of ozone generation and modern units now have selectable levels of ozone to match a variety of field conditions.

Piland says the best way to visualize how ozone and scent work is to imagine a stream with rocks and eddies that disrupt and change the flow of water. That’s a lot like how wind works as it moves across the landscape. Now imagine pouring red dye (your scent) into the stream. It won’t flow consistently downstream. In some places it will move faster, in others it will stop and pool. Lastly, imagine dropping purple dye (the ozone) into the stream on top of the red dye. In some places the purple will completely blanket over the red (effectively destroying your scent). In others, the red and purple will blend to make a slightly different color (altering your scent).

“[With ozone] sometimes you’ll see deer and they’ll definitely smell something, but they don’t panic and run away,” Piland says. “It’s more like, ‘Oh, I’ve never smelled that before.’”

And finally, in some places the red dye and the purple dye will never overlap. The same thing can happen with your scent in the wind. The faster the flow of the stream and the more eddies it has, the more purple dye you’ll need in order to obscure or change the red. In the field, this means more wind and more unstable wind means you need more ozone to neutralize your scent.

“So what you need to do [while hunting in higher winds] is figure out how to best dump your ozone … by adjusting the angle of the unit and the distance it is from you,” Piland says.

All our hunters reported that Ozonics either had a “very noticeable positive impact” on their hunt or “some noticeable positive impact” on their hunting. All of them said that they would continue to use Ozonics in the future.

Combined, they had approximately 435 deer encounters and were clearly busted by deer a total of 24 times. That’s a rate of only 5.5 percent, with many of the encounters occurring downwind. Some hunters had zero deer bust them throughout the entire season. Their anecdotes from the field provide examples of how the units performed.

“A good example of the Ozonics helping was an evening hunt in late October. Four doe and fawns came in upwind. A mature buck followed them in about 15 minutes later and started pushing them a little. Three of the does eventually got downwind of me. They definitely noticed a smell they didn’t like, but never were able to get enough scent to spook. They spent 10 to 15 minutes walking around with their noses in the air trying to smell me. Meanwhile the buck spent close to 10 minutes within 20 yards of me making a scrape and just watching the does. I decided not to shoot the buck, because he had a smaller rack, but there is no doubt in my mind that I don’t get that opportunity without the Ozonics.”

“Yes, even when trying to play the wind, deer still often manage to get downwind at times.  I have noticed that with the unit on, their reaction is much less of an issue when they do get downwind. My experience has been that deer either walk right through my scent cone or if they do stop and try to wind me, they are unsure of what they are smelling and eventually continue past without snorting or blowing. The unit is not foolproof but it certainly helps, based on my experiences.”

“We had a questionable to flat-out-wrong wind a few times this season while sitting over food plots. Normally I would hunt something else or stay home in this situation, but I was curious about how well the system would work in this scenario. In one hunt, the deer entered the field, and they fed into my downwind side. The younger deer had zero idea that we were there. An older doe picked up enough to know that something was off, but she couldn’t seem to pinpoint our location or gather enough scent to sound the alarms. She moved about 15 yards, slightly alerted, but was calm and feeding again within a minute.

I was very skeptical before using the system. It’s impossible to completely fool a deer’s nose. However, hunting from the ground and having deer downwind of me on multiple occasions, and not having them blow out of the field in most cases was a bit mind boggling to me. The deer that would detect something seemed to be confused about what, or where, I was. And that definitely bought me more time to make a shot. I killed a nice buck in the bluffs of Minnesota where my wind was swirling fairly bad. He came to 20 yards and didn’t have a clue I was there. I’m fairly certain that scent was pushing up into the ravine at the time he came in, as I could feel the wind shift onto my neck blowing into his direction. Judging from my encounters with hundreds of deer and countless ‘scent destroying’ products, Ozonics was the only one that I believe to work as they advertise, in most cases.”

“I had many encounters with deer coming in downwind, with zero instances resulting in any deer blowing. I did, however, definitely have some encounters where I do believe the deer smelled something — whether it was the ozone or a hint of me.”

“I had deer walk to 10 yards downwind. They knew something was up but never busted.”

The hunters in our survey had a clear-eyed perspective on Ozonics. They all felt that it worked, but no one said that it was a silver bullet for fooling deer. They also agreed it was not a perfect unit — most agreed that it would be better if the unit was quieter. It didn’t spook deer, but it made it harder to hear deer approaching. It’s a bit of a hassle to set up. Plus, there are minor health concerns involved with using ozone. You should make sure to educate yourself on those issues if you’re considering springing for a unit.

But the numbers don’t lie. The hunters in our survey encountered a ton of deer and spooked very few. They all attributed at least some of that success to the Ozonics units working effectively. That might not count as scientific data, but in the mysterious world of scent control, it’s as good of a field test as you’re going to find.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.
