#8314. Why Québec is the Ultimate East Coast Ski Destination

Owl's Head Ski Resort at sunset. (Photo: Cantons-de-l'Est © Cantons-de-l'Est/BBT Productions)

Nope, it’s not too much to ask: You can get great snow, both natural and man-made, wild terrain, incredible food, historic architecture, and rich cultural immersion all with just a short drive and no time zone change. That’s right. In Québec, winter is so good it feels like it should be hard to get to, but it’s just across the border.

Let’s start with the snow. Canada’s French-speaking province boasts some of the nation’s highest annual snowfall, with up to 250 inches per year. And you’ll find it in every form: deep powder, groomed tracks, and perfect corduroy, spread across terrain that varies from steep and wild to mellow and peaceful. And all that snow comes with dozens of vibrant mountain towns and more than 70 ski resorts—all within a stone’s throw of the Lower 48. (Montréal is just a 90-minute flight or six-hour drive from Boston, and New Yorkers can reach Québec City in less than two hours by air.)

Next, enjoy the rewards of going wherever the path of adventure takes you. The size of the province means you have lots of choices, but rest assured you can’t go wrong: in Québec, skiable terrain unfolds in nearly every direction. The only question is what kind of ski experience you’re looking for. Here’s what you’ll find in the four ski regions featured here—plus which resorts to hit to make the most of it

Looking for spectacular scenery? Unbelievably long runs? Buttery maritime snowpack coming in off the St. Lawrence River? Northeast of Québec City, you’ll find all three in Charlevoix, where the steep slopes of Le Massif de Charlevoix hover over the water, serving up mountain-meets-river views that are totally unique, and plunging valleys and sweeping bowls attract skiers looking to test their skills amid the serene quiet of a Québécois winter. Le Massif serves up the biggest vertical drop east of the Canadian Rockies, while Mont Grand-Fonds offers a compact layout, laid-back atmosphere, and terrain for all ability levels.

Use Québec City as your base camp and you won’t have to choose between good skiing and vibrant arts and culture. The province’s capital is an enchanting maze of European architecture and historic neighborhoods. An evening walk downtown feels like a wander through a snow-draped fairytale. The food and bar scene reflects a similar blend between time-honored traditions and modern flair. And at just 30 minutes from Mont-Sainte-Anne, it’s close enough to the slopes that you can fully immerse yourself in the true Québecois lifestyle without cutting into your ski time.

Close to Montréal, the Laurentian Mountains are speckled with charming, Alps-style villages—complete with classy accommodations, spas, bistros, and microbreweries—that support a robust après-ski tradition. Mont Tremblant offers a stunning variety of terrain, including both gentle runs and enough steep-and-deep to challenge the experts. Meanwhile, Mont-Blanc and Sommet Saint-Sauveur boast quieter settings, family-friendly atmospheres, and five-star night skiing.

The lush, forested mountains southeast of Montréal are densely packed with ski areas, making this the perfect region for some serious resort-hopping. Even better: with the L’EST GO Pass, you can nab discounted lift tickets on four of the zone’s best hills. If you like night skiing, head to Bromont, a local favorite that opens more than 90 runs after sunset. Prefer the solitude of the deep woods? Head to nearby Mont Sutton for world-class tree skiing and a far wilder feel. Laid-back resorts like Owl’s Head cater to families, while Mont-Orford’s high elevation makes it a motherlode of high-quality snow.

Each of the four ski regions featured here has its own distinct personality. What connects them is Québec’s unmistakable joie de vivre: a love of local flavours, lively après-ski, and taking fun seriously. It’s what makes a ski getaway here so full of character.

Québec isn’t far from America’s East Coast, but it feels like another universe. The province boasts a unique culture defined by its French language, historic neighborhoods, local cuisine, and a dynamic craft beer scene. In its urban areas, you’ll find 17th-century colonial architecture, complete with narrow streets, turrets, and flagstone courtyards.

Leave the urban centers, and historic brick quickly gives way to winter’s snow-flocked evergreens and white-blanket pastures. Barns and silos dot the countryside, and just beyond, mountains rear into the skyline like 5,000-foot beacons calling skiers home.

Québec’s unique combination of proximity and novelty make it one of the most unique ski destinations in North America. And yet it’s not nearly as pricey as some of the other life-list destinations you might have on your list. With the American to Canadian Dollar exchange rate, accommodations and food in Québec tend to offer a strong value on a complete ski trip, especially for U.S. travelers. To make the most of that value, explore ski packages and resort offers across Québec on maneige.ski to find the right getaway for your next winter adventure.

Between its vast and varied terrain, deep snow, rich culture, easy access, and affordable prices, Québec has everything skiers need to squeeze more adventure out of winter. Whether you’re looking for more terrain, more culture, or more discovery, you’ll find it here.

Ready to take your ski adventure further? From breathtaking mountain views and exhilarating runs to vibrant après-ski and charming resort villages, Québec offers much more than great skiing. Explore the regions and plan your winter getaway with Bonjour Québec.

#8313. Vanja Matijevec Gave Up His Own Everest Summit to Save Three People

Vanja Matijevec on the Lhotse wall during his 1981 Himalayan expedition (Photo: Aleš Kunaver, kept by the National Museum of Contemporary History of Slovenia)

Vanja Matijevec belonged to a generation of Slovenian alpinists who pushed onto some of the biggest walls in the Himalayas, but one of the defining moments of his climbing life came when he chose not to summit.

On his legendary 1979 expedition to Everest, Matijevec gave up his own planned summit attempt to help Stipe Božić, Stane Belak and Ang Phu, who had become stranded above 8,000 meters during their descent. Božić later remembered Matijevec’s selflessness as helping him survive after he lost a crampon high on the mountain.

Born in Ljubljana on October 14, 1946, Matijevec first encountered the Slovenian mountains as a child, tending cattle on pastures above Tržič. He came to alpinism later, after meeting climber Jože Hočevar through his field work, and began training as a mountain guide in 1975. In 1979, Matijevec, Lado Vidmar and Blaž Oblak made the first ascent of Lucifer (WI4+), a roughly 200-meter frozen waterfall in Gozd Martuljek. The climb, completed with equipment Matijevec later remembered as rudimentary, helped usher in the era of modern ice climbing in Slovenia.

But Matijevec’s ambitions stretched far beyond Slovenia. In 1981, Matijevec and Franček Knez climbed to the rim of Lhotse’s immense South Face, then considered one of the great unsolved problems of Himalayan alpinism. Over the course of his life, Matijevec accumulated more than 30 first ascents, including a direct new route up the West Face of Trisul in 1987. Despite his achievements, his peers remember his kindness more than anything. Fellow Slovenian alpinist Viki Grošelj, who had known Matijevec since their early climbing days, remembered him after his death as a distinctive personality and, simply, “the right man in the right place,” he told Slovenian newspaper Delo.

#8311. How Two Bored Belgians Broke the Backyard Ultra World Record

Trail Runner contributing photographer Jacob Zocherman drove 15 hours from his home in Sweden to document the Belgian team at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship in Retie, Belgium. Unlike a typical race with a predetermined finish and a predictable narrative arc within it, backyard ultras only end when there is one runner left. Zocherman spent the five days and four hours of what ended up being a world-record-breaking run on the course, sleeping in a camper van when he could. He spoke with managing editor Abby Levene during and shortly after the race.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts had been running for 98 hours at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, and they were bored. Never mind they had each run over 400 miles on the same 4.167-mile course. Never mind they hadn’t gotten more than a few minutes of sleep at once in over four days. They looked fresh, the nights were long, and blah blah blah, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports. But with the 100th lap on the horizon, something clicked.

“You could see something happen to them, like a spring flower waiting through winter,” Zocherman tells Trail Runner. “Suddenly the sun comes and nothing happens, nothing happens, and then in a specific moment everything happens and the flower comes out in bloom. That’s what I saw in them—suddenly they were happy to be there, cheering with the audience, laughing with each other and joking.”

It was like colleagues going out to the bar on a Friday afternoon: They’ve found their happy place, Zocherman says. Except in this case, their happy place was a park in Retie, Belgium, aka the middle of nowhere.

“It’s very touching to see, because they are so humble and so easy to like,” Zocherman says. “At that point, I felt like the race would go on forever. But it also feels very fragile—when there are only two runners left, there is no room for error.”

Per backyard ultra rules, runners must run the 4.167-mile lap on the hour, every hour, until only one runner remains and is declared the winner. In case that isn’t nutty enough, the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is an even nuttier spinoff of this format: Each participating country (of which this year there were 67) simultaneously conducts its own backyard race with 15 participants, and the country with the most cumulative laps wins. This backyard team world championship now alternates every other year with the individual championship, held on the original backyard ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Team USA would go on to win the team world title, with Mark Dowdle leading the stars and stripes to a collective 1,120 laps, also known as “yards,” for its second world title in six years. Australia took second, 51 yards behind, and Belgium took third, 11 yards off of them. While the team competition inherently shaped the dynamic of the race, with runners sacrificing their own best interests to slow down and pull teammates along, Steyaert and Geerts had several additional goals on their minds.

They’d each run over 100 laps multiple times—four times for Steyaert and six for Geerts. But neither had ever run through a fifth night. Belgium’s fourth-place runner Kenneth Vanthuyne was long gone after hallucinating that he was at work when Steyaert and Geerts put on their headlamps for the fifth time.

“That was the critical moment,” Zocherman says. “It was the one thing they had always wanted to do.”

As the sun rose over the dewy fields surrounding the dirt road of the race course, they both looked unscathed.

“I was like, ‘OK, nothing can stop them,” Zocherman says. They turned their attention to the Belgium national backyard ultra record of 115 laps, held by Jan Vandekerckhove. They checked that off and reset the goal to the world record of 119 laps, set by Australia’s Phil Gore at Dead Cow Gully in Queensland last year. That, too, proved to be seemingly no problem.

At 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, October 22—over five days after they started running—Zocherman heard rumors that Steyaert and Geerts were setting out on their final lap.

“I think they could have continued. They looked fresh, they looked really good,” Zocherman says. “But I also know they wanted to finish together. And the longer you go, the smaller the margins are that something will happen and one will finish over the other. And they wanted to avoid that. But they wanted to finish together.”

Sure enough, when the pair returned to the start/finish arch at 5:57 p.m., they did not go back out when the clock reached the top of the hour. Instead, the two friends, standing side-by-side in matching red shirts, grinned to the crowd of cheering onlookers, each raising a hand and joining them together over their heads in the shape of a heart.

Together, they had accomplished what no one had done before: Run 124 laps of a 4.167-mile course every hour, on the hour, for a total of 516.7 miles and a new backyard ultra individual world record.

“They are like brothers and have run many times as the two remaining runners,” Zochermans says. “So to them, it is not a competition that late in the race. They are doing it together. And they want it to remain like that. It’s kind of beautiful. It’s poetry.”

From the start at 2 p.m. local time on Saturday, October 17, until Steyaert and Geerts concluded their record-breaking run five days and four hours later, Zocherman was on the ground to document it all. It’s a stroke of good fortune that of the 67 backyard ultra team competitions happening around the world, Zocherman—who lives in his native Sweden—chose to go to Belgium. It’s also not a coincidence.

In fact, Zocherman almost didn’t make the 15 hour drive to Retie after his mother was unexpectedly diagnosed with an aggressive form of cancer two weeks before the race. The only reason he did go, Zocherman tells Trail Runner, is because that random campground in a foreign country is like home. Zocherman had been at the same course in April for the Legends Backyard Ultra, and the mini-universe environment of these events bring people together in a special way that’s hard to describe.

“It was an emotional rollercoaster and a logistical battle,” Zocherman says. “I wouldn’t have gone if it wasn’t this backyard ultra. It was a personal reason to be among people I know and like. I didn’t think it would be the crazy result that it was.”

Zocherman made the trek with his dog Balou, who he says keeps him grounded at these events with no predetermined end, or even rhythm. (She’s now witnessed three world records and could not be less impressed.) They did two laps of the course every day and got a decent amount of sleep for the first few nights before squeezing in 20 minutes at a time between loops by the end.

“I also know it will be a very long race and I have to drive home for 15 hours after so I can’t be crazy wasted,” he says. “Although you become crazy wasted anyway.”

Here’s how this world-record-setting run unfolded, through Zocherman’s eyes and words.

The first out of 372 whistles marks the start for the team world championships, by whistler Eilis Lanclus.

Matthias Pelgrims, one of the top runners the Belgian team is preserving his energy during the first loops of the competition.

Never a dull moment for the crews in between the loops. Always something to worry about.

The hula skirt. Once in a while there is a loop with someone wearing a hula skirt in order to break the monotony.

Resting runners in-between the loops with the watcher waiting to collect.

The puzzle. Whatever brings joy to the table and something to do during the early days is welcomed.

Approaching camp on day three. It’s a misty and cool morning after a very wet and challenging second night of the race.

The runners don’t fear the rain so much during the race, they say. It’s the wind ripping over the exposed night loop that they worry about.

Willem De Troyer is suffering from pain in his legs and is screaming out in pain at every step during what would be his last loop before timing out.

The emotions are rising as the race continues.

Jelle Tielemans is having a hard time during day three, moments before he quits. After 45 hours of racing, only 13 runners of the 990 who started in 67 countries remain.

As the race goes on, usually runners move closer to the start area in order to save time in between the loops.

The intersection of the two loops. The night loop is more open and exposed, while the day loop is more sheltered but also a bit more technical in the forest.

Merijn Geerts takes a micro-nap in between loops.

Tanja Steyaert crews her husband Ivo throughout the race.

The control center with the camera feeds from different parts of the loops, as well as the race broadcast and other tracking sites.

A tense wait for the remaining runners to finish their loops and go out for another.

Sleep is grabbed when you can and where you can. Nothing is certain in a backyard ultra, other than knowing you will get little sleep.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts run through the fifth night. They are the only remaining runners of the 15 who started for Team Belgium.

The party is getting real in the Belgian countryside.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert’s backyard ultra world record is celebrated with the power cutting out (and the start/finish arch falling down) after heavy rain broke the electric circuits. But nothing, seemingly, can stop their progress.

The remains of the previous days. A lot of food, drinks, and beer.

Ultimately, Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert ran 124 loops—and set a new world record—before stopping.

#8309. Go Further in Québec’s Winter Wilderness

Snowshoeing in Gaspésie. (Photo: Gaspésie © Gouv.Qc / I. Roberge)

Let this sink in: More than 92 percent of Québec is public land. Come winter, those millions of acres of woods, trails, and open glades get absolutely buried in snow, turning the province into a sprawling winter playground where opportunities for ski touring, Nordic skiing, and multiday snowshoeing abound.

All that wild landscape would be nothing without a trail system to match—which is why it’s a darn good thing that groomed trails and skintracks cover the province, courtesy of Québec’s adventure-minded culture and infrastructure. Cozy rustic huts dot the high country, Nordic centers pepper the lowlands, and there’s an extensive network of designated ski-touring areas across the region.

Behind Québec’s extensive network of winter trails and refuges lies a long tradition of winter travel and exploration.

Long before winter travel became a recreational pursuit, Indigenous peoples used snowshoes and knowledge passed down through generations to navigate the territory now known as Québec. Today, these snow-covered landscapes offer countless opportunities for exploration, from Nordic skiing and multi-day snowshoeing to backcountry adventures.

Today, Québec boasts 28 national parks and dozens of Nordic and cross-country centers. It also boasts plenty of grassroots backcountry ski areas, each complete with trail maps and designated runs. There’s no avalanche mitigation at these sites—they’re wild at heart—but the effortless parking, signage, and basic infrastructure make them a perfect stepping stone between sidecountry and true backcountry. Always remember to come equipped with the appropriate training, equipment, and avalanche awareness. And if you’d rather explore with a qualified guide, you can find businesses certified through Aventure Écotourisme Québec’s Quality-Safety certification program, which sets recognized standards for risk management, guide training and service quality.

Looking to do a little bit of everything? Try Vallée Bras-du-Nord. This all-season adventure center maintains both groomed cross-country ski trails and designated backcountry terrain. Its varied slopes and jaw-dropping views guarantee an unforgettable outing, while a collection of yurts and cabins make it a true ski-in, ski-out getaway. You won’t find a backcountry experience like it anywhere else in North America.

For a more homegrown vibe, head to Sommets du Fjord, a blues-and-blacks zone just beyond the charming village of Petite-Saguenay. The town sits right on the edge of the legendary Saguenay Fjord National Park—yet another ski touring and snowshoeing epicenter—which makes it an ideal multisport base camp.

Want to turn a great day into a great week? Treat yourself to a fully immersive multiday traverse through Québec’s snow-draped winter landscapes. Robust hut systems in national parks like Mont-Tremblant and Monts-Valins make it easy to plan linkups via Nordic ski or snowshoe, and village-to-village trips in the Laurentians like those along Les Routes Blanches offer chances to discover culture and cuisine alongside the stunning landscapes. Simply choose a trail to one or more of the parks’ remote refuges and use them as stopover points to cook, relax, and connect with your adventure buddies—and recharge by a blazing woodstove before hitting the trail again the next day.

The adventure doesn’t end when the skis or snowshoes come off. Beyond the trails, Québec’s welcoming villages, local flavors, and cozy inns offer the perfect setting to unwind and reconnect. Share a well-earned meal, raise a glass of a local wine or brew with your fellow adventurers, and relive the day’s discoveries. Because sometimes, going further isn’t just about the distance you travel, it’s about everything you experience along the way.

Your next winter adventure starts here. Whether you’re seeking powder-filled backcountry descents, multi-day Nordic ski routes or peaceful snowshoe expeditions through snow-covered forests, Québec invites you to explore further. Discover inspiring winter experiences and start planning your next expedition with Bonjour Québec.

#8308. 5 DIY Climbing Projects to Get You Through the Long Winter

From garage-hammered pitons to swami-belt harnesses, climbers have been making their own equipment since the sport was in its infancy. Gear has come a long way since then. It’s also gotten a heck of a lot more expensive. While we can’t in good faith recommend you save money by making your own chocks and cams, there are still a number of things you can DIY for cheap.

Earlier this month, I went on a DIY kick and decided to hand-make a few pieces myself. Some were items I’d seen friends carry around at the crag. Other ideas came from online forums (and this magazine). With a single trip to the hardware store and a heap of old gear that’s been rotting in the trunk of my car, I was able to make five things—and saved $183 total. Here’s what I came up with, how much each item cost, and what I would do differently next time.

Usual cost: $39.95 for an Edelrid Spinner Leash on Backcountry

Dropped tools are no joke. At Colorado’s ice parks, losing one will typically earn you a swim in a very frigid creek. On multi-pitch ice, you could end up stranded. The trick is to clip your tools to your harness via a bungee system that’s elastic enough to preserve freedom of motion, but not so springy as to send your dropped tool boomeranging pick-first into your thigh

Purpose-made leashes are pricey. A DIY version is free if you have old tent poles lying around your house and only $5 if you need to purchase new shock-cord. I started by clipping the bar tack off an old piece of double-length tubular webbing. I then tied one end of the shock cord to a piece of wire, and shoved it through the tube (this took forever). Once I could access the shock cord from either end, I tied an overhand knot in the center to create a girth-hitchable loop for my harness. I then scrunched the webbing down as much as possible over the two legs of the shock cord, tied overhangs for both carabiners, and melted the edges to finish them.

(Note: For another $10, you can purchase a swivel from most hardware stores, putting the result on par with $80 swiveling leashes.)

Usual cost: $17 for a Personal Tool Tether on Gear Keeper

Some nut tools come with integrated leashes. These don’t add a ton of cost to the tool, but they are boring as all get out. Aftermarket versions from Gear Keeper, Amazon, and beyond aren’t much better. The answer: Make your own out of an old spring-coil keychain bracelet.

First, snip the bracelet in half and feed an electrical crimp onto either end. Next, fold one end of the coil around the inside edge of a nut tool, tuck the end into the nearest crimp, and squeeze the crimp shut with pliers or a crimper tool. Then do the same thing around a small accessory carabiner to complete the tether.

Usual cost: $94.95 for a Metolius Basic Stick Clip at REI

The cost of stick clips has always baffled me, especially since you can make one yourself with a tree branch, a small stick, and a bit of tape. However, I’ll concede that not everyone loves tramping around the crag looking for an appropriately sturdy stick. For those folks, try this trick.

You can buy a painter’s pole from just about any hardware store for relatively cheap. The ones at my local were $20 for 8 feet or $40 for 23. Once you’ve got that, use a couple of stainless steel hose clamps (basically big metal zip ties) to attach a small spring-loaded clamp. Voila!

Usual cost: $54.95 for a Panic Quickdraw on Kong

The internet said I could make one of these by stuffing a piece of webbing into a section of transparent vinyl tubing and tying carabiners to the ends. I tried this and found the result upsettingly floppy. Vinyl tubing is also much more expensive than heavy-duty housing wire, which you can purchase by the foot at Home Depot. Tubing has the added benefit of being foldable.

So, after my first attempt failed, I went back to an old Matt Samet recipe and shoved a section of wire into the hollow core of a length of tubular webbing. I then tied the ends with a water knot to make a continuous loop, and duct-taped a Mad Rock Trigger Wire Carabiner and a bent-gate carabiner to either end. It’s not quite as long as other purpose-made stiffy draws, but it does the trick at a fraction of the price.

Usual cost: $24.95 for a Trango Cord Trapper on Backcountry

I first saw a DIY rope tarp like this at the notoriously dusty Vail Amphitheatre. It’s incredibly lightweight and astonishingly cheap. All you have to do is cut a four-by-four section from a painter’s plastic drop sheet and affix loops to opposite corners. (Note: I used 1 mm-weight plastic, but it felt a little flimsy; 2 mm would be better and only costs $1 more. Tyvek House Wrap would also be superior, but it tends to be more expensive if you don’t happen to have a housing contractor in your life.)

I found that heavy duty plastic shipping tape (especially the kind designed for long-term storage) sticks better than just about anything else. Tape a loop to either corner, and add colored tape to distinguish the belay end from the climber’s end when the rope is stacked.

#8307. 10 Tips for Hunting Pheasants Without a Dog

Before I ever owned a gun dog, I walked up pheasants on the family farm by myself. While I wouldn’t go back to hunting without a dog, I remember the special thrill of dogless hunting: there’s no warning before you see the bird. Every flush is a jump-scare, especially when those roosters burst out of the grass almost directly beneath your feet.

Dogless pheasant hunting was common in the days of high pheasant numbers. Solo hunters walked fencelines and road ditches. Gangs teamed up to drive and block cornfields. Those tactics still work with the right cover, but you’ll walk far more miles between pheasants than your parents and grandparents ever did. They had enough birds to take pheasants for granted. You’ll work for every rooster you scare up, and you’ll want to treat it like the trophy it is. Here are ten tips for hunting pheasants without a dog.

Small covers, like brushy waterways, center-pivot field corners, draws, road ditches (where legal), and fencelines are a dogless hunter’s best bet. Pheasants run, they sit tight, and they fly. You need them to fly. If you can push them to an edge, they’re out of running room, and they’re more likely to slip up and flush. Start at the wider end, if there is one, and push to the narrow end. Always imagine you are driving pheasants ahead of you, because you probably are.

Dogless hunters don’t get as many chances as hunters with dogs. That’s a simple truth. You have to make the most of every opportunity. All that money you save by not paying vet bills and buying dog food? Spend it at the range. Trapshooting is good practice for the straightaways and quartering shots that make up the majority of the chances you’ll get in the field. Skeet teaches you how to hit all the angles, and it’s a game better suited to using your hunting gun. Shooting from a portable trap is good practice, too, and it lets you focus on keeping your eye on the target and your head on the gun.

Compared to most other upland game birds, pheasants aren’t hard to shoot. They are hard to kill. When you hunt without a dog, you need your birds to hit the ground dead. There’s no retriever to bail you out if you only break a wing. The best shots at pheasants are close, going-away shots, and quartering or crossing shots where the head, neck, and vitals are exposed. Ideally, you want to shoot pheasants between a little less than 20 and about 30 yards. Long, going-away shots risk a poorly hit running bird. I don’t even take that shot with a dog, especially in heavy cover.

Dogless hunters don’t have the early warning systems that a flusher’s buzzing tail or a pointer’s rock-solid point provide. When you hunt without a dog, pheasants can pop up at any time. You can’t react well to the flush if you’re trudging along looking at the toes of your boots. Be on constant alert. That doesn’t mean strangling the gun in a death grip and jumping at every sound. It means your eyes are always up, you’re carrying your gun comfortably in a way you can get it into action, and you’re visualizing a pheasant in the air. I used to liken the alertness you need for walking in a field to driving a car, where you watch the road with part of your mind alert that something might happen fast, while also carrying on a conversation or listening to the radio.

Don’t kid yourself. Pheasants almost always know right where you are. Still, there’s no need to advertise your presence any more. Dogless hunters do have the advantage of stealth because they aren’t yelling at dogs. Ease the truck door shut. Keep talking to a minimum. The one time you can beat a pheasant’s hearing is on a very windy day when everything rustles. Sometimes, days like that make them impossibly skittish, but other times, you can get right up on top of them in the wind.

In the days of bountiful pheasant numbers, hunters often formed big groups. Many didn’t bother with dogs, or if they brought them, they used them primarily for pick-up duty. A large party can hunt big set-aside fields effectively. Detail several hunters to serve as blockers. They go to the far end of the field and space themselves along the cover. The larger half of the group walks from the other end. The drivers should stay in a straight line for safety and move toward the blockers. Some birds will flush along the way, and if you do this right, pheasants will be in the air everywhere as the drivers get close to the edge of the field. Obviously, safety is extremely important, and you can’t shoot low birds in a hunt like this. If you can see the sky below the rooster’s belly, you can safely shoot.

A big field presents a daunting challenge for one or two dogless hunters. Chasing pheasants in a large grass field is like trying to grab minnows in a bucket. To trap them, walk from the inside of the field out to the corners. If you push them ahead of you, they will have to sit or flush (of course, they might just loop back around you in the grass. No one said dogless hunting was easy). But your odds go up if you can corner the birds. Working the field edges is always worthwhile, too, as you might catch a bird that’s moving back and forth from food to cover as it lingers too close to the edge.

Pheasants hear a steady drumbeat of footsteps and hunker down to let danger pass by. They have excellent hearing, and they have bones in their feet that sense vibration. You want to make them uneasy. The way to do that is to pause periodically. If they don’t know where you are, they may get nervous and flush. Vary your pace, too. You want to get into their heads.

Any time you reach an edge or corner, or meet a blocker, don’t relax immediately. Birds might be crouched right there. Give them a minute or more to flush. Just last fall, I met my hunting partner, who was blocking, at the top of a terraced hillside. I am not sure what our dogs were doing, but they weren’t there, and we stood, chatting, guns broken open for several minutes before a rooster flushed at my feet and flew off.

Two or three hunters can borrow the hammer and anvil tactics of big groups on a small scale. As I mentioned, you always imagine you’re pushing running pheasants ahead of you. A blocker at the end of a piece of cover sometimes prevents those birds from sneaking out the back door or flushing wild. Give your blocker time to work into position, then drive toward them, pausing and zig-zagging as you go.

When you shoot a bird, mark where it fell as best you can, then go straight to it. Dead pheasants can stay alive just long enough to bury themselves in the grass, and you’ll want to know exactly where to search. Dead pheasants can also come back to life. With about fifteen minutes left in the last day of last season, I shot my final pheasant of the year. It fell on the other side of a stout woven-wire fence and post-holed into a snowbank. The tail feathers stuck up out of the hole, and when I saw that, I thought it would make a great end-of-the-season picture. I decided to hunt the last few minutes of the year, then go back for my photo and my bird.

When I got there, the pheasant was gone. If I had been hunting dogless, as I did so many years ago, the bird would have gotten away. Zeke found it, and I relearned the lesson that any hunter, especially hunters without dogs, needs to go to their birds right away.

#8306. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8305. Red Bull’s Newest Ski Film Is Made By Pros—But Is Surprisingly For Everyone

(Photo: Courtesy of Hai Yen / Legs of Steel / Red Bull Content Pool)

Unless all of your friends are die-hard skiers, you’ve probably endured the unfortunate experience of trying to explain ski films. For those used to tidy narratives and strong plots, it can be hard to see why a film that relies mostly on epic drone photography and loose plot development is worth several hours of someone’s time.

Thankfully, now you don’t have to. Filmmaker and pro skier Paddy Graham and his motley crew have done it for you. In his newest film, “We Can’t Not,” Graham writes a love letter to his favorite format, the ski movie. It’s also a message to his family, who appear in the film. The premise: This is Graham’s last hoorah, and before he steps away from the wild (and dangerous) world of steep skiing, he wants to help his family understand what exactly making a ski film entails.

“Paddy has been asked a lot about what he actually does, and why,” Red Bull Media House executive producer Sarah Stow told SKI. The film is essentially a response to the question Graham is trying to answer: Why keep making ski films? Why keep skiing such big lines? Why do you even do this? He can’t not.

The film opens up as many others do: a montage of big mountain skiing set to rock music, a few yew soundbites, and close-up shots of freeride jackets with sponsor logos. Then it takes a turn. We meet our protagonist and start to see the film’s thesis unfurl.

That’s the first moment that I realized this film was going to be different.

The idea of answering a legitimate question is what separates “We Can’t Not” from other films: the journey that the audience follows as Graham sits around a dinner table trying to explain to his children and parents what he does when he says he makes ski films is not unlike conversations we’ve had with our ski-film newbie friends.

The issue with many ski films is they’re created for an audience that already loves to ski; in “We Can’t Not,” the audience can be anyone. One way in which Graham does this is by introducing his cast to the audience like we’re meeting for the first time. Each castmate has an intro that explains his distinct “why”: why he loves to ski and why Graham chose to feature him in the film.

“We really wanted to introduce the athletes so audiences connect with them,” Stow explained, “which is such a smart move in a sport where we often only see goggles and helmets.”

The four other skiers: Kye Peterson, Markus Eder, Tom Ritsch, and Finn Bilous, all complement Graham’s conceit: They’re all a little maverick themselves.

But really, the story isn’t about the group of irreverent skiers—it’s about what compels a group of irreverent skiers to do something as outrageous as shooting another ski film. And, for that matter, why ski films ought to keep existing into the next generation. After all, Instagram and TikTok are full of more short-form ski clips than one could ever get through.

The response, at least according to these diehards? A passion for the sport that runs several standard deviations deeper than your average weekend warrior.

A point made clear by the team’s decision to rent out Hyperbowl, a VR film studio outside Munich that, according to Stow, is “more used to Hollywood productions than a bunch of pro skiers turning up.”

At Hyperbowl, a studio outside Munich that Stow says is “more used to Hollywood productions than a bunch of pro skiers turning up,” the cast found that sometimes the most radical lines exist many miles away from the mountain. The Alaska backdrops had to be scanned on location in advance, and Stow says it was the studio’s first indoor mountain ski shoot. Her verdict: the team was “pushing innovation in this film, not just taking the classic safe route.”

The film’s other big swing is its narrator. Sean Bean, a voice that Game of Thrones and Lord of the Rings fans may recognize, narrates the film. Stow says Bean, despite not being a skier, got so into the project that he became a method voice actor. For one of the final scenes, where he tells the audience the film isn’t over yet, she says he ran in from another room to get the tone right.

Ultimately, the meta-filmmaking in “We Can’t Not” helps to underscore the point of not only their ski film, but all ski films: If you love something deeply enough, no lark seems crazy.

While the film could have used a few female voices—there are no female skiers in the film, though many women lined the production teams for Red Bull — the bigger lesson of “We Can’t Not” resonates in its pure obsession with the art form.

For those who’ve struggled to wrangle their non-skier friends to the theaters, there is a story worth seeing here. For you and for them.

You can watch “We Can’t Not” for free on Red Bull TV, and in select theaters across the world.

#8304. 9 of the Most Impressive Undercover Crushers in Climbing Right Now

Shanjean “SJ” Lee sending on the Liberty Bell massif. (Photo: Mikey Schaefer)

The climbing world may love its celebrities, but they also love their underdogs. Which is why we all seem to collectively lose our minds when an undercover crusher emerges from the undergrowth, sends some famous project, and then once again vaporizes into obscurity. The silent crusher archetype has been around since the beginning of climbing history, but in the days of climbing influencers and social media, they seem rarer than ever. To prove the paradigm isn’t dead, we decided to track down a handful and show them a little love.

The trick with finding undercover crushers is that many of them are, indeed, undercover. I initially put out a request for nominations on Instagram and watched the recs pour in. At that point, I figured writing this story would be easy. But many of the people recommended to me were impossible to find. Others were findable but declined to be mentioned. A few, I learned, were undercover because they had been canceled, and I decided that crafting their PR comeback was very much not my job. So, below you’ll find nine climbers who were recommended by one—if not several—of their friends, are in excellent social standing, and were kind enough to dip a toe into the spotlight for this story.

Here are nine of America’s most impressive undercover crushers.

This Bozeman-based young gun is responsible for establishing the hardest climb in Montana: Fox-Like Creature (5.15a), which has yet to see a repeat. But the 20-year-old says his proudest send to date is World Without End (5.14d). “It’s not my hardest route ever, but I think it took me the most effort, in terms of projecting as well as bolting,” he says. “It was also the first 9a [5.14d] route in Montana, which I’m proud of.” In between FAs, McIntosh works as a routesetter at local climbing gyms and spends his weekends cragging in Refrigerator Canyon. “I think it’s one of the best crags in the country and no one’s caught on yet,” he shares.

A lifelong climber based in Squamish, B.C., the 23-year-old Quinn Mason cut her teeth on the U.S. competition circuit before diverting her attention to outdoor pursuits. Last fall, she sent her hardest sport climb to date, Spirit Quest (5.14d), and this spring sent Squamish lines Tainted Love (5.13d R) and Free Dimensional (5.13d PG-13), both on gear. When she’s not climbing, Mason’s either plowing through her coursework for her filmmaking degree or coaching the local youth climbing team. She also does a bit of brand photography and has two sponsors—which means she might not be undercover for long.

One of the few Americans to send V16, Eli Perry learned to climb at a young age but didn’t get serious until he was 15 (he’s now 21). In that time, he started ticking through the grades at a frenetic pace, sending Pegasus (V15) in Joe’s Valley, Utah, and Grand Illusion (V16) in Little Cottonwood Canyon. “Both of them I spent a lot of sessions on and multiple seasons,” he says. In between sessions, he busses tables at an Italian restaurant, does ceramics, and reads. Perry is currently based in Salt Lake City, which he calls “definitely the best spot to be for climbing in the States.”

In between shifts as an orthopedic surgeon at the VA Medical Center in Reno, Nevada, Shanjean “SJ” Lee, 42, manages to send hard across multiple climbing disciplines. She’s redpointed sport routes up to 5.14, boulders up to V10, and is no stranger to Yosemite big walls: In 2021, she notched a free ascent of Free Rider (5.13a; 3,000ft). Lee is also a developer herself. “I put up a route on Liberty Bell in the Washington Pass area called The Dark Side of Liberty with my partner Mikey Schaefer [in 2020],” she says. The 10-pitch pump-fest clocks in at 5.13+, making it the formation’s hardest route to date. Liberty Bell was her local crag at the time, and the opportunity to add to its legacy was invaluable, she says. “It was really special to add a new testpiece route to a place that had given me so much.”

Tadros “Teddy” Eyob isn’t just a connoisseur of long finger cracks—he’s a master of them. The Squamish-based climber recently sent the Joshua Tree triple—Asteroid Crack (5.12d), Equinox (5.12c), and Acid Crack (5.12d)—a trio of stout finger cracks first freed by John Bachar. “I love lines that have finicky gear and keep you feeling like every piece you place is what’s keeping you from decking,” he says. “Something about the level of focus those lines demand really gets me excited.” Before that, he became the first Black climber to free El Cap (NBD), nabbing a proud, ground-up free ascent of Free Rider in early 2026. Now 31, Eyob has climbed all over the world, but his backyard crags remain his favorite place to climb. “The more I travel the world, the luckier I feel to get to call a place like Squamish home.”

Lani Chapko started climbing 12 years ago when her friends convinced her to take an outdoor adventure course for physical education credit in college. She fell in love with the sport right away, became a guide, and went on to establish big routes around North America, including La Sombra de Muerte, (5.12b; 1,500ft), which she and her partner recently authored in El Portrero Chico, Mexico. Chapko, 32, now lives in Index, WA, which remains her favorite place to climb. “There is always another 4-star route, a new way to get humbled, and something to learn from the climbing there,” she says.

Based in Truckee, California, the 33-year-old Sam Daulton is a modern-day Sierra legend. “I was incredibly psyched to make the first flash ascent of Grand Illusion (5.13c) in January 2026,” he says, referring to the finger crack corner near Lake Tahoe, CA. “Grand Illusion was the hardest climb in the world when Tony Yaniro made the first ascent in 1979.” He also bagged the second gear ascent of Tahoe’s Empath (5.14c/d). Daulton first learned to climb as a toddler and grew up training alongside future phenoms like Michaela Kiersch and Isabelle Faus. “At the time, I was a little punk, more interested in shenanigans than training, but after a hiatus in high school, I got back into it.” Now, Daulton works as a research scientist for Meta, a remote gig that allows him to maximize his time in Yosemite, the Sierra, and the French Alps.

Born and Raised in Durango, Colorado, and now a physics Ph.D. student at UC California, Berkeley, Liam Foster is one of the kindest (and most obsessive) rock climbers you’ll ever meet. His meticulous approach to training has served him well, propelling him to redpoints of Line Above the Sky (D16), the hardest drytooling route in the world at the time of the send; Dures Limites (5.14b) in Céüse, France; and The Arsonist (5.14d), a Connor Herson line on California’s Jailhouse Rock. As for what inspires him? “It doesn’t have to be aesthetic as long as the holds are cool and the movements are cool,” he says. “I think people get snooty about climbs, and only want to climb good climbs. But there are so many good bad climbs. It doesn’t have to be perfect to be worth a weekend out.”

West Virginia-based guidebook author Andrew Leich was on the verge of sending his project, Green Magic in the Hills (5.14c) at Seneca Rocks when a rattlesnake bite almost killed him. While he survived, a slow recovery forced him to start over, slowly building through the grades until he was back to authoring new 5.13s, his previous baseline. Then, in December 2025, he finally sent Green Magic, more than three years after bolting it with a friend and nearly two after his near-death snake encounter. Now 32, Leich works as a part-time climbing guide and is the author of two guidebooks: Cheat Canyon Bouldering and Cheat Canyon Rock.

#8303. At This Resort, the Owner is Driving a Snowcat, Turning Wrenches, and Fixing Broken Fences

I’d never ridden a ski lift with the person who owns the mountain below us before, so I’m not sure if this is common.

But as we chugged from the Ski Santa Fe’s base toward its 11,075-foot peak, Ben Abruzzo noted a chairlift returning to the base that sounded squeaky, a groomer that needed tending, and an orange safety fence that had fallen over. Abruzzo—whose day was charged with showing this writer around the mountain his family has owned since the mid-1980s—interrupted his responses to any of my questions on more than a few occasions, apologizing before speaking into a small walkie-talkie mounted on his chest. He instructed this person or that to address the various tiny issues that must pop up a million times a day on a mountain, acting more like a manager than the guy who owns the mountain.

Over the course of a single lift ride, it became clear how much Abruzzo not only cared about the experience of the roughly 250,000 visitors who enjoy his family’s mountain every year but also about the mountain itself. It makes sense once you realize that Ski Santa Fe is, in a way, woven into the very fabric of the person Abruzzo is.

“It’s all I’ve ever known,” said Abruzzo, as the lift neared Ski Santa Fe’s peak, the mountain he described as his “lifelong backyard.”

Owners and CEOs often love to say that their businesses are like a family. However, for the Abruzzos, Ski Santa Fe is not only their family business, but it’s their ancestral home.

Abruzzo is the third-generation owner of Ski Santa Fe, following in the footsteps of his grandfather, his father, and two of his uncles, who finalized the purchase of the mountain in 1985. It was hardly a lark, as the elder Abruzzo purchased the Sandia Peak Ski Area in nearby Albuquerque in the late 1950s.

Their familial sensibility permeates much of Abruzzo’s staff. His grooming manager has worked at the mountain for thirty years. His operations manager as well. The mountain’s ticketing manager bests them both, with 32 years of service.

“I think it’s because we treat our folks right,” Abruzzo said, pointing out that when he says ‘we,’ he doesn’t just mean his father, his late grandfather, his uncles, and any other Abruzzo who’s spent time working the mountain. “Our mountain manager, our operations manager, all of our full-time staff; they’re all invested because they’re all part of this community.”

Abruzzo started working on the mountain when he was 12, building mountain bike trails in the summer and working in the rental shop during the season. After commissioning as an infantry officer in 2001, Abruzzo deployed to Afghanistan with the Army’s 101st Airborne Division during the height of the Global War on Terror. Abruzzo returned home in 2005, working as an area manager at Sandia Peak. He relocated to Ski Santa Fe in 2010, eventually taking over the mountain shortly before the Covid-19 pandemic.

And even though he owns the ski area, Abruzzo still drives snowcats and still turns wrenches when chairlifts need tending. And he requires the same of all the mountain’s senior staff.

“We expect all of our managers to be well-versed in the blue-collar side of things,” he said. “And that includes me.”

Sitting high in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, Ski Santa Fe is about a 30-minute drive from the heart of the famously artsy city in northern New Mexico. Of course, snowy days and weekends might impact that commute time, Abruzzo admits, despite the fact that the mountain has its own dedicated road crew charged with plowing the two-lane road leading up to Ski Santa Fe. Still, as Ski Santa Fe is the only ski area in the vicinity, it’s a drive that never feels out of reach for locals and visitors alike.

In a more corporate environment, that dearth of options could provide owners an excuse to rest on their proverbial laurels. However, Abruzzo sees that scarcity as an honor to uphold. If people only have one option, it’d better be a good one.

With 88 total trails, almost evenly split across blacks, blues, and greens, a trio of terrain parks, and 1,800 feet of vertical drop, all serviced by a double lift, two triple lifts, two quad lifts, two surface lifts, and a high-speed detachable lift, the mountain is far bigger and more diverse than you might think when you hear “family-owned ski area.”

But beyond all that, Ski Santa Fe is known by locals and regulars for two main reasons: first, its off-piste skiing. And second, its snowmaking capabilities.

On the day we spent together, snow fell from the sky in big, thick flakes. It was one of the 20 or so powder days Ski Santa Fe gets each season. The tops of tall pine trees, buried in some 200 inches of snow, poked out of the thick layers of powder. It was a relatively unfamiliar sensation to this lifelong East Coaster who is far better versed in riding ice than powder.

Still, Abruzzo assured, even when it’s human-made, Ski Santa Fe’s snow is some of the best and most consistent there is.

“We make very dry snow,” he said before pointing out how the mountain’s 42 snow guns and five-million-gallon storage tank allow them to cover most of the mountain in snow throughout the season. “It’s dry to the point where we have had snow gun companies write us a custom setting. And what you get is a much nicer surface to ski on that stays nice longer.”

A little shy of halfway down one of our day’s runs, Abruzzo cut from one groomer to another and, suddenly, a rustic, two-story shack stood surrounded by a small sea of skiers and snowboarders, each of whom seemed to have a beer, a cocktail, or a hot chocolate in hand.

At 10,500 feet, on-mountain restaurant Totemoff’s sits higher than the peaks of many ski areas in North America.

And while there was no entertainment beyond some music playing over the speakers, Abruzzo assured me that Totemoff’s often plays host to live music. Above the bar, apartments for Abruzzo’s family and staff really hammer home the idea of how deeply entwined the Abruzzo family is 0n this mountain.

As we sat chatting over a pair of light beers, the talk eventually came back to the Abruzzo family, their lifelong marriage to this mountain. I ask him what it’s been like having three generations of Abruzzos run a mountain together. He quickly corrects me.

“Both of my kids work here,” he said with a laugh. “So, it’s actually four generations.”

#8302. Last-Minute Costumes for Trail Runners

It’s Halloween week and you still have no idea what you’re going to be. Trail or ultrarunning is your entire personality, but you can only toss on some last-minute split shorts and a fake beard to go as Forrest Gump so many years in a row. Everyone is “pretty tired” of you responding to what you are with an exhausted, “I just felt like running” in a goofy accent. It’s OK; we’ve all been there. And Trail Runner’s resident doodler and creative character costume expert, Bobby Peavey, has your back. He’s put together a curated list of archetypes from your local run club and Instagram feed that are sure to be a hit this spooky season.

This costume is perfect for your most bonk-vulnerable friends.  Dress them up as Bonkenstein and enjoy a night of constantly bringing them back from the dead with salty and sweet snacks.

Do you have the patience of a saint and the multitasking skills of Leslie Knope? Then the Race Director costume is the perfect choice for you. Your night is going to consist of making sure there are ample snacks for all, that trick or treating/holiday party schedules stay on track, that everybody stays safe and healthy, and about a dozen other things that everyone else surely overlooks.

When you select this costume for the spookiest night of the year, the assignment is clear: only speak in the past tense for the entire night. You’re full of nostalgia and cynical disdain for anything modern. You’re basically the Uncle Rico of the evening.

Time to update your watch to the current model, recharge your heart rate strap, and cover every inch of exposed skin with wearable storage.  Because the funnest part of your Halloween is going to be teaching all your friends about the newest and techiest gear on the market.

For this costume, it is crucial that you log more photos than miles.  You are in this costume purely for the likes and kudos. If you exit Zone 1 at any point, you’re doing it wrong.

No pacer or muling needed with this costume. Thanks to your vampire diet and a steady dose of nipple chafing, you’ve got all the nutrition you need to conquer any ultra distance!

#8301. 17 Campfire Recipes to Make Your Next Outdoor Gathering a Hit

At the end of a long day, there’s nothing like sitting by the campfire, watching the flames dance and hearing the wood crackle (as long as the fire’s made safely and legally, of course). The only way to make it better is savoring a Michelin-star-worthy meal while sitting fireside. When preparing your menu, it’s easy to opt for a go-to hot dogs and s’mores combo, but there are so many more delicious meals out there. With these revolutionary campfire recipes, you won’t want to settle for anything less than all-plates-scraped-clean delicious. All you need is a burning campfire and a rumbling stomach.

This hearty combo tastes even better in the woods than it does at the diner. Whip it up over a campfire, and you’ll not only impress your buddies—you’ll have a no-pot meal with zero cleanup (eat right out of the bag!).

Got a relaxed morning? Make this tasty combination of sweet pears and crunchy granola.

Drizzle these fluffy pancakes with maple syrup for breakfast or top with chives and sour cream for a savory dinner.

“Just like Mom used to make,” says our editor of this simple, not-too-sweet pastry that’s perfect for breakfast or a healthy dessert.

A few simple spices elevate your already-delicious, fresh-caught trout to sublime, says Charlie Borrowman, Washington-based cooking instructor.

Pizza at camp? We’re in. This prep-ahead pie is an easy crowd-pleaser.

With fresh, handmade pasta in your repertoire, you can go as far out as you want without ever leaving behind the taste of a home-cooked meal.

Spice up this classic Turkish dish with shelf-stable Spanish chorizo, roasted right on your campsite coals. Best part? Eat straight out of a zucchini, so there are no dishes to clean.

Prep these at home for a delicious first-night treat with south-of-the-border flavors.

Take your fireside fish skills to the next level with this savory salmon recipe.

Apple pie is a classic flavor for a reason. The mixture of ripe apple and warm spices (cinnamon, cardamom, and ginger) work as well on warm summer nights as on chilly fall ones.

Hear us out on this one. All Backpacker editors have an opinion on what cheese works best in a s’more (mine is a Dubliner cheese). Try it out and find out for yourself.

This camping-friendly take on a classic Italian confection is so good, you’ll probably dream about it.

Craving ice cream? This take on a frozen classic is the next best thing.

This decadent treat is a welcome change from typical backcountry desserts, and requires almost no clean-up.

Throwing a campsite party? This treat satisfies any sweet tooth. Tip: In place of the English toffee bits, you can use four chopped 1.4-ounce chocolate-covered toffee bars (or plain toffee). Don’t overfill your cones or they won’t melt properly.

To turn this Thanksgiving staple into a portable treat, use a combo of graham crackers, instant sweet potatoes, marshmallows, and fall spices. The result delivers all the flavor you love in a outdoor-friendly package.

#8300. How I Got Benighted (Twice) on Yosemite’s ‘Lost Arrow Chimney’

In the first installment in our Benighted series, Shino Jomoto shares with Climbing the weird and spooky tale from her night in the chimney on September 17, 2023—and what all climbers can learn from her epic.

With over two decades of climbing experience, Jomoto specializes in epics, which she defines as getting sandbagged on adventure multi-pitch climbs and big walls that take far longer than anticipated. But her biggest epic of all occurred in the storied chimney route (5.10a) up Lost Arrow Spire in Yosemite.

Earlier this week, a Yosemite Climbing Association (YCA) newsletter detailed the history of the Lost Arrow Spire, including the chimney route. First ascensionist John Salathé himself bailed near the top in 1946. The next year, he came back “for an all-out effort” that took over five days. “Pushing through the claustrophobic shadows of the Lost Arrow Chimney, Salathé and [Anton] Nelson endured searing heat, dehydration, and brutal physical exertion,” the YCA shared. “They spent four bivouacs dangling from crude hammocks tied to pitons driven into the wall.”

The Lost Arrow Chimney is also believed to contain a human skeleton. On March 19, 1961, 17-year-old Irving Smith died in a rappelling accident from the top. An American Alpine Club trip report shared that Smiths’ body remains in the chimney: “While a ranger and volunteer rescue party was preparing to attempt the difficult and dangerous removal, Smith’s parents and Park authorities determined that no further life should be risked, and that the body should remain at rest where it lay.”

A comment on the Mountain Project page of Yosemite’s Lost Arrow Chimney (5.10a) foreshadowed what was to come: “Don’t let the moderate grade fool you. After pitch 7, you are halfway done.” The Lost Arrow Chimney is 10 pitches.

Poor fitness, dehydration, and sleep deprivation conspired, and by pitch eight we needed headlamps. Too tired to continue, we did the only sensible thing: slept inside the chimney.

I started climbing in 2005, mostly out of a hatred for my corporate job. That led to years living out of a station wagon, trying to figure out how to rock climb. Fast forward decades later, I’m in the business of going on epics—a lot.

Jim Herson said you could write an entire print edition on just my epics alone. I’ve had near-death epics like lightning and hypothermia on a big wall. But I’ll put it this way: I can climb El Cap faster than I can climb the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The reason why I wanted to share this is that nine out of ten climbers will have an epic on the Lost Arrow. You might be able to climb 5.13, but try to climb 10 pitches of old-school chimney—see if you can still call yourself a 5.10 climber. I think everyone goes in with the confidence of the grade. Then they just get gut-punched by the old-schoolness of the climb.

On my Lost Arrow Chimney epic, we weren’t in danger. We never called YOSAR (Yosemite Search and Rescue). You’re just humbled in a silly way because it’s such a silly grade.

Aside from the likes of Chuck Pratt or old-school climbers, I don’t know anyone who’s ever redone this route. When you do a climb, you usually redo it. You want a redpoint or you go back again. Nobody is dumb enough to redo this climb. We’ve done it three times, so it really goes to show either how incredibly stupid we are, or how memorable of an epic it was that we just needed to clear the record.

The lore that Jim Herson shared with me was he knew a guy who climbed the Lost Arrow Chimney and then never rock climbed again. The reality is he went to med school and gave up climbing. But that was his last-ever climb. It just embodies the spirit of the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The first time John and I did Lost Arrow Chimney in 26 hours on October 5, 2019 as a party of three, and we were actually in decent shape.

The time we slept in the chimney a few years later, we were a party of two. We thought we were fit. But we did all the classic gumby moves. We got up too late and got lost on the approach. To get back on route, we had to rappel. It’s obvious on a topo where you should go, but at four o’clock in the morning, you get lost. And we didn’t bring enough water.

On the climb, we started losing daylight. My boyfriend started dry heaving from dehydration and lack of fitness. He stopped mid-pitch in a chimney—he couldn’t go on.

There’s nothing you can really say in the dark. We’re not Rocky Talkie people. We have too much pride for that. So we just had to communicate with a rope. Finally, I was on belay. I went up to him. We were mid-chimney—this wasn’t even a belay station.

John was like, “I can’t. I can’t do this anymore.” And he’s a 10-times better climber than I am. So I was like, “All right, I’ll go.” He was like, “Are you sure?” I was like, “We can’t sleep here. We can sleep in a lot of places. This is not a place to sleep.”

It’s always scary when a very experienced person says, “I’m scared.” John rarely says he’s scared. It takes courage to say that. When you’re in the dark, there’s nothing you do. You can’t start yelling and placating, you know? You just realize in that moment like, it’s a serious climb. And you’re still having to reconcile that with 10a.

So I went questing and found this chimney that was adjacent to the climb. It wasn’t a chimney you go through on route, but everyone goes by it.

We were two pitches from the notch. Should we suffer for six hours, then rappel and call it a day? Or suffer through the whole night? You make those calculations. We decided we might as well stay put, rather than burden resources to call for YOSAR or any sort of search and rescue. I think that’s the number one thing: Can you self-rescue?

We had brought a salad that we thought we were going to eat at the base. So we ended up at the bivy with a salad, but no water. It’s kind of hard to eat a salad without water. So all of my swear words were salad- or foliage-related. It doesn’t matter if you have a whole buffet, if you have no water, you don’t want to eat anything. So we were just staring at this salad in the chimney. It’s one of those things with the Maslow’s hierarchy—if you don’t have water, you can’t do anything.

We laid out both climbing ropes so that we were a little bit insulated from the ground. We did the bivy dance. It was flatter than most bivy spots I have slept on. We were really depressed, just waiting for daylight.

Back sleeping was impossible, so we were relegated to side sleeping for the next six hours. There was no way to sleep besides big spoon, little spoon. The walls were very cold. I put a giant sad face in chalk where I was. Another group went and did it later and said, “We knew where you bivvied ’cause there was a giant sad face.”

But we were so thirsty, the epic wasn’t over. We could hear Yosemite Falls. Our brains went: Maybe we can just hike over there. Another lesson is you’re not rational when you’re having an epic. So we lost another half day going to the falls. We were sitting in a pool of water that we couldn’t drink. And we realized we couldn’t cut over. So we had to go back. A day and a half later, we got back to the car.

Finally, on June 2, 2024, we got our redemption. We did it in a day and tagged the summit where people do the Tyrolean. It still took us all day—and we didn’t even free it. We had to pull on gear. It makes you respect the history of the first ascensionists—the lineage of people who have tried it and who have bailed. There’s an insane amount of really, really old bail slings.

You’re in there and it’s a vortex. It’s spooky. I’m not a mystical person, but there are hexes that have been kind of swallowed by the rock. It’s a freaking spooky museum of gear. When you’re in there, you have an appreciation for who climbed this before you and the style in which they climbed it, because it is terrifying.

I feel like I’ve gotten my chimney badge in Yosemite. There should be a club for it: the Lost Arrow Chimney Support Group. If you can summit the whole climb and rappel in a day, I would have mad respect. More people climb the Nose than the Lost Arrow Chimney. Anyone who’s dumb enough and adventurous enough to sign up for that level of masochism will resonate more with me than if you’re C1ing a 30-pitch climb.

If you survive nine or ten pitches of chimneys with your partner, you will be bonded forever, for better or worse. They’ve done all these studies about reality TV shows, like for love matchmaking. You put people in intense situations and they confuse their endorphins as romance, but it’s really just adrenaline. Part of it is trauma bonding. Some couples are more willing to climb the Lost Arrow Chimney than go to couples therapy.

The beauty of epics is there are way more fun memories than sending. Every sending story is so ephemeral. But when you’ve been sucker-punched so hard by something scary, or that requires lack of sleep, or incredible amounts of suffering, you remember those experiences for decades.

If you don’t have some delusional optimism, you will never get off the ground. That delusion will catch up to you at some point. But you have to have a little bit of fuel. As long as it’s not over your head or dangerous for you and others. Can you live well and safely enough to live another day? Go do it.

Delusion meets reality at some point, like when you’re having an epic. Benighted is a subcategory of epics—it’s in the taxonomy. There has to be some darkness involved, generally speaking, but you don’t need to have slept.

The easy way to know is when you end up at the parking lot, you see your best friends, and they’re like, “How was it?” The face doesn’t lie. You actually don’t need to say words. They see your face and they’re like, “That was an epic.”

John and I have an epic grading scale. It’s the reverse GPA.

Every time we finish, we rate them. The Lost Arrow Chimney was like a 5.0.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#8299. I Hike With a Flip Phone. Here’s the Tiny Camera I’m Bringing Along.

Over the past few years, I’ve learned I’m much happier when I don’t have my smartphone on me—I’m not sure the human mind evolved to have 24-hour access to all of the Internet’s information on demand. In an effort to disconnect and be more present, I took a page from the Gen Z playbook and started carrying a flip phone instead. It’s been great—except for the camera.

A while ago, I started testing a potential solution in the Life Camera S168, a thumb-size digital camera built to compete with the Kodak Charmera. How did it actually perform on the trail? Check out this video to see what kind of photos and footage this $30 gadget is capable of turning out and read our full review for more.

A while ago, I swapped out my smartphone for a flip phone. I was getting tired of how distracted I was—doomscrolling, checking my emails—and I wanted to simplify things. This has really done the trick. On the trail it’s pretty much everything I need. It can send messages, make calls, if I need to get a hold of 911 in an emergency, it can do that. It has an MP3 player, so I can listen to podcasts at night, and it even has a rudimentary mapping app, although I’m not sure I’d trust it, I always bring a paper map and compass as backup.

However, it does have one big shortcoming: the camera on this thing really sucks. The pictures are grainy, blurry, and usually blown out. It’s not how I want to remember my trips. I often find myself hiking with my smartphone just so I can get better pictures and video. I’ve been looking for a solution, since that kind of defeats the purpose of ditching the smartphone, and I think I’ve found one.

This is the Life Camera S168. It’s part of a crop of new thumb-sized digital cameras that are designed to appeal to the retro crowd, they’re kind of like old digital cameras or old film cameras, you know, the disposable you used to take to summer camp with you. The most familiar one is the Kodak Charmera, you may have seen that in stores.

However, according to a lot of online reviews, the Life Camera’s photos and video quality is significantly better, and it has, from what I’ve seen, a fairly decent camera, you’re not going to confuse it with an iPhone or anything, but it may be enough for my purposes.

So, is the Life Camera a gimmick or a game changer? Well, that depends on you. If you’re like most hikers and you have your phone in your pocket most of the time, it’s definitely a gimmick. Your phone can do anything the Life Camera can do, and probably in better resolution.

If, however, you’re part of the small subset of hikers like me, who find they’re happier when their phone is off and in their pack, or if they’re just carrying a flip phone, you might give the Life Camera a try. No, the resolution isn’t anything to write home about, but it can capture your life on the trail in adequate detail, and if you don’t mind that retro vibe, it’s kind of fun. I’ll be carrying one on my next hike.
