#8298. The Best Ski Boots for Wide Feet—From Resort to Backcountry

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

A lineup of alpine ski boots clicked into skis on snow. (Photo: Re Wikstrom)

Overview: Wide feet often need a high-volume ski boot, meaning a last of 102 millimeters or wider, though some wide-footed skiers do fine in medium-volume boots with lasts of 100- to 101 millimeters. We highlighted seven boots with lasts from 100 millimeters to 103.5 millimeters, including men’s and women’s options and one backcountry touring boot.

Wide feet are a problem for skiers. Take it from someone whose bootfitter once called hers “platypus feet.” My forefoot is wide, I have basically no arch, and my heel, ankle, and calf are skinny. That wide forefoot points me toward a wider last and “high volume” boots, but my flat foot swims in them, with way too much room between my instep and the boot ceiling and around my ankle and calf. So what do I do? I stuff my platypus feet into low-volume boots that keep them snug, then work with a bootfitter to stretch and grind out the toebox.

For skiers with more typical wide feet (a wide forefoot, a higher instep, and proportionally bigger ankles and calves), the fix is usually far simpler: try on a few boots with a last of 100 millimeters or more, either a generous mid-volume or a high-volume model, and see what fits.

Why do so many of these boots all have BOA dials, you ask? Because whether you like them or not, you can’t argue that BOA makes it easier to fine-tune the fit and wrap above the instep. Here are our testers’ favorite boots for skiers with wide feet, high insteps, and thicker calves, all available in multiple flexes for men and women. And remember: boot fit is highly specific to your foot shape. To find the best boot for you, visit your local ski shop and work with a professional bootfitter.

Sizes: 24.5-29.5 Last: 102 mm Flexes: 120, 100

Pros and Cons + Convenient entry and BOA lower closure + Performance on par with stiffer boots + 100-flex version offers big value – Fit out-of-box was more snug than expected

One tester called it the best 102-millimeter-lasted boot ever made, and the fit balance explains why: secure and pinch-free through the rearfoot, roomy up front without going bucket-wide. A new lower-shell BOA dial lets you fine-tune the wrap across your forefoot and instep, and entry is among the easiest around. The reworked R-Go Fit liner grips just enough to hold your heel, snug at first but relaxing after a couple of runs. The 120 flex skied like several 130s, so if you like a softer boot, look at the Rossignol Hi-Speed HV BOA 100.

Sizes: 23.5-30.5 Last: 102 mm Flexes: 85-130

Pros and Cons + Lots of room, everywhere + Very square toebox shape + Foot feels planted for good edge control – Potential for quickness requires high volume foot and leg

Plenty of wide boots drift toward medium width or ski like the box they came in. The Premio BOA doesn’t. It averaged a 5 (roomiest) across all eight fit zones testers scored, and its toebox is the most noticeably angled they’ve tested, letting toes spread out for comfort, warmth, and grip. Stance angles and shell construction keep the foot planted flat through every edge angle, even on lower-volume feet. The only knock was quickness, which a thicker, higher-volume foot should close by filling the boot out. Available in flex options ranging from 85 to 130.

Sizes: 22.5-30.5 Last: 100 mm Flexes: 130, 120; 115, 105 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extra room in toebox, forefoot, instep and calf + Performance snug in heel and ankles + Double BOA offers fine adjustment to an already good fit – Testers said DD might stand for difficult donning

A true medium, the 100-millimeter-last Speedmachine 3 still has room for higher-volume feet to pack in and feel secure, with the performance payoff of a snug fit. The shell follows the foot’s natural shape while the liner cushions the wider, bony spots. Once your foot settles in, it’s held firmly, with just enough breathing room left in the toebox, forefoot, instep, and calf. A strong rearfoot hold keeps narrower, pressure-sensitive feet happy too. Entry takes more effort in the tested 115-flex DD (dual dial) than in the 105-flex model with buckles up top and BOA below.

Sizes: 23.5-30.5 Last: 101 mm Flexes: 120, 110; 105 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Flawless medium fit for average feet and legs + Particularly good shin and toebox fit + Skied as strongly and accurately as 130-flex models – A bit difficult to get on

The Veloce Space Dual’s 101-millimeter last runs a smidge wider than true medium boots but fits just as snug for average and wider feet alike. Its cabrio design keeps things friendly for higher insteps, and testers praised the snug shin fit and just-right toebox. Dual BOA entry can be a cable-tangled hassle, but testers called it worth the cover charge. On snow, it handled icy groomers to crud with ease, even outperforming stiffer boots. Available in two flex models for men, one for women.

Sizes: 24-31.5 Last: 101 mm Flexes: 130, 120, 110; 105, 95 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Easy on, easy off + Extra room over top of foot and through instep + Skis predictably with good stability – Might be too high-volume for skiers with low insteps

A 101-millimeter last makes the Nexus 130 BOA a higher-volume boot that balances comfort with performance, and the shape works for wider feet and higher insteps alike. The ankle break sits high and slightly forward, which accommodates higher insteps, and heel hold is excellent on genuinely high-volume feet. Even a low-volume skier barely noticed slop once the heel was driven into the pocket. Mid-entry means you lift the spine lever and step in hands-free, yet it skied like a true 130 flex, with a lively, springy rebound.

Sizes: 22.5-31.5 Last: 102 mm Flexes: 130, 120, 100 (men’s); 105, 95 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Accommodating fit + Comfortable + Skis more powerfully than expected – Might not be high-volume enough for some

Salomon’s wide-fit answer isn’t a soft, cavernous compromise: it skis like a performance boot. A 102-millimeter last gives wide-footed skiers plenty of space through the forefoot and instep, with ample cuff room for thicker calves. Once the BOA is dialed in, tension feels smooth and even from shin to toe, and even mid-volume testers felt locked in rather than sloppy. It’s plush inside yet quick, lively, and efficient edge to edge, scoring on par with narrower, more technical boots. Truly wide feet may need a bootfitter to tune the heat-moldable Custom Shell.

Sizes: 22.5-31.5 Last: 103.5 mm Flexes: 120 (men’s); 120 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Flex is progressive, you never feel the “brick wall” + 60° range of motion has almost no friction + New Vibram sole extremely grippy on rocky terrain – Wide last will be too cavernous for some

A touring boot for wide-footed skiers who want one boot for big missions, the mid-weight Radical Pro walks well and skis hard. The forefoot and heel pocket run wide, and our tester kept the scaffo clamped a bit to snug them up, so narrow feet should beware. The instep sits low enough to hold the heel even on a skinny-footed skier, leaving toes cozy and the descent locked in. On multi-day tours and a three-day Eastern Sierra traverse, the progressive flex muted vibrations in wet, manky snow, and the walk mode pivoted freely.

Fit makes or breaks a ski boot, and wide feet make it harder to get right. Expert skiers vetted and tested every boot here, but the best one for you depends on your own feet. A professional bootfitter is still the fastest way to narrow the field. Until you get there, here’s what to know.

Boot width is listed as the last: the internal width at the forefoot, in millimeters, measured on a size 26/26.5 shell. The number also hints at overall volume—the height over your instep and the room around your lower leg in the cuff. Narrower boots generally have a lower instep and a snugger cuff, while wider boots have a higher instep and a roomier cuff. Boots sort into three groups:

Not always. Some skiers with wider feet are comfortable in a medium-volume boot. Everyone’s tolerance for a snug fit differs, so try several widths at a ski shop and go with what your feet tell you.

Feet and legs come in too many shapes for one tester to speak for everyone. A boot that feels custom-made on one skier can feel punishing on another. That’s why we partner with professional bootfitter Mark Elling, who leads the Masterfit/America’s Best Bootfitters annual ski boot test. Every brand, large or small, is invited to submit models. Over two weeks, 10 expert testers—evenly split between men and women—skied 50 boots, averaging three runs per boot across a range of conditions.

Mark Elling has worked full-time in the ski industry for more than 35 years as a writer, a level 3 PSIA-certified instructor, a snowcat skiing guide and a professional bootfitter. He runs a year-round specialty bootfitting lab in Bend, Oregon (BootRX.com), and is a former board-certified pedorthist. Elling coordinates Masterfit’s annual boot test, and he’s the author of The All-Mountain Skier: The Way to Expert Skiing.

#8297. To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

Author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22. A rough start forced the team to abandon the fundamentals of competition and ask for help, be honest about their problems, and sacrifice for others. It paid off: the U.S. came from behind to defeat Australia and Belgium, who took second and third, respectively.

Early into the second night of the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S. teammate Levi Yoder and admitted that he was so tired he might fall asleep and into the nearby ditch. Yoder replied that he was so tired he was hallucinating and might wind up in that same ditch.

Before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S. squad thought of as their de facto captain, told his teammates to lean on one another. But Dowdle hesitated the first day, and so, he thought, did many others. It made sense: Backyard ultras are usually individual events predicated on you staying strong while others give up.

For the uninitiated, backyard ultra rules are pretty simple: Run a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour, until only one remains. (That runner must complete one final loop, also called a yard, to be declared the winner.) At the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, which alternates every other year with the individual championship, each participating country simultaneously hosts its own backyard ultra with 15 runners. The team with the most cumulative laps wins.

Typically at backyard ultras, competitors are wolves looking for the elk with a limp. No one wants to look weak. No one demonstrated this formidable exterior better than Dowdle in the Last Soul Ultra this April, when his gamesmanship created the event’s most talked-about moment. But his competitive side was ubiquitous among the 15 elite backyard runners on Team USA. They each won backyard ultras to qualify; they were wolves, not elk.

Yet Team USA struggled from the start. With daytime temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, it felt warmer than they thought it would. The course was hilly, with over 400 feet of climbing per loop, costing them a minute or two per loop in a format where extra seconds are precious. Indeed, over the first 40 laps when all runners from all 67 countries were still in the race, the U.S. had the slowest average lap speed of 52:21—nearly seven minutes slower than the fastest country, Slovakia.

Struggling through that second night, the U.S. decided to try a different tactic. They decided to be vulnerable.

Lewis urged the team to be honest about how they were feeling because there was a good chance others could help. It took Dowdle a bit to believe, even after watching how others supported each other.

“It did take encouragement from my team to even be more of a teammate,” Dowdle told Trail Runner.

But Dowdle was enthused when, after his admission that he was struggling, Yoder suggested that they look out for each other over the next 3 miles they had to complete to keep going. Dowdle got the message: This would be a different backyard than he’d ever run before. They talked to each other through the loop and by the end they had caught up to their teammates.

“That turned the corner for me,” Dowdle said. “In a normal race, I would never say that I was falling asleep to another runner. You just would never give up that information. But that opened the door for me to be more vocal about how I was doing.”

Several other members of the U.S. squad admitted that being honest with each other and asking for help when they needed it was key to them winning the world title. Instead of acting like individuals in a last-man-standing race, they were a unit. That helped many of them run farther than they ever had before—eight Americans ran over 80 yards, or 333.3 miles—when it looked like Australia might literally run away with victory.

“When some were feeling strong, we would help those who were not feeling OK,” said Megan Smyth, who set a PR with 82 yards and was the last woman standing. “I’m pretty sure that’s how so many of us got over 80 yards.”

The backyard, despite its do-or-die nature, lends itself to camaraderie because of the way runners all start the next 4.167-mile loop together on the hour, every hour. Jon Noll qualified for Team USA by running over 440 miles at the individual world championship last year. Even there most competitors congratulated each other after each lap. “The ultra community, in general, is not exactly a cutthroat environment for the most part,” Noll said. He especially felt that sense of camaraderie this time as the miles piled up.

This is why Smyth loves the backyard format.

“There’s no incentive to win a lap, so you really do wind up cheering for each other,” Smyth said.

Still, Team USA had to get comfortable with each other in a hurry. Even with seven returning members from the third-place 2024 team it was a little awkward at first: Some had previously competed against each other, and some called each other friends. Some were rivals. Other first-timers felt a sense of awe: Smyth had imposter syndrome, which doesn’t make it easy to talk about, say, a sore ankle.

But she also welcomed the unique race set up. If a typical backyard ultra can feel crowded and chaotic, the team race with its 15 competitors feels sparse, even intimate. Smyth got her wish right away.

“I haven’t gotten to do true team running since my cross-country days,” she said. “It was just a magical experience.”

A couple team meetings over Zoom, as well as an in-person meeting before the race, helped shoo away some of the awkwardness, Lewis thought. But Smyth said Lewis helped bring the team together during the event, too, with little (even corny) things like running in a fighter jet formation and chanting “U.S.A!” for a lap.

Smyth remembers walking at night and nearly falling asleep before the Ron Express came up behind her. Ron Wireman, competing in his second team championship, struggled early in the race and needed help from others. That first night, he was eager to pay his teammates back and named himself after a train to help them through the dark.

“He said, ‘MEGAN ARE YOU AWAKE?,’” Smyth said.

Smyth, just like Dowdle, learned how to ask for help. Later in the race, as the prospect of doing another lap on the steep trail, she requested a “hill sherpa.”

The team cohesion would be tested right away as Lewis insisted they answer a question democratically: Should they run the road or the trail?

Team USA competes on the original Big’s Backyard Ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s literal backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee. On odd years during the individual championship, racers run a trail loop during the day and a road loop at night. This time it was runners’ choice throughout the race.

The road was flatter and easier, but the hard, smooth surface can be problematic for trail runners. Smyth, for instance, said she didn’t bring many pairs of road shoes. But Laz recently made “improvements” to the trail loop that made it steeper, tougher, and slower. The precious minutes saved on the road loop could be the difference between having time to recover, fuel, sleep, and even go to the bathroom, and to DNF.

“There isn’t a lot of wiggle room in a backyard,” Lewis said.

Communication was key as the team tried to accommodate runners struggling with the trail by adding more laps on the road.

“We were changing things as the race went on,” Noll said. “Sometimes you didn’t know what course you were doing [on the next lap]. Mentally that can be hard.”

Ultimately, the back and forth paid off. Eventually emphasizing the road over the trail helped the team squeeze yards from people who may not have been able to continue otherwise.

“If we hadn’t moved to the road, I don’t know if we would have won the race,” Lewis said.

As the third day burned off its final few hours, Australia had a commanding lead of 58 yards over the U.S. The Aussies still had 11 runners in the race; the U.S. was down to 9. Nicholas Steel kept announcing to his U.S. teammates just how far behind they were. More than one American admitted later that they found these updates annoying. Dowdle told himself he didn’t care and tried to enjoy the experience.

But backyard veterans will tell you that the race doesn’t end at hour 70; that’s really when it starts. One Aussie dropped at yard 70, another at 72, two at 73, and two more at 75. By yard 80, nine Aussies had dropped. They had only two runners left—a precarious place to be, given the final runner can only complete one additional lap after the penultimate runner drops. Sure enough, Australia was out by yard 88. We’re not being judgy about this: They were on their third day of running without sleep. But that brutal attrition gave the U.S. a shot.

Suddenly Steel’s updates were inspiring. They would need Dowdle and Noll, the workhorses, to keep doing their magic. But the Americans realized that they could win if they got at least half their runners to yard 75 and several past yard 80.

“The possibility that we could catch up lit a fire under my belly,” Dowdle said, “and I remember thinking, ‘Oh, maybe I do care.’”

Even the Americans who dropped relatively early decided to stay at the campsite to cheer. This was big: Dowdle finished one lap with 15 seconds to go, riding the wave of exhortation to get him across the line in time.

Lewis did what he could to keep as many runners out there as possible. He ran with those who were close to dropping, even to his detriment. At times he finished the lap with less than three minutes to go. Lewis, famously, sleeps for a few minutes after every loop, but running with others meant he wasn’t able to do that. Ultimately, he went out for yard 84 but didn’t finish it, a result that Lewis found disappointing.

“I didn’t have my own rhythm because I was helping others,” Lewis said. “My ultimate goal was to be there for the team, so I sacrificed myself and my own best race for that.”

That kind of support from teammates, along with the competitive boost the Americans got chasing down Australia, helped push some to their backyard ultra PRs. Nick Petterson made it to 84 yards, 19 more than his previous best. That’s nearly a full day more of running.

“The team needed you, and that was a really easy thing to grab onto,” Petterson said. “We needed everyone to crank up the numbers. That motivation outside of just myself was really helpful.”

Petterson thrives off that external focus anyway. During backyards, he enjoys asking others how they’re doing, even though it’s not always reciprocated.

“The team factor was a major driver when times got hard for me,” he said. “I might have gone out earlier if it wasn’t for that.”

Yoder made it 86 yards, 11 more than his qualifying mark. Ryan Snickles went 69 yards after qualifying with 55. Smyth set a PR by five yards and quit only after her ankle swelled like a balloon. Jeff Walker got 75 yards, 30 more than his qualifier. Even Steel seemed inspired by his own updates. He went 94 yards—177% of his 53-yard qualifier.

Ultimately the U.S. won by a landslide with 1,120 yards to Australia’s 1,069.

It’s the second world title for Team USA in this rapidly developing sub-sport. When the U.S. won in 2022, it was with only 860 yards. Belgium, which has won the other two team titles, took third this year—although two of their runners set the individual backyard ultra world record of 124 yards, or 516.7 miles over five days of running.

“When other runners are hanging on longer,” Lewis said, “it impacts everyone to hang on longer.”

Ultimately, Dowdle was the last American standing with 107 yards—a personal best by 13 yards, or 54 miles. Noll got the assist with 106 yards. Despite his initial reticence, Dowdle says he values moments with his teammates more than his individual national title.

“There was one lap where I broke down crying,” Dowdle said, “and Nick Petterson saw me and put his arm around me and was just with me during that time.”

Dowdle wouldn’t want the backyard format to be flooded with team events, but he wants to go back:

“I’m bummed that you have to wait two years for it again.”

#8296. After Testing 122 Pieces of Gear, We Found the Best Climbing Gear of Fall 2026

Gear testing above 12,000 feet on the golden granite of Chamonix's Aiguille du Midi. It's a hard job, but someone's got to do it. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

Rock climbing season doesn’t end when snow hits the high country. Some of the best conditions of the year are right around the corner: cool temps, ample shade, and just the right amount of humidity in the air. Unless you’re sharpening your ice tools, don’t give up on the rock (or plastic) season just yet—with the right gear, you’re in for the best season of your life.

Climbing’s gear-testing team has spent all summer sweating it out with the latest and greatest so you don’t have to. We tested 28 harnesses, 27 pairs of climbing shoes, 30 pairs of approach shoes, 9 ropes, and 28 backpacks—a healthy mix of new items and longtime favorites. Some of the gear was good, some was great, and a lot of it missed the mark: bruised hips, sore feet, exploding packs—it’s all part of the gear-testing game.

2026 was the year of the hyper-specific shoe. Although notable all-arounders made it onto our list, the real highlights were the shoes who didn’t try to do too much. One shoe felt about as stiff as a crampon, with its new-age carbon insert, and powered us up numerous vert testpieces; another had about as much support as a woolen sock (but, like, in a good way!); and the best shoe I’ve ever used for offwidths is absolutely terrible for finger cracks. Perhaps 2026 is the year of the shoe quiver.

The harness is the one piece of gear that will make or break your day on the wall. In an effort to find the best climbing harness available, we put everything from fast-and-light alpine G-strings to beefy big-wallers to the test this year, taking them on trips from the cold Canadian alpine to the steep walls of Devil’s Tower to overhung sport routes at The Red.

Unlike this year’s crop of rock shoes, my favorite climbing packs worked hard to serve multiple niches. One versatile alpine-climbing pack carried anywhere from one to four days of mountain kit with ease. And a new haul bag might just be the last pack (and airplane carry on) a rock climber will ever need.

The best climbing ropes are a tough category of gear to review because, these days, almost all are well made and perform great right out of the package. It’s only after hard wear—climbing pitch after pitch in rain, snow, and ice, coiling and uncoiling on dirt and sand, and taking some big whippers—that a rope reveals its true colors.

Helmets are our best defense against rockfall and weird whippers while climbing outdoors. And after years of writing accident reports—often of climbers who took a seemingly benign fall, before something weird happened—I regularly note how fortunate the climber was to be wearing one. When shopping for a helmet, take the time to find one that’s comfortable, lightweight, breathable, and fits properly—because actually liking your helmet makes you far more likely to wear it.

#8295. Nearly Half of US Hikers Use Cannabis, And Other Strange Findings From the ‘Hiking While High’ Survey

Most hikers have experienced a natural high at some point in their outdoor adventures. Whether it’s the buzz of an athletic flow state or being straight-up stupefied by an amazing view, we’ve all been there. Endorphins fire, oxytocin floods the brain, and you’re overwhelmed with energy, good vibes, and a general sense of peace.

It’s also not news to anyone that some hikers use drugs in nature. People smoke weed on the trail, eat edibles, drink beer, and even take psychedelics. Every year it seems like we publish at least one story with a headline like, “Hikers Rescued After Mushroom Trip Goes Bad” or “Two Hikers Reported Their Friend Dead. It Turned Out They Were Just on Mushrooms.”

But how many hikers are actually hitting the trail under the influence? Those questions and several others led the team at Climbing Kilimanjaro, a Tanzanian guide company, to conduct its “Hiking While High” survey. It polled U.S. adults who hike to find out once and for all how many of them use cannabis, mushrooms, alcohol, and other substances, and importantly, in what circumstances.

The results surprised the folks at Climbing Kilimanjaro. Not just because of how many hikers admitted to using substances on the trail, but because those who do are “surprisingly disciplined about where and when,” Brian Raffio, Kilimanjaro consultant for Climbing Kilimanjaro, says.

“On one hand, we expected to get some respondents who were very into using substances while hiking, and others who were as sober as sober gets,” Raffio says. “What we ended up with was much more of a grey area.”

For the survey, Climbing Kilimanjaro polled 1,008 U.S. adults between September 1 and 3, 2026. The sample was 52 percent women and 46 percent men, all of whom counted hiking as a core interest or hobby. They also grouped respondents by experience level. Hikers self-reported as casual hikers (people who hike a few times a year), regular hikers (people who hike roughly monthly), or avid hikers (people who hike weekly or more).

Of the 1,008 U.S. hikers surveyed, 44 percent said they have hiked under the influence.

Cannabis is far and away the most popular trail substance. A notable 35 percent of respondents admitted to having used it while hiking. Of hikers who take anything, 80 percent said they are reaching for weed. Behind cannabis, alcohol was the second most popular, with 23 percent percent admitting to having drunk beer or liquor while hiking. In third were magic mushrooms, with 15 percent admitting use (and another 24 percent saying they are curious to try psychedelics in nature but never have).

However, a majority—56 percent of hikers—said they have never used any substances on the trail. And while 7 percent of hikers who enhance their hikes say they have felt judged for doing so, surprisingly more of the sober hikers (9 percent) said they have also felt judged, but for their choice to abstain.

“Hikers feeling judged for staying clear-headed rather than for using something was a bit of a head-scratcher for sure,” Raffio says. “Apparently ‘no thanks, I’m good’ raises a few eyebrows.”

What surprised the Climbing Kilimanjaro team even more wasn’t these reported use rates. Instead, it was the level of caution users claim to have when they’re hiking high. More than half (51 percent) said they seek out shorter, easier hikes, and would never try to hike under the influence at high altitude. And nine out of 10 who hiked under the influence said: “There’s at least one place they would never use a substance.”

“In the end, hikers seem to be a fairly self-policing bunch,” Raffio says. “The summit push is where folks want to stay sharp and have their senses fully alert. Whatever [substance] a hiker packs, the trail rewards you when you know the terrain, and you understand your limits.”

The final result that stuck out to Raffio was how many people use hiking to recover. Roughly half of the hikers surveyed said they hit the trail sometimes “to reset after drinking or a night out.”

According to the Outdoor Industry Association (OIA), there are roughly 63 million hikers in the U.S. That makes this sample size anything but definitive. The most obvious takeaway is that people like to enhance their hikes with substances—whether it’s cannabis, magic mushrooms, or something else.

Climbing Kilimanjaro’s results also suggest that hikers are fairly split when it comes to substance use on the trail. While the majority of the respondents had never used anything while hiking, a 56/44 split isn’t that wide of a margin.

For those who do partake, it’s clear (and unsurprising) that cannabis is hikers’ substance of choice—by a long shot.

The Hiking While High survey didn’t poll hikers on their feelings around the topic, and that was intentional. The guide company didn’t want to present opinionated data. It just wanted to open up an honest conversation around the rates of drug use on the trail.

“We asked ourselves: What if this was discussed more openly?” Raffio said. “We wanted to come from a place of curiosity, not judgement.”

#8294. Backyard Ultras Are Booming. Here’s Why.

In quite the feat of boots-on-the-ground journalism, author Dan England raced Jess’ Backyard Ultra on August 9, 2024. (Don’t ask him about the race name grammar.) He also spoke with backyard ultra mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell, several other backyard ultra race directors, and key backyard ultra runners, including Harvey Lewis and Maggie Guterl. What he found is that the format of running a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until only one runner remains is about so much more than running in circles. Since this article was originally published on Outside Run in 2024, backyard ultras have further entered the mainstream with the rise of figures like Mark Dowdle, Belgium resetting the world record, and Team USA winning the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship.

It’s 8:55 P.M. on Friday, August 9, and I’m with a small group of runners huddled together in a tent on a farm near Greeley, Colorado, that momentarily shelters us from our bad life decisions.

Outside the tent awaits pouring rain and a mushy race course complete with the “Plank of Doom”—a pink makeshift “bridge” adorned in purple twinkle lights suspended four feet over a drainage ditch full of stormwater.

Before the starting gun of this backyard ultra goes off in five minutes, Jessy Nelson needs to make an announcement. I’m assuming it will be about safety. Instead, she tells us that she is not a narcissist.

Yes, Jess’ Backyard Ultra does carry her name. But she named the race for about a dozen friends, all named Jess. (Seriously!). She met them all in an online chat group during a 1,000-kilometer Great Virtual Race Across The States.

Nelson started the race on her farm for them in 2021 with the hope that one Jess could run far enough to qualify for Big’s Backyard Ultra—the original Bell Buckle, Tennessee, “backyard ultra” event that pioneered a quirky new kind of endurance racing format in which runners must complete a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until they can no longer accomplish the task.

For the record, this event is Jess’ Big Backyard Ultra, not Jessy’s. Understand?

We nod as the rain comes down harder. It would be a fun, goofy, quaint little race that seems to match the aesthetic of many backyard ultras across the world, except it’s been raining for three days, transforming the dirt roads on which we will run into what seems like gooey Jello pudding.

Nelson is worried. The Plank of Doom is seriously dangerous, she tells us. Sure, it’s pink and twinkly, but the four-foot fall that could result with any misstep could mean a broken ankle or, according to Nelson’s narrowed eyes, instant death. Nelson is so serious about the plank that she forces the four of us competing to vote to keep it on the course instead of bypassing it through a paved road 100 yards to the south. We vote to keep it, 3-1.

It’s hard to take anything Nelson says seriously, given that this is a race seemingly held on the set of Little House on the Prairie and that a stuffed toy squirrel named Skittles awaits us in a rocking chair at the turnaround to our 4-ish-mile loop. One of the Jesses befriended a squirrel in her backyard, you see, and that’s a tribute to her. Nelson once befriended an eagle, who would follow her during her daily 10-mile loops around her property. But now, she presumes, the eagle is taking cover. We are about to do the opposite.

Nelson’s odd race is now one of an estimated 500 backyard ultras held around the world that are certified by concept creator Gary Cantrell. You may know him as Lazarus Lake, or simply Laz. He is  probably the sport’s most famous race director and certainly  the quirkiest. Cantrell is known first and foremost for creating the Barkley Marathons, a grueling 100-plus-mile largely off-trail race in Tennessee that’s considered to be the world’s hardest running race to complete. While there’s only one Barkley Marathons, Cantrell’s backyard race format has boomed over the past five years or so.

There is no predefined end length or time in a backyard ultra, as long as multiple runners can complete each 4.167-mile loop within an hour. (Cantrell chose that peculiar distance because running 4.167 miles per hour is exactly what it takes to run 100 miles in 24 hours.) A race ends when only one runner remains to complete a lap and is declared the winner, while all other runners are relegated to did not finish (DNF) status with whatever total number of laps they are able to complete. The runner who completes the second-most laps in a race is often referred to as the “assist,” in the sense that their effort is ultimately what determines how long the race is allowed to continue.

Most backyard races are not like Cantrell’s Big’s Backyard Ultra, which, even though it maintains a grassroots feel, has gained worldwide fame and is filled with elite runners. Most backyard races are more like Nelson’s: small, fun and grueling little get-togethers that last a couple days and bring most runners to tears. Most backyard race directors are like Nelson, too; they have“real” jobs outside of race directing and simply love the format and camaraderie their events foster amid runners of all ability levels pushing  themselves beyond what they ever thought possible.

When Cantrell started his race and named it after his pit bull, Big, in 2012, he hoped to have enough interest for just one event. He was pleasantly surprised when people asked if there would be another race the following  year. Now tens of thousands will likely tune in to the livestream to watch this year’s race on October 19. Cantrell guesstimates more than 25,000 people have run in a backyard ultra event this year, and those are just in the races he’s certified: He knows there are probably dozens more who don’t bother with the paperwork.

“The continued growth really has been a surprise for me,” Cantrell said. Indeed, there are backyard races in 83 countries now.  Even the renowned Tarahumara tribe of Indigenous people from Chihuahua, Mexico, (aka the Raramuri people, who were profiled in the 2009 New York Times bestseller Born to Run,) have their own race, Cantrell noted.

Cantrell relishes putting on the world’s hardest events, almost to a sadistic degree. Only 20 individuals have finished the Barkley Marathons since he began it in 1986. It’s a race as ominous as its location, Frozen Head State Park in Tennessee. The race, over 100 miles with a staggering 65,000-feet-plus of elevation gain, is a miserable quest for survival through thorn-infested bramble, often terrible weather, and ridiculously steep hills on a “course” with no real route.

He started Big’s as another way to test people, and at times, it resembles Stephen King’s The Long Walk, a fictional horror story about 100 walkers who are forced to trudge hundreds of miles and are shot when they quit. Big’s format is also horrifyingly simple: Run 4.167 miles, a “yard,” in under an hour, and then line up and do it again, and again, and again, on the hour, until one person is left. No breaks from the on-the-hour start are allowed, not even to use the porta-potty, but if you finish the yard early, you can eat and drink to your heart’s content, sleep a few minutes, and yes, answer nature’s call. Last year’s winner, accomplished Cinncinnati ultrarunner Harvey Lewis, set a world record by running 450 miles over 108 hours—or four and a half days.

Cantrell now finds himself surprised not only by the race format’s popularity but also the allure many runners have found in the design. These backyard races are, like Nelson’s race, more about community and the comradery of people pushing each other to go farther than they ever have than about fighting your competitors to the near death. While the format becomes exponentially more grueling over time as variables like sleep deprivation escalate, for the first 24 hours or so, the backyard ultra format is an approachable way for many to cover a very long distance. And Cantrell admits that he likes what these mom and pop backyard races have become.

“There are a lot of aspects to it that I didn’t really consider,” he said. “I do know we get a lot of people who never thought they could ever run an ultra. It’s a race for everyone.”

Cantrell thought of the idea for a backyard race close to 50 years ago, when he was in high school struggling to keep up with the fast kids on his track team during interval workouts. He noticed by the end of an interval he was often a little closer to their heels.

“I’d get left in the dust early, but eventually, I’d wear them down,” he said. “So in a 4-mph race, I thought I could beat everybody.”

The idea stayed in the recesses of his mind until he could do something about it on his property in central Tennessee. He didn’t have the money to put on a big race, but with the format, all he needed was a stopwatch.

“This format doesn’t require very much,” Cantrell said. “I think that’s why it’s caught on.”

It’s also caught on because it’s spectator-friendly—both online and in person—perhaps more so than any other race not on a track. It not only made a household name out of Lewis but acted as a coming-out party for Courtney Dauwalter when the two went head-to-head for nearly 20 hours in 2020 and ran a total of 283 miles before Dauwalter outlasted him by a lap and won. Cantrell said this was another aspect of the race he didn’t consider, and it’s partly what makes it fun.

“Women are on an equal competitive footing with men,” he said, and indeed, Maggie Guterl also won Big’s Backyard Ultra, now considered the format’s national championship, in 2019.

The format, Cantrell said, is supposed to measure willpower, not VO2 max or speed or other aspects of physiological talent. There are enough races for that. Instead, Big’s measures grit—the one thing he had over those speedy, more talented guys on the track in high school.

“The most challenging part,” Cantrell said, “should be the distance between the chair and the starting corral.”

Tens of thousands were captivated last year by Lewis’s win, his second at Big’s Backyard, which Cantrell now livestreams and provides real-time written commentary. Lewis was already well known for winning the 135-mile Badwater Ultramarathon in 2014, but he wasn’t taken seriously as a trail runner when he first entered Big’s in 2017, he said.

“I like the trails though,” Lewis said. “I’m very strategic. They were doing it wrong. Everyone was running up the first hill, and I was in the back, just walking up. The next day, everyone walked up the hill.”

Lewis kept going even after making a lap by just a second. He eventually gave in after 200 miles, taking the assist, but it made him wonder just how far he could go. He decided to devote part of his life to it.

“Big’s is so great,” Lewis said. “You’re walking into an ultimate game board, with strategy, perseverance, and skill level. The course itself is nothing special, and it’s usually that way with a lot of them. The genius is behind the format.”

Lewis races at Big’s to win, no doubt, but as a teacher at the School for Creative and Performing Arts in Cincinnati his living does not depend on it. (Good thing, as there’s no prize money anyway.), Despite his competitive drive, he’s learned to relish in the non-competitive moments on the course and treasures his two assists as much as his wins.

Last year, he says his goal was as much to help get runners through the third night as it was to outlast them all. He remembers 2020 mostly for the way he and Dauwalter spent nearly a full day and night taking turns leading the race and pushing each other to approach 300 miles, a number that was, at the time, unheard of to run in this format. Lewis called it a “collaboration” instead of a race. It was a much-needed feel-good story during the pandemic delivered by two nice people.

“We were very encouraging of each other,” Lewis said.

This is one of the evolutions of the race that took Cantrell by surprise: Backyard races build community among runners with different ability levels because of the unique format. Many other ultras around the world are in intimidating places for beginners, but the accessible four-mile loop obliterates those fears.

Mandy Mullen, the owner of run.Windsor in Windsor, Colorado, changed the format from a 50K to a backyard race for her Weld Your Mettle ultramarathon because it helped foster that community aspect.

“There’s so much more to running than just running,” Mullen said. “In this the competition goes away, and it’s more teamwork. There’s zero of, ‘I want to beat this person.’”

Katie Stroud is the president of a running and walking club that’s existed since 1979 in Alice Springs, a small town in the desert of Australia. She hosted the second annual backyard ultra this year as a part of the races the club puts on.

“It’s such a terrific format for people to push their distance in such a wonderful and supportive way,” Stroud said. “It’s so much more than people running in circles.”

Indeed, Cantrell believes more people ran 100 miles in 24 hours, a benchmark so elite that races usually give out special belt buckles to those who do it, this year in backyard events than all the other ultramarathons around the world combined. The final two left standing this year in Alice Springs, Stroud said, were running buddies who just wanted to push each other to 100 miles.

“There are all these little moments like that in our event every year,” Stroud said. “It’s really cool to be there for that.”

Carl Worth was another one who caught the backyard bug. Even though he’d never run more than a half marathon, he ran the virtual backyard race during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020 and astonished himself by covering 54 miles. He liked the camaraderie and community of backyard running so much he began organizing the Banana Slug Backyard Ultra the following year in Oregon’s Champoeg State Park.

At this year’s event, the winner ran for 49 hours and 200 miles for a “Silver Ticket,” which qualifies him for Big’s Backyard, since the Slug was one of the six events where the winner qualified him for the World Team Championships.

But Worth prefers not to focus only on the winner. During the race, he puts up a spreadsheet on a TV—he’s a software engineer by trade—and posts everyone’s longest distance they’ve run. Whenever they break it, and many do, they can ring a bell, a tradition that Cantrell established at his own race. At this year’s Banana Slug event, 34 runners surpassed their personal bests.

“It’s a really satisfying thing to put on as a race director,” Worth said. “You get to see some amazing things.”

This is true for Jess’ Backyard Ultra as well. The sun rises, illuminating the gray sky and shining some welcome light on our muddy trails. Nelson decides to take a small nap at the house. Our fourth competitor rolled her ankle in the wee hours of the morning, making my friend, Bret Naber, the winner after 30 miles, but we decided to run through the night and see how far we could go. At 9 A.M., after 12 hours and 50 miles of running through the mud, we go home for a shower and some sleep.

This year’s Big’s Backyard Ultra on October 19 is the biannual international team competition, called the World Satellite Backyard Team Competition. Team USA will compete at Cantrell’s event in Tennessee, and the 15-member U.S. roster will have at least two women, Megan Eckert, who won the Saguaro Showdown Backyard Ultra in Mesa, Arizona, and Jennifer Russo, who won Ohio’s Backyard Ultra, as well as Lewis and Scott Martin, the three-time winner of the Banana Slug race put on by Worth.

Cantrell said there are 68 national teams, the members of which will compete simultaneously in backyard ultras in their home countries to earn points for their teams. It’s much like the Olympics—with each country enjoying a home field advantage—and it makes you wonder if this event will finally get ultrarunning there.

“I think you have to reasonably see how it goes,” Cantrell said. “A lot of things start up, and they are really popular, and then they fade out. Maybe somebody more politically skilled than me could get it there.”

But Cantrell’s favorite part about the race format isn’t the superstars, even if his own includes some of the most elite ultrarunners in the world. It’s that time isn’t a factor. It’s about the distance you run, and if you run a personal best, you get recognized for it, even if you finish 30 seconds before the bell.

“The age groups in other races are won by the same people over and over,” Cantrell said. “But in this one, everyone has their day.”

#8293. Is Yellowstone National Park (Back) in Its Wild West Era?

A crowd waits for Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone (Photo: Grant Faint / Getty)

I was sitting on my tailgate, listening to the sounds of songbirds and car honks, when a scuffle broke out in a nearby picnic area. Shouts echoed from the woods as a crowd swarmed two dudes who were shoving and swinging at each other.

Welcome to a hot summer day in Yellowstone National Park. The tussling group seemed to be a motorcycle club, based on their headwear and matching T-shirts. Given their sweaty disposition, I’m not sure “staying hydrated” was listed in the bylaws.

“This place is nuts,” said my wife, returning from the restroom as the two dudes were separated. “What happened here?”

“Fist fight at the Old Faithful corral.” I shrugged.

Then we embarked on a long trek through the semi-apocalyptic parking lot. Frantic drivers whipped around corners, cutting each other off. Exasperated families double-parked and hurried away. Frustrated sightseers returned to their blocked vehicles and laid on the horn. Finally, my wife and I breathed a sigh of relief as we reached the safer confines of the world’s most active hydrothermal zone, the scalding Upper Geyser Basin.

Yellowstone seems to be having a moment as the poster child for rising threats facing the National Park Service (NPS), including bad visitor behavior. While the parks attract record-setting crowds, the Trump administration simultaneously gutted the workforce, cutting NPS staff by nearly 25 percent since 2025. Interpretive signs about important topics like Indigenous displacement and slavery were torn down and replaced by nationalistic propaganda. More trash than ever was recently pulled from Yellowstone geysers, including strange stuff like fidget spinners, fake nails, and a baseball cap displaying the words cowboy hat.

For outdoor enthusiasts watching these disturbing events, it can feel like there’s never been a worse time for national parks such as Yellowstone. My wife, who’d never been there before, was shocked by the wackier things we saw during one high-season day. I arrived better prepared, having come to Yellowstone a grand total of TWO times. My first visit happened 20 years before, when some young whitewater paddlers and I came through on a cross-country road trip. The park felt somewhat calmer back then, but by no means sane. There were about 3 million visitors that year, instead of about 4.5 million now.

Back then, occasional thrill seekers with camcorders chased wildlife, while today’s park paparazzi are influencers with smartphones. Then, like now, I saw a few tourists hopping off boardwalks and stepping across dangerous thermal crusts. I don’t think I’ve ever witnessed anyone stick their fingers in toxic waters, but I’ve definitely seen videos on Tourons of Yellowstone. Each time I’ve gone, we talked about the poor souls who fell and the impulsive daredevils who flung themselves into acidic hot springs, where they were fatally burned or entirely dissolved.

After my first visit, I mostly gave Yellowstone a wide berth. Later, I returned to the mountains and canyons of Wyoming, exploring real places and stories from the Wild West era for a book, Discovering the Outlaw Trail. That’s how I learned that Yellowstone National Park never saw any “good old days,” though some periods have been better or worse for various reasons.

In 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed the first national park into law, word had already spread in the East. Yellowstone was a landscape like no other, filled with abundant wildlife, erupting geysers, and plunging waterfalls. For ages, it was home to nomadic and resident Native peoples like the Mountain Shoshone. Now this volcanic plateau in the Rocky Mountains was threatened by westward expansion of the United States.

For a decade, no more than roughly a thousand visitors made the long and jolting stagecoach journey. Yet the bad behavior started immediately. Seeking souvenirs, vandals hammered away at mineral deposits. Poachers slaughtered countless bison, elk, and bears for their hides, leaving fields of carcasses. Squatters built illegal cabins within the boundaries, hoping the park law would be repealed. Tourists tossed trash, timber, and soap into geysers like Old Faithful. When the erupting fountains sent foaming debris sky high, onlookers cheered. The handful of park staffers watched on, horrified.

After the railroad arrived in 1883, things only got worse. With growing crowds came petty pickpockets, horse thieves, and gunslinging outlaws. Bandits hid behind bends in the road and robbed the passing tourist wagons one by one. The largest stagecoach robberies in U.S. history were said to have happened in Yellowstone. Not once, but three times.

The reason for the mayhem? During the lean federal budgets following the Civil War, Congress had been willing to establish the park, but they weren’t willing to fund it. With limited rules and near-zero enforcement, Yellowstone developed a reputation as a fun place to get away with things.

During our summer day in Yellowstone, my wife and I managed to break away from the crowds. To start, we took a six-mile hike through quieter parts of Upper Geyser Basin, which reminded us why this is a special place worth protecting.

We watched the angled eruption of Daisy Geyser with maybe a dozen fellow visitors. Then we walked past Punch Bowl Spring to a unique feature that few visit, Black Sand Pool. Under our feet, the ground tremored with loud thumps, the result of steam implosions happening beneath the pool’s surface.

During our hike, we met a friendly Oregon family that ranks Yellowstone among their favorite parks. To avoid the craziness, they devised a unique itinerary, staying a few nights each at several park lodges and hiking outward during the quieter mornings. In most ways, this family resembles the majority of parkgoers. Hikers who love the parks, follow the rules, and appreciate the rangers. While poor behavior may be increasing again, such offenders remain a highly visible minority of visitors.

That said, without a few key decisions made during the fading days of the Wild West, Yellowstone might have gone bad altogether.

Tucked away in the woods bordering Norris Geyser Basin, there’s a log building overlooking a small river. Today, this old Army post ironically holds the Museum of the National Park Ranger. Inside, a bronze bust depicts Harry Yount, a legendary figure from Yellowstone history. If the frontiersman’s face looks particularly tired, well, there’s a reason for that.

In 1880, as this nascent national park was being overrun by poachers and miscreants, the meager budget was enough to hire exactly one game warden. He was expected to single-handedly patrol over 3,300 square miles of parkland. Instead, Yount quit in protest after 14 months, reporting that one guy couldn’t do a job that required a well-funded ranger service.

And guess what, the government listened! It just took 35 years. In the meantime, they tried pretty much anything else. They invited some vigilante cowboys, offering them half the collected fines. Naturally, these volunteers avoided the gunslingers and targeted wealthier tourists. So, the U.S. Army was sent in. For decades, half-hearted soldiers chased outlaws beyond park boundaries. The soldiers went back to their posts and waited until the villains cartoonishly returned.

In 1916, the National Park Service was established. Finally, professional rangers assumed responsibility for management, interpretation, and enforcement within an improving park system. Disorder gradually decreased across the West and in Yellowstone, but not entirely. The national parks went on to become a beloved feature of the U.S.

The story of Yellowstone’s destructive early days, and its first park ranger, offers a cautionary lesson that’s easily forgotten: when crowds increase and park budgets and staffing decrease, lawbreakers rise again. We’re seemingly back where we started, with Yellowstone in its Wild West era again.

#8292. This Sound Map Will Transport You to the PCT From Anywhere

Most backpackers memorialize their trips through photographs. But when LA-based hiker Tom Kelly hit the PCT in 2023, he wanted to document a different, more sensory experience of the trail. Kelly, a nature sound field recordist, composer, and musician, toted 40 ounces of audio recording equipment during his 2,650-mile thru-hike, pausing along the trail to capture the acoustics of the journey. Kelly set up his microphones along burbling creeks and amid chirping insects; he recorded the rustling of grass in the wind, rain on a tent fly, or the chatter of passing hikers. Upon completing his thru-hike, Kelly spent two years compiling his recordings into an interactive and freely accessible sound map.

Reporter Amelia Arvesen spoke to Kelly about his project, the challenges of capturing sound in the backcountry, and what he hopes listeners can gain from the map.

Tom Kelly: It was beautifully calm, really nice day. And we all went to bed, and I woke up to the sound of a great horned owl calling across the lake. And so, the last thing I want to do is wake up and do something, you know? It’s hard enough to wake up to go to the bathroom, much less take your recording equipment, go hike, set up, and you know, do the whole recording process.

I’m a nature sound field recordist, I’m a composer, and music performer based in Los Angeles, California. What led me to recording sound on the PCT is kind of the natural history I have of recording sound in spaces that I would travel to in general. Leading up to the PCT, I’ve always had a field recorder with me because it is just very natural for me to bring it along as my way to interface with the space that I’m in. Getting to the Pacific Crest Trail, I knew that this was going to be my method of creativity while I was hiking. When I set out, I didn’t necessarily know what the project was going to be, or if there was even going to be a project to begin with. But I knew that I wanted to engage in the practice of listening and recording sound along the trail.

In the Mojave Desert, on the north side of the LA Aqueduct, I just sat down on the ground, pulled out my recorder, and started listening. And it was in that moment that I became very aware of where I was and what I was doing. And honestly, I could not be happier in that moment. Comparing the scale of these things—like this massive trail, and then here’s like this little moment—and it’s just, for me, taking in kind of just the depth of those small moments all along the trail is something that’s been really rewarding for me, and has been something I’ve worked through this project to try and convey, and offer as a gift to everyone. I hope that when someone sets out to interact with the sound map that I’ve put out there, that they’re able to get just a little piece of what I was able to experience out there. And that is just the ability to slow down and just really experience nature along the Pacific Crest Trail in this kind of embodied sort of way.

#8291. A Conversation Between Alex Honnold and Jim Morrison on ‘Everest: The Other Side’

At first glance, it might not seem like Alex Honnold’s free solo of El Capitan has much in common with Jim Morrison’s first ski descent of Everest’s north face, which is documented in Jimmy Chin’s new film Everest: The Other Side, which releases today, October 30.

But in a conversation during a live recording of Climbing Gold in May, it became clear that several parallels exist between these historic firsts:

Despite their shared sky-high risk tolerance, both Honnold and Morrison also agree with the general public on one thing: They consider each other “crazy.” Morrison called Honnold’s ropeless ascent of El Cap “totally insane.” Meanwhile, Honnold struggled to identify the line one might ski down Everest’s north side in a photo. Once Morrison pointed it out, Honnold declared: “That seems like death.”

The Hornbein Couloir on the northern Tibet side of Everest has taken the lives of several climbers, including the snowboarder Marco Siffredi who attempted to make the first descent of the couloir in 2002; his body has never been found.

Two Americans, Thomas Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, made the first ascent of Everest’s north side in 1963. The north side’s first ascent came just 22 days after Jim Whittaker became the first American to climb Everest via the south side. The 9,000-foot couloir they took to the top was colloquially known as “Hornbein’s Avalanche Chute.” Jimmy Chin also attempted an ascent of Hornbein’s in 2003, but was caught in a near-deadly avalanche.

At the age of 50, after two failed attempts and the staggering loss of Hilaree Nelson, his partner in life and mountains, on Manaslu, Morrison skied down Hornbein’s Couloir on October 15. He pulled it off just four months after undergoing a partial knee replacement. Before Morrison’s ascent last fall—which included a 12-person team of Sherpas, Ecuadorian fixers, and filmmakers—no human had successfully ascended the line since 1991.

Honnold’s conversation with Morrison about his historic ski descent was part of the first-ever live recording of Fitz Cahall’s and Honnold’s Climbing Gold podcast. The interview took the stage at Outside Days on May 31 in Denver, CO. The podcast episode dropped today, alongside the release of the film. You can watch an excerpt above, and read on for Honnold’s and Morrison’s thoughts on grief, the question they dread most, and risking their lives for sport.

Morrison conceived of the goal to ski down Everest’s Hornbein Couloir with Hilaree Nelson. The two ski mountaineers met on Makalu (8,463m) in 2015 and fell in love.

“We were on a tear,” Morrison told Honnold and Cahall, “ticking off these dream runs all over the planet.”

The two had been trying to get to Everest to attempt their ski descent. But COVID delayed their plans, making it impossible to get to the Chinese side of the mountain. To stay in 8,000-meter-peak shape, in 2022, they headed to Manaslu (8,163m) where Morrison recalls they “had a pretty incredible day all by ourselves up on the mountain.” He started skiing down first; Nelson followed, but when Morrison stopped to wait for her, she never appeared. She had set off a small avalanche. “What ensued was a multi-day, horrific rescue of her and trying to find her,” he said. “And it changed my life.”

At first, Morrison wanted to hang it up—never ski or head into the mountains again. But eventually, he began to realize “this is part of me, this is in me.” And he returned to the goal they’d started together. “I wanted to do it for her, and her legacy, and us.”

On the summit, Morrison spread some of Nelson’s ashes. “It was a really emotional moment for me, looking off at mountains I had skied with her, Lhotse and Makalu,” he reflected. “I really felt like she was there.”

In 2011, before losing Nelson on Manaslu, Morrison’s wife, daughter, and son passed away in a plane crash. While he has experienced unfathomable loss, he continues to try to push past the grief to keep living. On stage, he shared a metaphor he uses to grapple with loss:

I’ve described grief as a big heavy wet blanket that gets put on you. It’s just really hard. You go through a process of losing a loved one or spouse or child and it’s a really heavy weight. I like to think over time you take that blanket and you dry it out and you begin to fold it up. And eventually, you put it in a backpack and you carry it with you.

After free soloing El Cap, Honnold said his life became “a crazy whirlwind.” A week and a half later, he was on an expedition in Alaska. Then the film came out, thus marking his “six month deployment to Hollywood” of screenings and award ceremonies.

The effect was that his memories of free soloing El Cap blurred with the scenes from the film as he watched himself on the big screen, again and again. What he’d set out to do for himself became a messy, public experience. As Chin releases his film, Morrison may undergo a similar experience of distorted memories and mayhem.

Honnold also recalled the dreaded question punted at him on his Hollywood deployment: What’s next?

Morrison received the same question after his Everest descent and gave an answer Honnold wished he’d come up with years ago: Isn’t this enough?

“I just achieved this 10-year life dream,” Honnold joked of receiving the “what’s next” question. “I don’t have another life dream lined up on the back burner.”

Morrison called achieving his Everest ski descent goal an “incredible journey” and noted that he appreciated the team that supported him throughout the process.

Cahall teed up his last question by warning that “some of this is triggering to some people.” Meaning, this talk of visualizing fatal falls, of risking it all for the goal. But, Cahall wondered: Are we mistaking complacency for safety?

Morrison said that he doesn’t really see it as complacency versus risk. It’s not an either/or situation. “This is what I’m drawn to and this is what my life’s goals have been centered around,” he said. “I’m not going out there to make a mistake and not come home.” He added that while his ski descent might seem like a “horrendously risky thing,” it was the culmination of extensive planning and preparation, just like Honnold’s El Cap free solo.

“It’s really hard to look at you climbing El Cap without a rope and rationalize it and understand it and be able to relate to it because it is so totally insane,” Morrison said. But at the same time, he said he held “deep respect” for all of the preparation and focus Honnold put into ticking the goal.

“Without taking some amount of personal risk, you just can’t lead a rich and fulfilled life,” Honnold added. “People watch the film Free Solo or a film like that and they’re like, ‘Well, that’s crazy!’ Yeah it’s unusual, not the sort of risk taking you normally see, but it’s still making smart choices in their life in order to lead the most fulfilled life that they can.”

#8290. The Best Hiking Child Carriers for Travel, Day Hikes, and Long Trails

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Before our daughter AJ arrived, my wife and I braced for the end of an era. We figured our adventurous lifestyle would be long gone (or at least forever changed); our family trips would revolve around nap schedules instead of trails; and our days of spontaneity and exploration would grind to a halt. Turns out, we couldn’t have been more wrong.

At eighteen months, our daughter has probably logged more trail miles than the average adult. She’s joined us on ridgeline hikes in the Blue Ridge Mountains, alpine lake loops in the Rockies, coastal walks in New Brunswick, red-rock rambles in Arches and Zion national parks, and plenty of urban outings around Chicago.

And all the credit goes to the unsung hero of our gear closet: the hiking child carrier.

While she loves to explore the trail on foot in short stints under a mile (for now), we’ve found that she’s most content at longer distances taking in the view from above our shoulders. And when we’re lucky, she’ll even doze off for an afternoon nap mid-hike. We’ve tested several kid carriers on dozens of hikes, looking for the ones that balance comfort, fit, and storage. These are the ones we reach for again and again on our hiking adventures.

We take a lot of hiking-centric trips, and packing for them with a toddler is already a puzzle. Between a Pack ’n Play, a car seat, and a week’s worth of diapers, there’s not much bandwidth to lug along a bulky carrier. The Osprey Poco LT is the exception. At five pounds, nine ounces, and a whopping twenty-five liters of gear storage (nearly double what you’ll find in the Kelty and Deuter carriers below), its weight-to-capacity ratio stomps the competition.

Its internal aluminum frame keeps the pack light but provides enough structure and strength to carry a toddler up to forty pounds. There’s a massive lower zipper compartment that fits extra layers or a change of clothes, a soft cooler with snacks, and diapers with room to spare. And a built-in UPF 50 sunshade unfolds and clips to keep the sun off our kid’s sensitive skin.

But the real magic is in how it packs down. The Poco LT folds completely flat and can easily fit into an airplane’s overhead bin or other tight spaces like a jam-packed trunk on a road trip. I can’t say that about any other child carrier I’ve tested. Since getting this pack, we’ve completely ditched the stroller at the airport in favor of this pack as a lightweight transport option for our kiddo.

The tradeoffs? Thinner shoulder straps and a minimalist design mean it’s not the pack for very long days on the trail. Its shorter hip belt and slim profile also don’t fit larger bodies as well as some of the alternatives below. But for traveling to a place you expect to hike or walk five miles or less, it’s the ideal pick.

For smaller babies not big enough for a full-blown backpack carrier, Osprey also makes the Poco Soft Child Carrier. It cradles your young’un on the front of your body, and once they’re big enough, they can face outward to enjoy the view.

Gearing up for a day hike (especially with a kid) means bringing plenty of extras along for the ride: snacks, layers, sunscreen, bug spray, more snacks, and diapers—to name a few. Two pounds heavier than the Poco LT, this pack certainly feels bulkier. But what it lacks in packability it makes up for in convenient features. If you care less about cutting weight and more about pockets, comfort for your kiddo, and space, the Kelty Journey PerfectFIT Elite is your best bet.

Nine total pockets—including three front zippered pockets in different sizes, dual zippered hip pockets, and large mesh side pockets—offer ample storage for a day hike. We’re big fans of the zippered “dirty” compartment on the underside of the pack to stash soiled clothes, like when an unexpected diaper blowout strikes mid-hike. Six chunky grab handles make it easy to hoist the carrier (with some help from a partner or friend) onto your back or set it down gently. Once it’s down, an oversized kickstand keeps the pack sturdy and balanced, even when your kiddo’s kicking around inside. Kelty clearly cut no corners on the details with this pack.

A pack suitable for sleep is non-negotiable. Who wouldn’t want the serenity of their kid snoozing mid-hike? More miles, fewer meltdowns, as I like to say. AJ zonks out in the Journey PerfectFIT Elite more than in any other carrier. I suspect it’s the roomy seat and oversized chin pad (perfect for resting her head like a pillow), which seem to make settling in for a nap that much easier. We took her on numerous day hikes in the Blue Ridge Mountains around Asheville this fall, and she fell asleep on nearly all of them when we timed our outings around her usual naptime. Now, I’m not promising this pack will put your kid to sleep. But I’m confident its cozy, supportive setup will make a mid-hike nap that much more likely.

Backpacking families and peak-bagging parents who want to take on bigger mileage need a carrier that balances weight, capacity, and comfort. For longer hikes, I grab the Deuter Kid Comfort because it fits like a classic backpacking pack. Think of it as an overnight pack that happens to carry a kid instead of your tent, sleeping pad, and stove.

Fit is where the Kid Comfort shines. A sliding torso adjustment lets whoever’s wearing it (Mama, Momzie, Grandma, or Uncle Daniel, in AJ’s case) dial in a precise fit. And as a notoriously sweaty hiker, I appreciated that the back panel’s raised and ventilated mesh kept air moving without trapping heat on my back. The Kid Comfort’s height-adjustable seat has a cushion that widens as your kid grows. We started AJ in it at ten months old, and at eighteen months, she still rides comfortably with plenty of room for continued use over the next couple of years.

It’s eight ounces heavier than the Journey PerfectFIT Elite, but its greater adjustability and plusher padding make it that much more comfortable on longer, more technical routes. On a recent trip to Arches and Zion national parks, we spent long days exploring the trails. I noticed far less shoulder and hip fatigue with the Kid Comfort compared to the Osprey Poco LT and Kelty Journey PerfectFIT Elite packs, especially given all the scrambling over obstacles or on longer hikes. Ergonomic hip wings secure the weight of the load above your hips. Because the hip belt locks the load in place and the pack doesn’t shift or sway with every step, I felt confident scrambling up and down sandstone, squeezing through slot canyons, and crossing exposed slickrock with AJ on my back.

The tradeoff is its limited storage. At fourteen liters, it holds roughly half as much as the Kelty and Osprey packs. Two stretchy side pockets, hip belt pockets, a large stretch pocket on the back, and a zippered bottom compartment hold the essentials but not much more. It’s enough for a day-long outing, but one of us always also ends up carrying a daypack in addition to the Deuter so we can have everything we need. All to say: This pack is by far the most secure and comfortable on technical trails, especially over longer distances.

#8289. The 7 Items That Got Me Through October (and the Rest of Fall)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare said on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”)

Anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

But tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:

Kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries quickly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

It’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

When it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a big back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!)

One-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he said he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.
