#8277. Does Anti-Stink Clothing Actually Work? We (Really) Wanted to Find Out

It wasn't easy, and didn't go as expected, but the no stink clothes seemed to work as advertised. (Photo: Sam Anderson)

I boarded a 3-hour flight wearing a T-shirt I’d worn for over three weeks straight.

By this point I only had a vague sense of what I smelled like. Sleeping bag sweat? Iso gas? Hot dog water? I listened to the crew make the “very full flight” announcement again and shifted in my middle seat. It wasn’t just that I had a dirty shirt on—I’d barely showered for the entire trip, and apart from a few bracing dips in rivers and ocean water, I had made little effort to clean myself at all.

Instead, techy fabrics from Patagonia and an innovative startup called HercLéon battled my oils and odors at point-blank.

Except for deodorant, all that guarded the packed flight from trail stank were various items of “laundry-free” or “anti-odor” clothing. My Patagonia pants and sun hoodie were treated with steam-extracted, food-grade mint oil. The HercLéon T-shirt and my boxer briefs were infused with charcoal and woven with copper fibers. I had used exfoliating nylon washcloths from Lunatec that “never need washing.”

When I planned to hike through the majority of Washington state on a former rail grade, I immediately thought it would be helpful to bring only one set of clothes. But if I tried it and anything went wrong, I could be exposed. As is the case on many long-distance hikes, I knew clothes shopping could be a tough ask depending on where I was.

Still, wardrobe weight is real, and weight quickly becomes the enemy of comfort. So could materials like Patagonia’s HeiQ and HercLeon’s HercCopper limit foul smells after days on trail? Could that improve my overall mood, along with the weight savings, and could it all help me with social graces along the way?

My target was a 330-mile segment of the Great American Rail Trail. It links old railroad corridors from the western Cascades to the Idaho border, dividing roughly into two halves that mirror Washington’s geography: rugged mountains west of the Columbia River and sparse deserts to the east.

I quickly realized small-town hospitality would be my only ticket through the eastern deserts. With no infrastructure or known water on the trail for 40 miles in some areas, networking with anyone willing to provide would be key. I knew I’d be more likely to score overnight stays or solid hookups if I didn’t roll into town smelling like Sasquatch.

Early on, though, the hike took a hard turn: I limped off the trail after 60 miles with a foot injury, but decided to stay in Washington anyway. Some supportive offers from friends could give me a runway to rest up until my original bail date, and maybe hit some rock climbing if I could recover in time.

Because that plan would still require a pretty deep level of dirtbagging, I knew I could keep stink-testing my clothes—which had amazed me to this point.

The accident led to a variety of activities I wasn’t planning on.

This demanded resilience and adaptation from me and everything in my kit, including my clothes.

Apart from activities, my clothing was also subjected to heavy chemical factors, including sleeping bag sweat, dehydrated meal sweat, fried food sweat, and beer sweat. Smoky campsites, rampant use of catholes and wag bags, many cups of coffee, and trash bags packed in vans directly alongside gear during rainy spells also played a role.

In short, I believe the textile engineering of several items made it possible to keep the same clothes on my back for the duration—without disgusting myself, visibly offending service workers, or prompting any business owners to kick me out.

To understand this question is to understand why a tiny startup like HercLéon would market a copper-infused T-shirt for $130.

TL;DR: Body odor happens because our skin is a Golden Corral for bacteria. And it’s open 24 hours.

No matter what we’re doing, our skin is always generating natural oils and shedding dead cells. Glands in areas like the armpits and groin constantly leech thicker protein- and lipid-composed fluids onto the skin. The resulting buildup becomes a body-sized feeding trough for potentially trillions of bacteria.

When those bacteria expel waste, that’s where stink comes from. That and the layers of old oil, decaying cells, etc. that accumulate until you wash them off with soap and water.

Imagine flooding this system with sweat, then draping a layer of clothing on top. Sweat itself is generally odorless, but it does help bacteria multiply. And when it touches the clothing, it allows them to swim, slosh, or spill over. If your skin is a microbial Golden Corral, your sweaty clothes are like a swim-up bar attached to the dining room. But not all textiles are equally hospitable.

Polyester repels water but attracts oil. Skin oils can bond tightly to its synthetic fibers, but the fibers naturally reject water, even in the washing machine. The oil, and anything else gummed up in it, gets welded to the fabric. (This is why some of your cheapest workout shirts get “permastink.”)

Merino wool is the opposite: It repels oil and attracts water. The thirsty fibers soak up sweat from the skin, but leave most bacteria behind, stuck in the oil. And because the merino is removing their water source, the bacteria have a harder time multiplying and farting out more odor.

Techy fabrics like those from Patagonia and HercLéon take this equation of moisture and bacterial transfer to the nth degree—they seek to wall off the swim-up bar.

The HercShirt felt great right out of the bag in a size small, and matched my sizing expectations. Field performance proved to be incredible.

The fabric felt slightly heavy, sliding across my skin with a gentle pressure that felt cooling and was never scratchy. I found it fit closely enough to help me look sharp in town, but it never lost its shape. After three weeks, the material still felt stretchy everywhere. The collar hadn’t bagged out, and even the shirt’s hem under my hip belt wasn’t sagging or creased. By the end of the journey, it was tie-dyed with sweat stains from pack straps, but still passed as a deep navy blue. It never developed pit stains.

Of course, odor did become noticeable. It’s hard to say whether it was on day 12 or 20, but I also made no effort to clean the shirt. So based on my testing, HercLeon’s stated 10-day freshness target is fair—especially if you take the punishing factors of my testing field into account. My shirt endured days of sweaty hiking, exposure to muggy northwestern rainforests, late nights out on the town, cold snaps, and rainstorms that kept me layered up for days on end. It survived nights wadded up at the bottom of a sleeping bag around my heinous feet. I have almost no doubt that 10 days of normal wear with regular showers would be feasible.

My HercUnderwear 2.0 Boxer Briefs were equally impressive. With the caveat that there is a wide spectrum of underwear hygiene tolerance in the population, my findings are below.

First, did I wear the same pair of underwear every day for over three weeks without washing them? No, because there are bacterial realities that command respect. I did take a backup pair of boxer briefs, and I wrung out the HercUnderwear once in a sink with hand soap and once in the ocean. With only this spartan care, the single pair of shorts served for up to nine days at a time. (I used wet wipes consistently.)

For comparison, I did test how long I could make my spare Hanes 92/8 poly/spandex units last. I found four days was my threshold, and wanted to incinerate them after that for the benefit of the trash workers. Meanwhile, crude handwashing rejuvenated the HercUnderwear to a satisfactory extent for the field.

I found fit and roominess to be on the small side. I opted for medium with my 29-30” waist.

Ultimately, I’ll keep the underwear in my kit for activities except hot-weather hiking. The fabric is a bit heavier than many boxer briefs, and can feel slightly warming depending on pants choice.

HercLéon’s engineering exists at every level of manufacturing. Instead of using a spray-on coating, the brand mixes tiny particles of copper and charcoal into its raw textile material before spinning that into fibers. It is called a “masterbatch.” Materials are chosen to control odor at three different points: bacterial growth, odor absorption, and moisture management.

The shirt starts with lyocell, a soft, moisture-absorbing textile fiber made from processed wood pulp.

Copper particles embedded in the fibers release antimicrobial ions when damp. This damages bacterial cell walls, limiting their ability to multiply and convert sweat and other food sources into foul-smelling compounds.

The next contingency is charcoal. Their highly porous carbon structure can trap odor molecules that do develop, HercLéon says, preventing them from escaping into the air.

Finally, “plasma modification”—altering the surface properties of the fibers with ionically-charged gases during manufacturing—causes sweat to spread out and evaporate across the garment, rather than accumulate. Less lingering moisture means fewer opportunities for bacteria to multiply. HercLéon recently launched the HercSock 5 on Kickstarter, which uses the same technology that’s in the shirt and the boxer briefs. However, I did not get to test them on this trip.

Stumbling into Cle Elum, Washington, with wobbly legs, an injured foot, and a calorie deficit, I lurched toward the nearest bar (a long, long mile away). It had been a 30-mile day, and I’d been walking since it was too cold to feel my fingers in the morning. The afternoon in the sparse Yakima River valley had reached 93 degrees. I hadn’t stopped to change clothes—I knew I was hurt and no comfort would amount to real relief.

Night fell, and I sat down at a park bench in a fugue state to put on layers. I reached for my shirt collar to pull it off, expecting to wrestle with a sweat-soaked sheet. Instead, it was bone dry.

My Patagonia Capilene Cool Ultra hoody slotted into the “go-to” position on the trip. The lightest of four entries in the Capilene line, Patagonia builds it specifically for summer temperatures. I confirmed this use case in an unseasonably hot, exposed ascent of the west face of Exfoliation Dome. But I also discovered the hoody had just enough weight to take the shiver factor out of a damp Pacific morning.

Features are limited but functional. I found that using the thumb loops didn’t stretch the sleeves beyond recognition, and I liked the single button to tighten the hood. There are no pockets. Wearing the hoody roughly as much as my HercShirt, often layered with it, I got the sense that odor control wasn’t quite as strong. But it did still generally meet the limits of social acceptability by the end of the trip. And since it was easy to rinse and dried fast, I had no problem dunking it and wringing it occasionally.

According to Patagonia’s anti-stink coating provider, this shouldn’t have worked to refresh odor-fighting capabilities. The coating is a handful of botanicals arranged in a bioengineered structure. HeiQ Mint contains essential mint oils and other “naturally derived deodorizing ingredients”—inside capsules the manufacturer claims are capable of trapping the oils and acids that cause odor. This proprietary “encapsulation technology” snatches odor-causing particles and encloses them during wear. Then it releases them during washing thanks to the alkalinity of soapy water. Thus, laundering duds like the Capilene Cool hoody restores them for their next use, according to HeiQ.

On the last day of the trip, we walked down from the base of Blueberry Buttress (5.8+, 1,000 feet). In just a half mile from the foot of the climb to the car, we lost 1,300 feet of elevation. Quads screaming, we reached my borrowed van and flopped. My climbing partner wrestled himself out of his soaking wet T-shirt, now two or three sizes too big, and hung it on a tree branch.

My Capilene hoody wasn’t stinking up the campsite, and it still fit around my shoulders. Plus, it was dry enough to continue wearing comfortably.

Lunatec’s “never needs washing” camp cloths were absolutely clutch in my kit. With no technology on board except a loose weave for fast drying, the two units thoroughly supplemented wiping and cleanup needs without creating their own.

The green “odor-free” dishcloth was abrasive enough to lift stuck-on burnt bits, and highly durable. Its diffuse weave made it economical to rinse after scouring cookware with sand.

The “self-cleaning” washcloth, slightly larger and stretchier, played well for more detailed work. It was minimally absorbent (I didn’t reach for it when I spilled an entire beer into my friend’s van carpet). But viscous bits like snot or soup remnants clung to it well, then vanished when rinsed. The elastic hang tabs doubled as gathering straps, making each cloth easy to pack up.

What is Lunatec’s secret to self-cleaning? According to the brand, nothing. Their washcloths are 100% nylon, and nothing else.

A backpacker’s world is a stinky one no matter what. So if you’re on an anti-gross-out program, how can you tell if your efforts have meant anything? How can you tell if you’ve kept the Golden Corral in the corral?

There is a device used to measure odors in clinical settings called an olfactometer. It works by, basically, establishing a control smell and then upping the ante in increments—approaching the threshold where the subject can’t handle it anymore. In everyday practice, though, you experience moments when you become suddenly aware of an odor. You lift a shoulder to reach an awkward zipper or squat fast to pick up something you dropped—and the wave breaks. A solid mass of stink floods your face, and you wonder how long everyone else has been able to tell.

For many of us, that’s the trigger. “I need to wash, somehow, now.”

Over 25 days living in a pretty dirty corner of the dirtbag life, I never had that moment. River plunges sufficed for bathing. Sink water rinses refreshed the hardest workhorses in my wardrobe. I didn’t take a microscope, but I think the makers of my clothing delivered on their broad promise: Science can help you not stink (or at least, stink less).

The maintenance burden of living outside full-time had been meaningfully decreased. I thrived in my unexpected program of outdoor and social events for over three weeks with a wardrobe that would fit in a McDonald’s bag, and I’d spent zero time doomscrolling at the laundromat.

Boarding my flight, I looked down at my disheveled rags and scratched at an itch in my neck—I also hadn’t shaved for the whole trip. Then, both of my neighbors arrived and settled in, smiled warmly, and relaxed.

#8276. In His Own Words, a Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain

Honza Špička on Huascarán (Photo: Courtesy of Matěj Žák)

My name is Jan “Honza” Špička. My climbing partner, Matěj Žák, and I are two alpinists, climbers, mountaineers, skiers, and endurance athletes from Nove Straseci, a small town in the Czech Republic. Although we have known each other since childhood through our families (and the local ice hockey team), our climbing paths only crossed a few years ago. Since then, we have spent three seasons together in Peru’s Cordillera Blanca and two seasons in Argentine Patagonia. We have roped up together a few times on Czech sandstone as well. We are no professionals, though; rather than extreme lines, what we have behind us are moderately difficult routes climbed in our own style: clean and fast.

Our speciality? Long days in the mountains and a fast, lightweight approach. We take nothing on an expedition that we cannot carry on our own backs.

Huascarán is the highest mountain in Peru and the highest point in the entire tropics. Its south summit reaches 6,768m and the north summit 6,655m; the two are separated by a broad col called La Garganta (“the Throat” in Spanish) at roughly 6,000m. Huascarán lies at the heart of the Cordillera Blanca, the most heavily glaciated tropical mountain range in the world, and it gave its name to the surrounding national park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985. Because the Earth bulges slightly at the equator, the gravitational acceleration on the summit of Huascarán is among the lowest anywhere on the planet’s surface; a person there measurably weighs a little less than at sea level, by a matter of grams. The summit of Huascarán is also the second most distant point on Earth from the planet’s center, right after Chimborazo.

The mountain is named after Huáscar, the Inca ruler who fought his half-brother Atahualpa for several years over control of the Inca Empire. Atahualpa eventually defeated his brother and had him executed. The American mountaineer Annie Smith Peck, then over fifty years old, climbed the north summit in 1908. The higher south summit held out until 1932, when a German–Austrian expedition made the first ascent.

Huascarán, however, also has a darker side to its history. In 1962, a huge mass of ice broke away from the mountain, and the resulting debris avalanche swept down onto the towns of Ranrahirca. Then, on May 31, 1970, an earthquake off the coast triggered a far larger and more extensive avalanche from the north summit, which within minutes buried, among other places, the entire town of Yungay. The earthquake and avalanche combined took the lives of approximately 67,000 people. It was the deadliest single avalanche disaster by death toll in recorded history.

This tragic event unfortunately also carries a strong Czechoslovak mark. It was right here, in the valley between Huascarán’s north summit and Huandoy Sur, that a Czechoslovak expedition was camped—and the whole expedition became a victim of this mountain.

If we take into account the victims of 1970 and all the climbers who have died on its slopes, it is probably the mountain responsible for more human lives than any other in modern history.

The ascent itself, via the Normal Route, is not particularly difficult, but Huascarán’s glaciers are retreating fast, and so today some routes that were relatively straightforward climbs just a generation ago involve significant objective hazards. In the six years that I have lived in Peru, I cannot remember a year when Huascarán did not claim another victim. There have even been years when it allowed no one at all to reach its summit.

The start of our trip began on Friday, July 11, in the evening in our favourite “pollo a la brasa” restaurant. Our whole group, which we called the “Cayesh crew,” met for a shared dinner to load up on a solid dose of protein before what was to be the main climbing objective of the season for all of us: Huascarán Sur. It has to be said, though, that for none of us was Huascarán the center of the universe. We all had it in “one day, maybe, I’d like to, if it comes to it…” mode, but there was certainly no obsession with this “fat one.” I already had three unsuccessful attempts behind me, but even so I wasn’t insisting on “bagging it.” Yet somehow the appetite, the motivation, the hunger for it arrived. And essentially by coincidence it arrived not only for Matěj and me but also for our friends from Peru. In the end we formed three teams of two.

I have known Saul—formally, Freddy Saul Mendoza Lizana—since 2021; he was essentially my first climbing partner here in Peru. Since then we have been through a lot together—in the mountains, on the crags, at home, and in the pub. He was like my Peruvian brother. We were so close that my wife Alča and I were already counting on a little room for Saul for when we one day return to the Czech Republic and settle down somewhere.

Agnieszka is a Polish “machine” with several 8a/5.13b sport routes to her name. She had seen plenty in the mountains, too. Definitely no lightweight.

Alejandro “Chicho” Ugarte Jordan was a professional photographer from Lima. His main interest was unique mountain images captured with his DSLR or his drone. We had known each other since 2022 through the Skiing Peru project, which we were both part of. We often spent time together with our girlfriends in Lima outside the season, too.

Artidoro “Arti” Salas Gaitan was a pure Huaracino—someone who comes from Huaraz. He was born in the town at the foot of the Cordillera Blanca and lived there his whole life. He ran the Big Mountain hostel, well known among climbers. I personally have known him since 2021, when I spent my first season in Huaraz at his hostel.

Our expedition began on the morning of Saturday, July 11, when we loaded the van with heavy packs. Under the watchful eye of—as Matěj called him—our adoptive father Paul, our friend and the owner of the cozy Cayesh Guest House bed and breakfast, we set off for our starting point, the village of Armapampa in the Yungay area. From Huaraz, it was about a two-hour drive. Besides the six of us, Alenka came along, too, having arrived from Lima that same morning, as did Míša, a Czech woman living in Nepal who had just popped over to Peru to see friends. The girls, however, were only going on a day trip to the hut and back down the next day.

On the edge of the beautiful village of Armapampa, we unloaded our gear from the van, ate the last gluten-free cinnamon rolls that Alenka baked for the trip, and shouldered our heavy packs. Matěj took a group photo and we set off towards Refugio Huascarán, our base camp. We reached the refugio at 4,650m spread out over quite a wide time range (Matěj first, at 2 hours 45 minutes, and Saul and Aga last at a little over 6 hours). Who knows where and why they lingered; apparently they were finishing off their avocados. Either way, the trail was easy and there was no rush, so everyone went at their own pace.

There was no one at the hut apart from us, so we enjoyed it immensely. The evening was a very friendly affair: dinner, beer, guitar, and singing in four languages mixed together. And, of course, planning the climb.

This is where the first, relatively pivotal moment came. Aga wasn’t feeling well—to be precise, she felt pretty crap—so she decided to walk down with the girls. That left the five of us Mohicans. Saul immediately arranged with the lads to form a three-person team. At the time, it seemed to me a good idea. Saul is the most experienced of the three, and the team would only be stronger for it. In hindsight, I blame myself that we didn’t tell him to stay with Agnieszka; Aga was his big “project.”

After breakfast at the hut, we packed our rucksacks, took a group photo, and set off. The girls headed down; the lads headed up. None of us had any idea that this would be our last photo together, and that the girls would never see Saul, Chicho, and Arti again. Just writing this sentence brings tears to my eyes.

The second day of the climb up Huascarán was easy going. A few hundred vertical meters led up to the glacier, then a few hundred more traversed over a gently angled and relatively safe glacier to the spot where Camp 1 is set, at about 5,300m. Matěj and I arrived first, and shortly after us Arti and Chicho, with Saul behind them. We pitched the tents, melted water, cooked food, took photos, rested, and fine-tuned the details for tomorrow’s summit push.

Huascarán is normally climbed via the Garganta col, where Camp 2 is placed at 5,950m, and from there climbers make for the summit. All of us, however, were heading for the El Escudo (“The Shield”) route, which is technically harder but objectively safer,and of course more fun. It is a roughly 600-meter long ice face at 60 to 70 degrees. Thanks to its shape, there are no seracs hanging above you, no cornices, and far fewer things that can come down on your head. Unfortunately, there is little room for a Camp 2 there, so the Escudo is usually climbed from Camp 1 straight to the top, with the descent via the Normal Route.

We set our departure time for 10 pm. While the sun was still up, we crawled into our sleeping bags to get at least a little sleep and recharge the batteries a bit. We all knew that brutally hard work lay ahead.

This was it: summit day. Matěj and I got up at 9:30 p.m. so that we could leave at 10. We could hear the lads sometime before 9. In the end, we left more or less together: the lads at about 10:15 pm, we a few minutes after them.

Given the profile of the route over the Escudo, the plan from the start was to climb in pairs. Later, we became a pair and a three. You cannot climb this with five people on one rope, and none of us ever suggested it. The same applies to the descent.

The first part of the route was probably the most dangerous section of the whole ascent. It was a zone of crevasses and seracs of a size you will not encounter in Europe. There were a few sections of steep ice, but it wasn’t outright hard; it was just that something could come down at any moment. This section was shared with the Normal Route, which then branched off to the left towards Camp 2, while we headed right towards El Escudo.

We reach the bergschrund in less than two hours, with the lads following an hour or so behind us. Here we re-tied onto the full length of the 60m rope and racked up all our gear. In the process, I dropped my radio somewhere into the bowels of the glacier, and Matěj set off upward. The terrain wasn’t hard, so we simul-climbed on a single rope. Matěj climbed three to four pitches this way until he ran out of ice screws. On his last two snow pickets, he built a belay and let me through. My section was more hard snow than ice:easier climbing, less fun, but with correspondingly worse protection. I had three snow pickets on my pack, but I wanted to save those for later, for the belay anchors. After climbing some six pitches on just a handful of screws, I topped out over the lip of the Escudo, where I brought up Matýsek. (Editor’s note: “Matýsek” is a Czech nickname for “Matěj.”) By then, we were at 6,300m. It was cold as hell, with the sun still nowhere in sight. I dropped a glove and started feeling properly ill from the altitude. From this moment on, I suffered like an animal. The section from the top of the Escudo to the summit was endless; it wasn’t as steep any more, but it was long, and the soft snow did nothing to help our progress.

Sometime before 9 a.m. on Monday, July 13, though, we stood on the summit of Huascarán Sur. We didn’t really feel much joy, because we knew the worst was still ahead of us: the way down. On top of that, the summit was a completely flat plateau. You could play soccer on it, only you’d have a long way to go for a stray ball. Even so, weakness came over me and I cried. It was my fourth attempt, with my partner and childhood friend, and exactly a month to the day since our dog, Pisco, was poisoned. I cried again just remembering him. But the joy was there, too, although the main part of it was supposed to come down below. And it did come. But only for a moment.

We didn’t linger on the summit. There really was nothing there. After a snack, a little tea, and the summit photo, we headed down. No one had been on the summit for about two to three weeks, so there were no tracks and no trail. Our only guide was the offline mapy.cz app, which traced the Normal Route. But it was the route that was walked an unknown number of years ago, so we treated it as a rough indication only. We re-tied into classic glacier-travel mode, roughly 15–20 meters apart, with the rest of the rope coiled around each of our bodies.

A few minutes from the summit, on the empty, white, flat plateau, I saw something that looked like the windblown hint of a trail. Before I even got there, something happened and I was falling through the air into an icy hell.

A crevasse. With no sign whatsoever of its existence, it had been waiting there silently for its victim. I remember precisely the feeling of flying into the void. It was as if I were falling for an eternity. Suddenly, I felt the rope come tight, and I knew that was Matýsek. But I keep falling. In that instant, I was certain that in a moment, Matýsek would come flying in after me and we’d both be dead.

But a miracle happened—a miracle called Matěj. The rope bit again and I stopped. He bloody well caught me. I was hanging about 12–15 meters down in a crevasse that runs 100m in each direction and could easily be 50m, 100m, or 300m deep. Who knows? Below me, I saw nothing but icy hell. The crevasse was completely covered with a cap of fine snow. Zero chance of seeing it.

To my own surprise, I didn’t panic; I knew exactly what to do. My only connection to our world was the rope I was hanging on and whatever Matěj had rigged up there to keep me in this world. I clipped a Micro Traxion onto my harness as a self-belay and climbed up the vertical ice wall towards the surface as far as I could. I felt so OK that I even took three photos inside the crevasse. When the line of the rope stopped me from climbing any farther, I swung out into space. I ascended the rest on prusiks.

In a little under half an hour, I was out, back on the surface, back in the world. Only now did I breathe out.

Matěj and I fell into each other’s arms and began to grasp what we just survived. It would have taken very little for him to come in after me, and no one would ever have found us. In hindsight, I see it as an enormous miracle and a measure of enormous skill on Matěj’s part. He saved our lives. And maybe it was at this very moment that we realized this really was no joke and that things were getting serious. We continued the descent very cautiously, and we were genuinely scared.

We reached the edge of an ice wall where the Normal Route was supposed to be, but there was nothing there—nothing at all. There was no question of searching for a way through this labyrinth. The wall looked to be about 20m high, with a ramp below it along which we hoped to traverse off left toward the Normal Route.

We rappelled off two snow pickets into a relatively safe spot surrounded by seracs. I remember looking at the leaning towers next to us and thinking that one deep breath would be enough to bring the whole lot down. Still, we felt a certain safety in our little hollow. Finally, we had a bit of time to catch our breath, eat and drink a little, and get in touch with the lads.

Before I could do that, they called me. They said they were about 200 vertical meters below the summit. But it was already late, around 12 to 1 p.m., so their plan was to traverse off towards the Normal Route and descend by it.

I told them to try to find our tracks and our rappel, and to really watch out for crevasses, because I had just fallen into one. We confirmed that everything was OK and that we would meet in the evening at Camp 1, or if need be, at base camp, depending on the time and our energy. If I had known that this was the last time I would speak to them, I would have told them so much more.

A little later, while searching for the route on the map, my phone slipped out of my hand and vanished somewhere below. But I didn’t dwell on it. I knew we had other worries. It was just a shame to lose the photos from inside the crevasse.

Another unpleasant rappel off a 25-meter serac, and we were on the slope leading towards the Garganta. By now the weather had turned and visibility had dropped to a few tens of meters. But we were already in the Garganta, at 6,000m. All we needed now was to find Camp 2, which was just a flat patch where tents stood two days ago. From there, there should be some tracks and a route down.

We wandered about a bit, but eventually we found Camp 2 and there really was a hint of tracks. Shortly before that, the summit shook off its cloud, and we saw the lads above us at about 6,300 or 6,400 m. It even looked to us as though they were closer to the Normal Route than we were. We were really relieved.

The route from Camp 2 to Camp 1 is the most dangerous crux of the climb. It is a zone of avalanches, collapsing seracs, and crevasses. Later, Matěj and I agreed that we both felt as if we were living in some kind of virtual reality, outside our bodies, just waiting for the video game to end. Maybe that was why I didn’t really register the risk.

We arrived back at Camp 1 at sunset. With our last reserves of strength, we packed up and continued down to the refugio. A hot dinner and a bed was, after all, a big draw. And it was only a little under two hours more.

We reached the hut sometime before nine in the evening, after 23 hours on our feet. We asked for something to eat and a beer, then went to sleep. We thought about the lads and somehow had no doubt that they were fine and that they were at Camp 1. After all, we saw them a short way above Camp 2.

In the morning, we woke up at the hut completely wrecked, but suddenly also happy with what we’d achieved. We expected the lads to turn up any moment, and then we’d race down into the valley. The news from the lads, however, was different.

Saul wrote that they couldn’t find the way down and had to bivouac somewhere above Camp 2. But they were OK, he said; they survived the night up there without any camping gear. They were tired, Chicho was apparently feeling ill, but all were OK. They would try to find the descent route. From then on, we were to communicate with Chicho, as Saul’s battery was dead.

We still had no idea that things were bad. But neither did the lads. Because things weren’t bad yet. We managed to download our GPS track onto a phone and send it to the lads as a mapy.cz link. Up above Camp 2, there was occasionally a signal, so we communicated with the lads via WhatsApp.

At 9:10 a.m., Chicho wrote asking us to send our route. At 9:15 a.m., we sent the mapy.cz link and it was delivered.

At 10:16 am, Chicho sent a photo and a video from where they were. They sounded fine; Camp 2 was visible below them. At 10:18 a.m., we sent them a crib sheet of roughly which way to go down, including a sketch drawn onto their photo. This was delivered. At 10:21 a.m., we asked Chicho whether he had our route on mapy.cz. This was the last message delivered to Chicho. After 10:21 am, no further messages were delivered. From then on, there was no communication from them.

Since the weather was beautiful, the lads were fine, and there was no signal lower down towards Camp 2, it never occurred to us that the lads might be in trouble. We were certain they had descended lower, lost signal, had flat phones, and so on—but were descending. There was essentially no reason to think anything else. They werebujacos”—tough guys. They had survived a night without sleeping bags at 6,400m, and now they would just run down to us, to the girls, to lunch, to a beer.

Given these assumptions, we knew we had several hours of waiting before they would appear above Camp 1, which could be seen from the hut. Meanwhile, we tried to contact them by radio and by phone, in case they happened to come into signal. But still, we were completely calm.

When about 3 p.m. came and there was no sign of them, though, it seemed odd to us. It had gone on too long. We decided we would go up and look for them. They were probably tired and frozen, and another night up there would be truly critical.

We ate, brewed tea, and took all the clothing we had. In the meantime, I called a friend, a guide, down in town so that he knew something was going on and could start rounding up help if needed. But there was still a chance alive in us that they were at Camp 1, asleep in the tent, and simply had no way of letting us know. Down in town, a group of volunteers was already getting ready to set out to help. There is no organized professional mountain rescue in Peru.

But there was no one at Camp 1. By then we sensed that things were bad; we just didn’t know how bad. On top of that, a snowstorm was moving in.

The message we sent down was clear: It was official, we needed help. The lads were somewhere up there. We were going up for them. We knew that down in the valley things were already under way and would keep going without us. But we had a different task: to find them and bring them down.

We pack all their sleeping bags as well and set off up into the gale. Matěj created a Garmin messaging group and made our position trackable online. He realized more than I did that we were heading into real trouble.

I have friends up there – my “churaks,” my “hermanos.” I registered nothing.

For the first time in my life, I was faster than Matěj. In my head, I knew they were up there, frozen and exhausted but alive, and that we were their only chance.

In these conditions I would turn around on any climb of my own; I would never go on. But now it wasn’t about me. It was about the lads. The moment we gave up, they would have no chance.

We got as far as above Camp 2, to 6,000m, but there was nothing anywhere. That was shortly before midnight. Just gale, snowfall, a temperature I’d estimate at around minus 30 degrees, and not a trace of the lads.

By this point I knew things were very bad. In this weather, no one survives up here for even an hour. Matýsek was very afraid of going down because of the avalanche danger and pushed for us to stay at Camp 2 and somehow sit it out with all those sleeping bags. I knew that if we stayed, we would be dead within the hour. In the end, I convinced him that we had to go down. That was about 50/50. But staying up there felt to me like 90/10.

The descent was horrific. Avalanche terrain was everywhere we looked, with giant seracs over our heads almost the entire way. Visibility was near zero, and our tracks drifted over with snow. Nevertheless, our guardian angel was on duty again and guided us down. We get back to Camp 1 sometime around 3 a.m. on Wednesday, July 15. There I well and truly collapsed, mentally and physically. We crawled into the tent for a while and waited for the first group of volunteer rescuers, who, as we already knew, were on their way from the refugio.

Even in the tent and in a sleeping bag, 700 vertical meters lower, the weather was terrible, and it was here that Matýsek told me we were one–all. He had saved us above that crevasse, and I had by insisting that we go down.

The first rescue team reached Camp 1 just after first light, sometime after 6 a.m. It was five people in all, three guides and two aspirant guides, and among them my good friend Szymon, who was the only one closer to me than Saul. That was all. We handed over all the information we had and let them go up. We would head for the refugio, where further teams were supposedly bound: one to set up a support base at Camp 2, another at Camp 1. Supposedly lots of people were coming.

Unfortunately, we were in Peru, where everything does not quite work. We met the Camp 1 team below the glacier—five lads, all friends, climbers, and volunteers from Peru, Colombia, Spain, and the Czech Republic. No Camp 2 team ever came, and in fact, there never was one. The five lads up above had packed late in the evening and set out from Huaraz to help friends in need. In a single push they climbed to over 6,000m. But because of the lack of support and the conditions up there, they had to turn back in the afternoon and descend to Camp 1. That essentially ended any realistic chance of finding the lads alive. I personally had known already at Camp 2, which we had climbed to in our attempt to find them, that there was almost no chance left.

From then on, great chaos set in across the whole organization of the rescue and search. As I already mentioned, Peru has no mountain rescue service; there are no rescue helicopters, no rescuers, no system, no protocol, no designated person to take charge of any coordination. Everything happened through the WhatsApp group that Matěj created when we set out for the lads. Everything was done on the basis of volunteers, friends, guides and family members.

Eventually, the police, the high-mountain police (Policía de Alta Montaña), and apparently even the army joined in to help. But their help consisted solely of transporting volunteers by helicopter from the town of Caraz to the refugio at 4,650m, and the first helicopter took off 24 hours after the official call for help. What’s more, it flew up empty, to assess the situation, only to find that another police helicopter had been sitting on the “helipad” by the refugio for several days, badly parked, and that its pilots were afraid to take off in it.

In the end, some transport up did take place, but effectively only on the following days. If someone down below had been able to coordinate it, they could have sent the line of volunteers towards base camp on foot, with a herd of donkeys, on the very first day of the search (July 15), and they would have been there far sooner than waiting until the next day to see whether anyone would get a place on the helicopter.

The entire rescue, and subsequently the search, was run by volunteers and the families. It was they who hired private companies with advanced drones, they who coordinated everything, mainly with the police, they who did everything they could. I myself went back with two volunteers a few days later to a point just above Camp 1 to attempt a further search with drones—without success. The zone where all the clues ended—GPS signals, the location of the last photos, the hint of the last tracks, and so on—is at around 6,500m. Camp 1 is at 5,300m, and most drones simply cannot fly that high and that far. Only the advanced police drones can, and they in turn lacked experienced pilots willing to risk it. Going higher wasn’t possible because of the conditions on the mountain. So, a stalemate. In the end footage from the suspect zone was obtained, but there was not a trace of the lads.

After almost detective-like work by many friends—using the GPS signal from their watch as requested from Garmin headquarters, footage from private and police drones, plus footage from the guides who went all the way up during the search, information from us, and the lads’ last photos—it appears that the lads missed our belay station by literally a few meters, and that while crossing a snow bridge over gigantic crevasse systems it collapsed beneath them.

When I first wrote this report, it had already been more than three weeks since I last saw the lads, since I last spoke to them. Still nothing has been found today, and in my view it will be hard for anything to be found. The scale of everything on Huascarán is utterly absurd: crevasses several hundred meters wide and deep, seracs the size of apartment blocks… Sure, this isn’t the Himalaya, and it doesn’t look like it, either. Huascarán looks like two lazy fat blokes lying side by side. But beware of it. That mountain is mean and hostile, and although on paper it isn’t hard—the Normal Route was reportedly graded only AD/AD+, the Escudo D—it is no game. You are playing for your life at every single step.

I don’t think that either we or the lads made any fundamental mistake; it was simply that Matýsek and I had a large dose of luck, while the lads had a little less of it.

I am not writing this story for sensation. It is just one real story with a tragic ending. If at least a few of you take something from it—ideally some kind of lesson—it will have served its purpose. As we all know, the mountains give, but sometimes they also take away. We unfortunately now know that this is no empty phrase but the hard truth.

Editor’s note: This trip report has been translated from the original Czech into English with permission of the author. Place names and local terms (La Garganta, El Escudo, refugio, Huaracino, pollo a la brasa) have not been translated from the original Spanish.

#8275. My 99-Year-Old Grandmother Built a Hidden Empire Around Flannel. Then She Lost It All.

When I was a child, visits with my Korean grandmother always began with the same ritual. She would place my left hand on her lap and trace the lines in my palm with her index finger, before delivering a prophetic verdict about my future. She’d tell me that when I became an adult, I would be a cheapskate. Apparently, the so-called “money lines” on my left palm were unbroken. “Your pockets won’t spill money, unlike your grandfather,” she would say.

After reading my palm, my grandmother would turn her attention to my shirt. Starting with the threads, she’d run her fingers along the seams and the stitches, analyzing the fabric for some soothsaying quality. Her hands would rub the material, and she would look at it closely. After pausing for a few seconds, my grandmother would announce her findings: “This shirt has good cotton!” or “I’ve never seen this weave!”

I lived with my family in Arkansas, worlds away from Seoul, which is where my parents had been born and my grandmother lived. Sometimes my grandmother would visit us in the United States, and sometimes we’d fly halfway across the globe to see her in Korea. I remember thinking that her fixation on fortune-telling and garment analysis was normal. I assumed that, across the U.S., grandmothers were greeting their grandchildren by gifting them candy and presents, before sitting down and studying the microfibers in their sweatshirts and blouses.

As I got older, I learned that my grandmother’s hyperfixation on fabric was the product of her younger adult life in Korea. According to my family’s fuzzy family lore, Grandma had once managed a textile factory. Well, no, maybe she had actually owned it. Did she simply work at the factory? Facts were hard to come by. Different family members visiting from Korea would tell pieces of Grandma’s life during their stays in Arkansas. And over the years, Grandma’s history in the garment industry became a source of my curiosity.

I’m now in my early forties, and my grandmother is 99. After years of hearing these mysterious stories, I set out to discover the truth of her connection to the garment industry. During one of my trips to Seoul, as we sat on her couch watching professional wrestling on TV—her favorite pastime—I asked my grandmother questions, in my second grade–level Korean, about her career in textiles.

More than half a century ago, she told me, she and my grandfather had owned a textile factory in Seoul that employed more than 50 people. They had helped pioneer the industrial production of a fabric that stills defines the style and culture of the outdoor industry: cotton flannel.

I wanted to know more, but my lack of Korean fluency kept me from truly interrogating this history. So, I enlisted my cousin, Spring, who speaks fluent Korean and English, as well as my sister, Mary, and my own mother to uncover the real story. Over the course of two years and a half dozen interviews, we interrogated Grandma, full name Sonia Shin, but whom we affectionately call “Hal-money” (grandmother in Korean). She told us stories, recounted memories, and helped us understand what her life was like more than half a century ago. We pieced together the tale of how she and my grandfather built a small empire of industrial flannel production in postwar Seoul. And then, how she lost it all.

Flannel is one of the most popular fabrics amongst outdoor enthusiasts—just try walking into an outdoors store without spotting a flannel shirt at any time of year. Over time, the soft, plaid, button-down shirt has become the unofficial uniform for those of us who work in the outdoor recreation industry. It’s the stuff of cozy pajamas and warm camping blankets, the foundation of the lumbercore fashion movement. Its cultural significance extends far beyond the campfire: flannel is synonymous with Kurt Cobain and grunge rock; with Snoop Dogg and nineties hip hop; with ranchers, tech bros, and city dwellers seeking blue-collar authenticity.

Despite its ubiquity, few wearers of the material ever stop to consider what flannel actually is. Most people associate it with colorful plaid designs woven into wool, but not all flannel is plaid, nor is it wool. The term “flannel” refers to any woven fabric, usually cotton or wool, that’s been brushed until it becomes fuzzy and extremely soft.

Imagine taking a metal brush and scrubbing down a spot on your khaki pants until a thin layer of fuzz forms on the surface. That layer is called a “nap,” which is made up of loosened fibers that, due to the brushing, now stand on end as a soft and warming tuft. The process of creating flannel makes garments warmer and softer.

Industrial textile factories use machines affixed with fine metal bristles to scratch fabric as it passes through the device, raising the nap evenly across thousands of yards of material. The technique used to make flannel is centuries old. Flannel’s origins have been traced to 17th-century Wales, where textile workers brushed fabric made from sheep’s wool into a material that was warm enough to survive the region’s wet, cold winters. Originally done by hand, the technique eventually became mechanized, and it spread across Europe during the industrial revolution. Cheap cotton from North America eventually flooded the European market in the 19th century. Mills quickly swapped out wool for cotton. Amid this evolution, cotton flannel became a fabric for working-class Europeans.

In the U.S., flannel’s connection to the rugged outdoor lifestyle came from Woolrich, the Pennsylvania-based company founded in 1830. The company introduced its red and black buffalo check shirt in 1850. The brand was a hit with hunters, loggers, and trappers, and the design became the official shirt of the lumberjack.

Steven Kurutz, author of American Flannel: How a Band of Entrepreneurs Are Bringing the Art and Business of Making Clothes Back Home, grew up 25 miles from Woolrich headquarters. Flannel was the uniform of the town, even on dressed-up days. His grandfather, a sheet metal worker and fisherman, owned a fancy flannel coat that Kurutz still wears today. “Everyone had one,” he told me.

Kurutz’s explanation for its popularity is that flannel lends a quiet humility and authenticity to those who wear it. The style, he says, has never belonged to any one kind of American. “Flannel cuts across races,” he reminded me. “It’s American, but not necessarily a white person’s garment.”

America’s production of flannel garments shrunk as the textile industry increasingly sought cheaper labor abroad. In 1980, approximately 70 percent of the clothing Americans wore was made in the U.S.; today, it’s about 2 percent, Kurutz wrote. The lion’s share of our garments is instead woven in massive factories in China, Vietnam, Bangladesh, or India.

The Woolrich mill, the oldest continuously operating one in the country, closed at the end of 2018 after the brand moved production overseas. Kurutz calls this a “quiet tragedy” in his 2024 book.

“It’s a deeply American brand, and now it’s not made here, not headquartered here,” he lamented. These days, the brand’s corporate headquarters are located in Italy.

As I spoke with Kurutz, my grandmother’s connection to flannel echoed in my mind. Her story seemed to become more compelling with every historical data point he explained. Decades before American textile manufacturers shipped their operations overseas, my grandparents built a flannel empire out of a half-burned factory in Seoul.

My grandmother is exhausted. Spring and I have just completed a two-hour-long interview session, and Hal-money is lying sideways on her favorite sofa in her apartment in the Apgujeong neighborhood of Seoul. She ignores us while we wrap up our camera gear for the day. I’ve turned on the TV to drown out the noise so she can sleep. WWE wrestling is, of course, playing on the screen.

“If I was just a little younger, I could do it again,” she mumbles before nodding off for a nap.

Spring and I have been aided by a sizable trove of documents, photos, and records from my grandmother’s career in the textile industry. While searching through her belongings, we found the incorporation documents for her business, as well as photographs of the factory, of the looms, of past employees.

These photographs and documents jog Grandma’s memory. She recites exact dates, locations, names of old friends, measurements of fabric. She describes scenes as clearly as if they’d just occurred.

Sonia Shin was born in the northern city of Pyongyang in 1928, back when Korea was under the colonial rule of Japan. Her father worked as a court clerk for the Japanese colonial administration, while her mother was a homemaker. She had an older sister who was academically astute and would eventually marry into Pyongyang’s elite class. Sonia, however, was, in her own words, “naive and mediocre. Obedient.” She found a supporter in her own grandmother, who would say, “The little one has it better in the end,” when referring to her. Sonia has repeated this phrase under her breath for 90 years.

In 1947 Sonia was married off by her father—a traditional custom at that time—to my grandfather, KwangDal Suh. Kind and gentle, KwangDal was from the city of Incheon, in the south of Korea, and had traveled to Pyongyang to work on a railroad project connecting the two cities. They spent the first year of their marriage in Pyongyang so he could be closer to work, but eventually, they decided to move to Incheon in 1948 to be closer to his family.

The move came at a pressing time in Korea’s history. The Korean peninsula was politically fracturing in the post–World War II years, as communism and democracy tore the population in half. Armies from the Soviet Union occupied the north half of the country while American troops were in the south, and the 38th parallel created the de facto border. The dividing line was supposed to be temporary.

Sonia had one child and was visibly pregnant with her second at the start of her journey to Incheon. Before she left, her mother sewed cash into her clothing, should she need it. Her father also hired a travel broker, whose job was to help her complete the journey without being arrested or stopped. As she and KwangDal awaited a train to take them south, Sonia had just a few minutes to say goodbye to her mother and father. She told them she didn’t want to go, that she would miss them.

“I had no idea what was ahead of me,” she remembers.

Her father turned and gently pushed her back onto the train. She would never see her parents, or her home, again.

The journey to the south was treacherous. The first leg, from Pyongyang to Namchon, was by train. From there, Sonia, her husband, and a group of refugees, led by the broker, traveled by foot. She strapped her toddler son, JungDuk, to her back. They hiked along ridgelines and through dense forests to a ferry on the Ryesong River, which they caught after crossing quicksand-like mudflats. They had to complete the muddy crossing in the dark, and bullets from border guards whizzed by her head as they trudged through the muck. Sonia nearly drowned in the crossing.

“My foot got stuck in the mud and I thought my baby and I were going to die,” she says. “Someone in the group heard me crying and pulled me out by my shoulder. I still remember how painful it was.”

They evaded border guards who lined the roads, ready to shoot at anyone seen moving across the boundary. They completed the final leg to Kaesong, in modern day North Korea, on foot, and then traveled by train and car to Incheon. They were safe.

But they weren’t entirely happy. Sonia and KwangDal found work in his family’s herbal medicine shop. Sonia performed the daily manual tasks of grinding roots and other plants into medication. She did not like the work. After six months, she told KwangDal that she wanted a different life away from his family.

“My husband [had] told me his parents were pharmacists. This wasn’t a pharmacy, it was a traditional medicine shop where they wanted me to pound roots all day long,” she says. “I was not about to spend the rest of my life doing that kind of physically demanding work for my in-laws.”

After weeks of arguing, KwangDal relented. They moved into a boarding house where they rented one room to sleep in and another for work. Their first job was to repair sewing machines and other mechanical equipment. KwangDal was a natural tinkerer, and he loved disassembling machines, fixing their broken parts, and reassembling them. He even innovated with the leftover parts, building prototypes, including a makeshift loom and a cotton candy spinning machine.

Eventually, KwangDal and Sonia started a repair business. They added a secondary business selling cotton candy from the machine KwangDal built by hand.

But being business owners came with its own stresses. KwangDal was terrible with money, often donating his time to clients without charging them enough for his duties. Undercharging customers frustrated Sonia. But with the cotton candy machine, she got an opportunity to run her own business selling sweets to kids.

“That was the pivotal point,” Grandma says. “A young naive woman became a business-minded woman. As it turned out, I had a business mind that had been hibernating.”

It’s dinnertime in Seoul, and the three of us sit at a small table and attempt to finish off the fish my grandmother has made for us. In Korea, when an older person places food onto your plate, not only are you supposed to eat it, you also have to show immense gratitude that they gave it to you. In previous generations, when food was scarce, this is how the older family members treated their kin, by picking out the best pieces of meat, or the most symmetrical looking pieces of kimchi, and placing it on your plate—or even onto your spoon. But Spring and I are too full to finish the meal. Grandma spoons more fish onto my plate. “Yellow croaker is good for your brain,” she tells me.

“Hal-money, you didn’t eat enough, you should eat this last one,” I say as I move the fish to her plate. Eventually, Spring finishes off the meal. Throughout dinner, Spring has shown Grandma old photos on her iPad. Grandma had recited addresses of the old factory and names of people she hadn’t seen in decades. I wonder: maybe if I eat enough yellow croaker, I’ll have a memory like hers when I’m 99.

Sonia and KwangDal’s first factory was located in Seoul, which, in the early fifties, was a city of transition and turmoil. War between North Korea and South Korea officially broke out in 1950, and during three years of battles and bloodshed, Seoul changed hands four times and was decimated by bombs and shells.

Sonia and KwangDal departed Incheon for Seoul in 1951. Millions of Koreans had been displaced as the city tried to rebuild during and after the war. Using their earnings from selling cotton candy and repairing machinery, plus some of the cash that had been sewn into her clothing years before, my grandparents purchased a partially burned, two-story textile factory in the heart of Seoul.

“We saved enough from the cotton candy business to buy the property, all while supporting our fast-growing family,” Grandma said. By this time, they had four children.

Inside the burned-out factory sat several metal looms for weaving cotton. KwangDal set to work repairing them. Cotton had been the fabric of Korean society for centuries, ever since the Chinese had introduced it to the peninsula in the 14th century. Most garments were made of simple, loom-woven cotton.

Ever the tinkerer, KwangDal iterated on his original loom design from Incheon. He wanted a device that could make cotton garments have the softness of cotton candy. Instead of spinning sugar, he used metal bristles to scratch tightly woven cotton fabric. The cotton strands, when pulled apart, would stand on their ends, making the piece of fabric fuzzy, soft, and warm. This process is still used today to manufacture cotton flannel.

Building the machine took several months, but after KwangDal finalized his design, he took it to a metalworking shop and had three identical devices built. In 1958, he installed the four machines in his factory and set to work producing brushed cotton flannel fabric. The textile was a hit.

“We made so much money that the bank had to drive to our factory and load the cash into their vehicle and count it at the bank,” Grandma said.

Within a year, the looms were pumping out 4,800 yards of cotton flannel every 24 hours. They stored the fabric on massive rolls in the factory. And, as quickly as they could churn it out, it was purchased by clothing makers across the city.

Sonia and KwangDal named their company Baeekyang Gimo, which loosely translates to “White Lamb Flannel.” While KwangDal operated the machinery, Sonia ran the business. She became the bookkeeper and inventory clerk, the quality-control manager and logistics coordinator, as well as the HR department. Perhaps most important, however: Sonia was head of the company’s sales department. She processed every order, negotiated contracts with clients, and signed off on deals.

“I had to see things for myself,” she said.

As the company grew—by 1959 it employed 50 people—Sonia also took over the finances. While KwangDal was a brilliant engineer, he was terrible with money.

“He spilled money everywhere he went,” she said. “He couldn’t walk past a beggar without emptying whatever he had on him.”

Sonia, now 31 years old, blossomed as a business owner and entrepreneur. Most of Baeekyang Gimo’s customers were wholesalers and garment manufacturers throughout Korea. Sonia took orders from small businesses in Seoul’s Pyeonghwa Market in the Dongdaemun district and sold large orders to garment factories in Daegu. Even the Korean military was using their flannel in standard-issue uniforms. Baeekyang Gimo was profitable in its first year. By the societal standards of the time, Sonia’s work was almost unheard of. Women in postwar Korea worked hard, but they toiled in the background: in fields, markets, or family shops where a husband or father was the face and the owner. Confucian tradition places a woman at the bottom of a social pyramid: under her father, her husband, and even her son, for life.

Placing a woman at the head of an industrial operation violated social traditions. The only reason Sonia was tolerated in her position was that, on paper and in the public eye, the business belonged to KwangDal. Sonia could run everything as long as everyone agreed that Baeekyang Gimo belonged to him.

My grandmother’s story has had a tremendous impact on my own sense of identity in the outdoor industry, where I’ve spent most of my professional career. I first attended Outdoor Retailer (OR), the official industry meetup for outdoor industry professionals, in 2010 in Salt Lake City. I was employed by an e-commerce company in the outdoor space, and was eager to get to know an industry I had long been wanting to join. I wore a three-piece suit—attire that would have been fine at a normal trade show. But at OR, I stuck out. Nobody wore formalwear. Everyone was clad in flannel.

That wasn’t the only reason I stood out. As I walked the showroom floor, I saw very few people of color, aside from the show’s director, Kenji Haroutunian, who later became a mentor and, now, colleague in my current venture.

Over the years, I came to understand many truths about the industry. Industry leaders love to talk about diversity and inclusion, and in many cases, they do follow these guidelines. These days, the people who are featured in marketing campaigns are diverse. The entry-level ranks are finally starting to get more diverse. Even the crowds you see at trailheads are less white than they were decades ago.

But the leadership in the outdoor industry and the people owning these brands haven’t really changed. For 15 years, I’ve been asking myself if I’m crashing a party I wasn’t invited to. So in 2015, I launched my own event, an outdoor conference called Outdoor Media Summit (OMS). Since then, it’s become the largest gathering of media in the outdoor industry. It turns out my grandmother’s prophecy was spot-on: bootstrapping a business has required me to become extremely frugal. It’s been a grind, and I’ve only recently been able to pay myself a livable wage.

But money was never the hardest part. My face was. Once, at a fly-fishing industry trade show, someone made a highly offensive racist joke to a group of people, and everyone in the circle laughed at me. To this day, I still consider changing my public-facing name to “Ian” in hopes that my email response rates improve.

Not long ago, the industry’s leadership decided that OMS didn’t belong on its list of recommended trade events. We’ve earned the right to be on that calendar. Yet these are the kinds of things that make me wonder if I can survive in an environment that is so overwhelmingly white-run, if I can overcome the structural barriers ingrained in our industry.

My perspective changed after spending time with my grandmother and unpacking the details of her history. I learned how she spent nearly three decades building a business in a country that didn’t want women at the helm. My grandmother didn’t have the luxury of asking whether she belonged—she just worked, because stopping was never an option. Yes, my grandmother lived in a different time, in a different country, and faced deeper discrimination than anything I’ve encountered in the outdoor industry. But hearing her story instilled in me a sense of perseverance that, otherwise, I may not have developed on my own.

Learning my grandmother’s story also taught me that I indeed do belong in this industry. I no longer view myself as an outsider, the one guy in a suit in a sea of flannel shirts. You see, those shirts—worn by almost everyone walking the showroom floor—are made from a fabric woven into my own family history. My grandmother produced countless yards worth of brushed cotton flannel, which made its way into thousands of shirts across the globe.

My grandmother’s sedan rolls through the streets of Seoul’s Sindang-dong neighborhood, past soaring apartment high-rises and modernized commercial buildings. Inside, I sit packed into the car next to my cousin, mother, sister, and grandmother. We’ve come to Singdang-dong to try and find the old factory that Hal-money and her husband operated. Our mission is to snap a photograph of the five of us in front of the building. But alas, we cannot find it.

We circle the crowded city blocks, driving past throngs of people and modern buildings. It’s been 30 years since my grandmother was last in Singdang-dong, and the neighborhood has completely changed. The factory has been enveloped by a city that no longer resembles the one that she and KwangDal helped rebuild from rubble 70 years ago.

“Just drive around,” Grandma keeps saying. “There’s an entrance somewhere. Circle the block.”

We park, look at the map, and then continue driving three different times. Each time, we get out of the car and wait for Grandma to follow us. But each time, she finds a reason to stay in her seat. No, this isn’t the correct block. Let’s check another street. She won’t get out of the car.

After a few stops, our situation becomes obvious: We’re not lost. My grandmother is simply stalling.

But we are persistent, and my grandmother realizes that we aren’t going to give up. Eventually we coax her out of the car and into her wheelchair. And as she settles into the chair, she looks deep into my eyes. “It’s because I’m embarrassed,” she says.

It takes me a few minutes to understand her emotion. Decades ago, these city streets had been the site of my grandmother’s lifelong triumph. She had been the boss. Everyone walking the sidewalks had known her, respected her, and worked with her. Now, she is an old woman in a wheelchair, pushed along by her grandchildren. To her, everyone was staring at her, and not in a good way.

The turning point in this transition had occurred in 1982. That year, KwangDal had turned 60 and decided he was ready to retire. Per Korean cultural norms, he handed Baeekyang Gimo to his eldest son, KwangDuk, and walked away to tinker with his next project, an electric car endeavor commissioned by the South Korean government.

There was no discussion about whether or not Sonia would simply take over the business from her husband. KwangDuk was the eldest male of the family and the only boy among nine children. By societal rules, he was the next in line.

Instead, Sonia retired the same day as KwangDal, but not because she was tired or ready to walk away from her position. She simply gave up the oversight, the management position, and her job inking contracts. This was despite the fact that she had financed the business in the early days with her money from selling cotton candy and with the money sewn into her own garments.

Baeekyang Gimo did not last long under KwangDuk’s direction. Eventually it shuttered amid tough financial times, and he sold the building.

I ask my grandmother how the business would have continued, had she stayed at the helm. She tells me that a woman approaching 60 deciding to run her husband’s business would have been considered “unsightly” by Korean society.

“I haven’t even thought about it,” she says. “What’s lost is lost.”

After some searching, we eventually locate the address of the old factory. The building was long ago transformed into residential real estate that blends seamlessly into the neighborhood. It’s just another apartment, housing some of the 10 million people who live in Seoul.

I stand behind my grandmother’s wheelchair in an effort to get a photo of us in front of the old factory. My sister and I are trying to get her to look at the camera, but she’s unable to hear anything we’re saying. The memories of this place are flooding her attention. Eventually my sister gives up and snaps a photo of just my grandmother. In it, she is reliving the years when all this was hers.

Spring B. Han, Mary Kim, and SangHyun Kim contributed to this story.

#8274. ‘Please Help Me.’ A Hiker’s Desperate Text Led to Her Dramatic Rescue on a Famed Colorado Trail

A Black Hawk helicopter. (Photo: patty_c / Getty Images)

A desperate text to 911 turned into a dramatic rescue in the Colorado high country after an early-season storm trapped a 37-year-old solo hiker in thigh-to-hip-deep snow on the Four Pass Loop on October 30.

The Four Pass Loop is a popular but rugged 27-mile route that travels through the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness while gaining about 8,000 feet of elevation. Most hikers tackle the route as a backpacking trip over the course of two to four days.

According to a release by Crested Butte Mountain Rescue (CBMR), the ordeal began when Pitkin County Emergency Dispatch received a text to 911 that read “please help me.” Before calling for help, the hiker had texted a family member that her phone’s battery was down to 10 percent. Shortly after that initial call for help, emergency services lost contact, leaving them with only a single coordinate to guide their search. With temperatures dipping into the teens, CBMR reached out to CareFlight of the Rockies to coordinate air support. The team also dispatched a ground team, reasoning the elevation and mountain conditions could make landing a helicopter impossible.

By 11 p.m., the helicopter team located the hiker attempting to climb over Frigid Air Pass, but they were unable to make a safe landing to extract her from the scene.

About four hours later, the first two party members of the CBMR ground team reached the pass and located the hiker struggling to make it over the pass near where the helicopter had spotted her. But neither air support nor ground support could reach the hiker: “The steep terrain, deep snow, and darkness presented legitimate avalanche concerns,” CBMR wrote. “The first two rescuers initially attempted to descend toward the subject but encountered concerning conditions. Recognizing the potential hazard, they made the decision to wait for the remaining team members before committing to the descent.”

When the remaining members of the CBMR ground team reached the pass at about 5:30 a.m., two team members descended somewhere between 300 to 400 feet to reach the hiker. Upon their arrival, they realized that her condition was potentially life-threatening since she was no longer ambulatory, she had cold-related injuries, and was showing signs of hypothermia. The rescue team placed the hiker in a bivy before realizing that the best way to extract her would be via a helicopter hoist rescue.

CBMR coordinated with the Colorado Search and Rescue Association (CSAR), who contacted the Colorado Army National Guard to dispatch a UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter from Gypsum. A helicopter lowered a rescue technician to the hiker, then hoisted both party members into the helicopter.

After the hiker was successfully transferred to the airport and flown to the UCHealth Burn and Frostbite Center in Aurora, the National Guard returned to the Frigid Air Pass to remove the remaining rescuers due to the pass’s dangerous conditions.

In the wake of the incident, CBMR reminded hikers to take extra precautions before heading into the backcountry since high-altitude rescues can be dangerous for rescuers, too. (“So throw that extra puffy in your pack!” the team wrote.)

The team noted that rescue came at the end of a particularly challenging week for CBMR, which responded to three incidents, two of them fatal.
