#8273. After an Accident Left Her Paralyzed, Brittany Chadbourne Found a Way to Keep Climbing

“I'm the giant asterisk at the end of ‘climbing is dangerous.'" —Brittany Chadbourne (Photo: Maya Silver)

For some climbers, campusing—climbing with only your upper body—is a training strategy. For Utah climber Brittany Chadbourne, it’s her only choice.

I met Chadbourne in early October at Momentum Millcreek, one of the gyms she regularly visits in the Salt Lake Valley. She pulled onto a V3 boulder problem angled at least 45 degrees, working her way to the top and back down in about a minute. Then she eased herself into her wheelchair, hardly out of breath.

Bouldering carries particular risks for Chadbourne. Because she can’t control how she lands, a fall could cause additional injuries, including damage to the rods in her spine. These days, she saves harder climbing for ropes and sticks to boulder problems she knows she can safely descend. Afterward, I belayed the 28-year-old on a 5.11c. Her powerful shoulders, arms, and back carried her up the route without the use of her legs or lower abs.

Four years ago, a routesetting accident left Chadbourne paralyzed from the belly button down, so she had to find a new way to practice the sport she loves. “I’ve always wanted to be in Climbing Magazine,” Chadbourne told me. “But I thought it would be for something way cooler than a V2 boulder. I’m still proud that I’m continuing with it and being positive, or at least as positive as I can be.”

Chadbourne discovered climbing while in school at Weber State University in Ogden, Utah, and really got into it in 2020. But before she started climbing, while growing up in northern Utah, she was a gymnast who had heard plenty of stories about gymnasts breaking their necks and becoming paralyzed.

“It was something that I always feared and tried to avoid,” Chadbourne says of paralysis.

On November 22, 2022, that fear became reality.

When Chadbourne began working as a routesetter in September of that year at The Front in Ogden, routesetters used a pull-through system of static lines, an alpine butterfly knot, and quickdraw anchors to access the wall. Chadbourne says the setup made her nervous from the start. She worried the knot could slip through the quickdraw carabiners. And the system differed from the one she’d used while routesetting at Weber State University.

“I was pretty new to all of it. So I was just like, ‘If this is what you guys have been using, obviously it’s safe. I’m sure it’s fine.’ Obviously, it wasn’t fine.”

Not long after she started, Chadbourne and The Front have stated that another routesetter reattached the wrong side of the rope when they were lowering and fell from the wall. According to both The Front and Chadbourne, the climber wasn’t seriously injured. After the accident, The Front retired the system and hosted trainings to get all routesetters up to speed on the new standards. Eddie Morillas, the gym’s director of routesetting, told Climbing via email that an updated fall-protection plan took effect on October 18, 2022, removing the alpine butterfly setup.

Under the new standard, Morillas explained that routesetters “are only permitted to gain initial access to anchors and remove working lines while on belay or connected to an autobelay unit, where applicable.” He added that Chadbourne attended two training sessions on the new standard before her accident.

According to Chadbourne, the head routesetter that day instructed her to use the alpine butterfly setup. The Front confirmed this, stating in an email to Climbing: “Our understanding is that the routesetter in charge let Brittany use the alpine butterfly system, which went against The Front’s fall protection plan and the training every setter on the team had completed.”

The precise cause of Chadbourne’s fall remains uncertain. Morillas told Climbing that The Front’s investigation found her knots were tied correctly, but that she pulled the rope in the wrong direction, preventing the knot from cinching around the anchor. According to The Front, the knot temporarily caught in the anchor before slipping through as Chadbourne moved up the rope.

Chadbourne says she followed the head routesetter’s instructions when setting up her static line correctly and had a coworker double-check it. Near the top of the wall, as she slid her ascender upward, she felt the rope go slack. She believes the knot slipped through the quickdraws, just as she’d feared.

“I immediately knew that I was falling,” she says. “So I just closed my eyes and fell 30 feet.”

When Chadbourne hit the ground, her left leg took most of the impact. She shattered her tibia and fibula, and suffered a burst fracture of her T12 vertebra and compression fractures at her C7, T5, and T7 vertebrae. The fall left her paralyzed from the belly button down.

Chadbourne says she receives workers’ compensation benefits that cover her medical expenses and equipment, including wheelchairs. She has chosen not to pursue a lawsuit, saying she was already overwhelmed by the aftermath of the accident and didn’t believe legal action would change what had happened.

Initially, Chadbourne felt embarrassed that her accident happened in a gym rather than outdoors. She’d spent years caving, exploring abandoned mines, and climbing outside without serious injury, only to suffer a life-altering fall inside a gym.

But that embarrassment didn’t diminish her desire to climb.

“I pretty much knew immediately that I would go back into climbing,” Chadbourne says. “Even as I was being loaded onto the helicopter to go to the hospital.” She didn’t know a lot about paraclimbing, but she figured there must be people out there climbing without their legs. “Campusing is a thing, so I’m sure somebody’s doing it,” she recalls thinking.

After two months in the hospital and another month adjusting to her new normal at home, Chadbourne’s doctor cleared her to climb. But her first time back on belay was “pretty rough.” She made it about 10 feet off the ground, partially hoisted up by her belayer. At first, she couldn’t climb high enough to experience the fear she’d felt during her fall. But as she grew stronger and began climbing higher, Chadbourne admits some of the fear came back.

Chadbourne still has days when she cries about her injury, sometimes even while climbing.

“Day to day, my life is just as hard now as it was four years ago [when I was first injured],” she adds. “I’m just doing more.” And she is. She’s traveling more, training more, and trying things she once thought were out of reach, including becoming an ambitious competitive climber.

Before the accident, Chadbourne loved technical slab climbing. Now, without the use of her legs or lower abdomen, she competes in the AL1 paraclimbing classification, also known as seated climbing.

In 2024, just two years after her injury, Chadbourne made Team USA. She earned bronze in the women’s AL1 competition at the 2025 Paraclimbing National Championships and silver in 2026.

But she found herself in a small competitive field. With so few women in the AL1 category, Chadbourne often faced just one or two other athletes. She and fellow paraclimber Carlie Cook advocated for mixed-gender AL1 competition, which would allow women and men to compete against each other. In March 2025, the International Federation of Sport Climbing released updated paraclimbing guidelines permitting mixed-gender competition in the category.

Competing against a larger field has made the sport more exciting for Chadbourne. “If it was just women, it would be like three or four of us in the entire world,” she says. “So to be able to compete against 20-plus people is really exciting. And it makes me want to beat the men!”

Now, Chadbourne has her sights set on making a World Cup final one day. She’s also working to bring more athletes with paraplegia, especially women, into the sport. One day, she hopes there will be enough female competitors to support a separate women’s category.

But there’s another stage Chadbourne hopes to compete on someday: the Paralympics.

“When I had heard rumors that [paraclimbing] was going to be in the LA Games, I got really excited,” Chadbourne recalls. But like many paraclimbing categories, AL1 was excluded from climbing’s Paralympic debut at the Los Angeles 2028 Games.

Chadbourne hopes that will change for the 2032 Paralympics in Australia. In the meantime, she’s also training in Nordic skiing and biathlon, with ambitions of making Team USA in both sports.

For Chadbourne, staying busy is one way of coping with the difficult days. “The busier you are, your brain just forgets to be sad,” she says.

“Continual motion builds on itself,” she adds. “I don’t really have any other choice but to just keep on going.”

Chadbourne’s momentum has carried into her work with other climbers. Between competitions and training, she teaches climbing and continues to set routes at Weber State University.

There, she’s become an advocate for safe routesetting and climbing practices, encouraging climbers to ask questions about systems before trusting them.

“I’m the giant asterisk at the end of ‘climbing is dangerous,’” Chadbourne says about teaching college students. “I want to prepare them that this is a possibility, but then I prepare them to avoid it in as many ways as they can.”

The most important lesson Chadbourne underscores is to always speak up if you don’t understand how something works. No matter their experience level, Chadbourne wants all climbers to feel comfortable raising concerns and asking questions.

“I want them to feel like they have a voice.”

#8270. 5 Wellness Trends We’d Like to See Go Away

Fitness tracking can help take your training to the next level, but know when you're taking things too far. (Photo: SimpleImages / Getty)

Calin Van Paris has been writing about wellness for more than a decade. Here, she breaks down a handful of wellness hacks and trends that, though beneficial for some, many of us could do without.

Let’s talk about wellness trends. More specifically, let’s talk about our collective penchant for “optimizing” the human experience.

Being a person is not always easy. We’re all in bodies that are designed to decay, with minds that tend to run amok and emotions that can seem like they have brains of their own. It’s only natural to try to control what we can—and self-care provides what can seem like an ideal platform for the pursuit.

Routines that can support physical, emotional, and mental well-being fall under the ever-growing umbrella of “wellness.” But many wellness trends begin in a beneficial place and spiral out of control from there.

A growing corner of self-care fads is overly focused on tracking, streamlining, and pushing extremes. And anything that makes you feel inadequate or anxious is one we’d love to fade into the background.

Take what, if anything, really works for you from the below trends and then notice when it’s time to let it go.

The concept of “sleepmaxxing,” or maximizing the quality of your sleep, began swirling around social media a couple of years ago. Sleeping better is a trend we can get behind—but you don’t need expensive gadgets or high levels of anxiety to do it. More importantly, putting too much focus on your sleep habits has the potential to backfire, transforming a restful part of your day into a stressful one.

Good sleep is essential. Nicole Moshfegh, MD, clinical psychologist and author of The Book of Sleep, notes that proper (or inadequate) rest can affect your physical health and cognitive function, not to mention your mood. Sleep is meant to be restful. Relaxing. Restorative.

Your sleep routine should not be causing you additional stress. If habits like evening restorative yoga, breathwork, or less blue light after dark improve your sleep quality, maxx on! But should you find yourself agonizing over a sleep score or lying awake calculating how many minutes of rest you’re losing—both examples of orthosomnia, an obsession with achieving the optimal sleep score—know that you’ve lost the plot.

Dunking your body into cold water might sound refreshing—and for some of the population, it is! Cold plunging is a Nordic tradition that some say boosts mental clarity and resilience (again, you are willingly submerging yourself in cold water) and is thought to reduce post-workout muscle stiffness, fatigue, and more.

Still, you may want to pause before adopting the cold plunge as your new cure-all. One study suggests that using cold baths for muscle recovery may be more of a placebo effect than anything else, as parsed by longtime Outside columnist Alex Hutchinson. And for those in female bodies, some research suggests that over time, exposure to cold water can adversely affect the reproductive system, and there is no proven boon to female muscle recovery.

Between phone apps, smartwatches, and Bluetooth-connected rings, it’s never been easier to know exactly what’s going on in your body, at least on a biological level.

Certain smart gadgets, like the Pulse Mindfulness Ring, can act as a little buddy, helping you breathe deeply, commit to daily meditation, and focus. And when used correctly, the Oura Ring can also be a mindful companion.

The issue isn’t the tracking devices themselves, but how they’re being used. Just as putting too much stock in sleep scores can be considered an obsessive condition (again, orthosomnia), too much preoccupation with the information provided by wearable devices may negatively impact psychological well-being. For some—including those with eating or health disorders—this sort of constant tracking can serve as a trigger, increasing rigidity and anxiety around otherwise healthy habits.

In short, try taking your smart accessories off sometimes, just to see how you feel.

We live in a world where the breaking news about what’s going on in our minds and bodies—and, usually, what we’re lacking—is practically non-stop. And usually, there’s a supplement for that. According to one report, the global supplement market is projected to be worth $300 billion by 2028.

Supplementing becomes an issue when you’re adding to your stack before looking at your diet and other habits. Studies have shown that supplements and weight loss pills offer a perceived sense of invulnerability, ironically leading to poorer choices in nutrition and fitness habits.

Another more obvious issue is supplements offered with no scientific evidence to back up purported benefits. Not all supplements on the market are even FDA-approved; in fact, many are not.

But if your supplements are thoughtfully chosen and supplementing an existing healthy lifestyle, you’re probably on the positive side of this trend.

The internet can make your life feel like a reality show. And if you make your living as an influencer, maybe it sort of is. But even with audience perception, brand deals, and showmanship at stake, your health and wellness routine can and should make you feel good.

At its core, self-care is for you. If sharing your journey feels beneficial for you and for them, go ahead. But when your wellness practices become more about the performance of tending to yourself and less about actually doing things that bring you peace and healing, you may want to reconsider your approach.

#8269. Forget the Florida Trail, These 6 Hikes Reveal The Wild Variety of The Sunshine State

The jungle foliage can get thick along many of these Florida Trails (Photo: Boogich via Getty)

Florida may be best known for its beaches, theme parks, and sprawling wetlands, but if you are willing to venture inland, you will find a surprisingly diverse set of hikes in an equally varied landscape. Trails along sandy ridges, shady hardwood hammocks that shelter wildlife, and deep ravines providing a welcome escape from the subtropical heat are scattered across the state. And you don’t even have to commit to a months-long thru-hike to experience them.

From ancient dunes to forested ravines, these six all-season, pet-friendly trails offer a reason to lace up your hiking boots and explore the wilder side of the Sunshine State. They are open from dawn to dusk, and some even allow camping for a small fee if you want to make your hike an overnight trip.

Mileage: 2.5 miles Location: 1600 Twigg St, Palatka Entrance fee: $5 per vehicle, $2 for pedestrians and bicycles.>Highlight: The trail is especially beautiful during azalea season, from late January through March, when the park’s flowering shrubs explode in splashes of pink, red, and white.

This part of Florida is unlike anything you’ll find along the coast, with steep paths covered with ancient root systems of Azalea bushes. The 2.5-mile Azalea Trail at Ravine Gardens State Park is a short but challenging loop that takes hikers along narrow dirt paths, over exposed roots, and down historic stone staircases. There are two suspension bridges over a spring-fed creek that flows through a shaded forest of ferns, mosses, and native trees.

Mileage: 39 miles Location: 13208 SR 72, Sarasota Entrance fee: $6 per vehicle, $5 camping permit per night.>Camping: Three campgrounds with 90 sites with water and electric hookups (check water conditions before camping) and six primitive campgrounds with three sites each Highlight: You may spot wild turkeys and alligators, so be sure to stay on the trail at all times, especially through the open prairies.

Myakka River State Park, just east of Sarasota, is one of Florida’s largest and most ecologically diverse state parks. The Myakka trail is a roughly 39-mile loop. It winds through pine flatwoods, oak and palm hammocks, open prairie, and wetlands. Several shorter day hikes like the 5.4-mile Bee Island and 8.7-mile Honore branch out from the main trail. Those are great alternatives if you don’t want to stay overnight.

Mileage: 5.8 miles Location: 13201 San Felasco Parkway, Alachua Entrance fee: $4 per vehicle, $2 for pedestrians and bicycles; dogs are not allowed in some sections frequented by birders.>Highlight: Birding is very popular here as species like the Wood Thrush and Red-headed woodpecker thrive in the park’s varied ecosystems.

The San Felasco Hammock Preserve State Park is home to one of the only remaining hardwood forests in Florida. The Spring Grove Trail is a 5.8-mile loop that passes through a variety of habitats and ecosystems within the park and is a great reminder that Florida’s natural diversity isn’t limited to its famous swamps and coastlines. This trail passes through shady hardwood hammocks, pine forests, and sandy hills. There are also both dry and water-filled sinkholes, adding interesting terrain features along the way. You can also hike a shorter 2.8-mile loop up to the Hammock cutoff.

Mileage: 7.1 miles Location: 5298 Michigan Ave, Sanford Entrance fee: None. Highlight: Explore a swampy jungle that is teeming with Florida wildlife of all shapes and sizes.

If you’re looking for that classic, marshland, jungle Florida experience, with rugged hiking and tons of wildlife, look no further than the Black Bear Wilderness Area. This 7.1-mile loop trail takes you deep into lowland habitats like wet prairie, hydric hammock, and cypress swamp. The trail is challenging in spots, due to roots, boulders, and muddy sections. Bugs and humidity are to be expected, but it’s worth putting up with those for the chance to see some wildlife. Hikers often encounter river otters, alligators, white-tailed deer, tons of bird life, and, if it’s quiet enough, even black bears.

Mileage: 5.8 miles Location: 4335 Firetower Road, Haines City Entrance fee: Free; $5 camping permit per night.>Highlight: It is home to 21 rare plants and 31 animals, some of which are not found anywhere else in the world. You might see scrub morning glory, pygmy fringe tree, and cutthroat grass, along with protected animal species including the Florida scrub-jay and gopher tortoise.

The Allen David Broussard Catfish Creek Preserve State Park is located along the Lake Wales Ridge. It includes Florida’s most unusual ecosystems—an ancient shoreline and sandbar dating back almost 350,000 years. The park protects more than 8,000 acres of scrub, sandhill, and flatwoods habitat. The Catfish Creek Trail is a 5.8-mile loop that is mostly exposed with little to no shade. This trail crosses a lot of sandy terrain, which can make even a relatively short walk feel strenuous. Be prepared with plenty of water and consider bringing your own shade.

Mileage: 7-13 miles Location: Torreya State Park Loop Parking Lot, Bristol Entrance fee: $3 vehicle entrance fee; $5 backcountry camping feeHighlight: Striking cliff formation and primitive camping for backpackers.

This hike follows the Apalachicola River and offers some of the most challenging terrain in this part of Florida. It can be completed as a 7-mile single loop if you want a shorter dayhike. Or, extend the hike by adding the second loop. It connects with the first and nearly doubles the distance to 13 miles. In total, you’ll gain a whopping 1,646 feet of elevation. If you want to make this an overnight adventure, there are three different primitive campsites along the trail. Campsites require a $5 backcountry camping fee and must be reserved at Torreya State Park or by phone at 850-643-2674.

#8266. 3 Expert-Approved Exercises to Build Power in Your Climbing

There’s a famous quote by Wolfgang Güllich, the German climber who invented the word “redpoint”: “There’s no such thing as too much power.” As a coach, I often see and hear this in the climbing community. I agree with the sentiment, but I think that by and large, power has been misused, misunderstood, and poorly trained by the vast majority of climbers.

Firstly, I think it’s misused and misunderstood because the general climbing population doesn’t grasp that strength and power are not the same thing. Secondly, as a result of this, the training methods climbers use when they’re trying to improve their power are often wrong.

So let’s start with a very simple explanation of strength and power. I’m also going to have to bring speed into the equation, as this gives context for how these all sit on a spectrum. Afterwards, we’ll look at some of the main things I think climbers are getting wrong when doing their own power training, how to solve these issues, and some examples of simple but effective ways to train power.

The reason that power matters so much in climbing is because not all moves are possible—or most efficient—when executed at a slower pace without speed and power. Trying to just use strength (slower movement) could mean that you’ll either fail on the move or you’ll climb inefficiently using excess energy, which ultimately means no send!

An easy example of this is completing a super long hard move. With just strength, we’re only able to lock to a certain depth of shoulder position and throw or deadpoint to a limited distance. Add in power and you’ll cover way more distance and end up latching that hold.

One additional note on the “power endurance” term: This one is a bit of a misnomer which caused us many issues over the years at Lattice, mainly because power endurance does not actually use power. It should have been named “strength endurance,” as that’s what it really is.

Strength is how much force you can produce. Think of a max hang on a small edge, or a heavy weighted pull-up. The movement is slow, but the force is high.

Speed is how fast you can move when there’s very little resistance. Think of how quickly you can move your hand from one hold to the next with only the weight of your own arm to overcome.

Power sits between the two. It’s force multiplied by speed, so you only have lots of it when you can produce a relatively high force quickly. Dynos, band-assisted pull-ups, and latching holds at the end of a deadpoint all fit into this category.

Think of it as a sliding scale. Heavy and slow climbing is at one end, light and fast climbing is at the other, and power is in the middle. You can’t produce your maximum force and your maximum speed at the same time, so where you train on that scale matters and I think climbers are continually getting this wrong.

None of this means strength doesn’t matter. Strength is the foundation of power. A stronger and bigger muscle can produce more force at every speed, so if you’re relatively weak, getting stronger will improve your power more than anything else. This is a really important point to grasp, for those of you who haven’t yet developed a foundation of high strength. Once you’re reasonably strong, though, specific power training starts to give you more benefits. As a rough guide, if you can’t do a pull-up with an extra 35-50% of your bodyweight, strength should be the main focus still (even though power training in addition is still useful). Once you’re above this threshold, power training should become increasingly important.

This is the big one. Power is extremely sensitive to fatigue and it drops well before you actually feel tired. Despite this, many climbers I see at the gym do their “power work” at the end of a session, after an hour of board climbing or a set of endurance drills. Unfortunately, if every rep is slower than your best, you’re practicing being slow. Power work goes at the start of the session, straight after a thorough warm-up, when you’re fresh. Prioritise this timing over everything.

Linked laps on the campus board, long sets of explosive pull-ups, and circuits of “powerful” moves can be useful, but they’re all mostly power endurance, not power. Power training means low numbers of high-quality reps. Stop the set as soon as a rep is noticeably slower, shorter, or messier than the first.

Ninety seconds between sets isn’t enough. You need at least three minutes, sometimes more, for the systems that drive maximal efforts to recover. If it feels like you’re resting way more than you should and you’re slightly bored, you’re probably resting the right amount.

The intention to move as fast as possible is a large part of what drives the adaptation, even when the movement itself ends up slow. So remember, if you’re doing a power pull-up, even if only the first 20% of the pull is fast, that’s ok. You should put in full intent, with complete focus on speed for each pull, and you’ll find that’s what really counts.

Some climbers only hang, push, squeeze, and lift heavy. Others love to campus, jump, spin, and dyno. The best results come from working across the scale. Heavy strength work (for the foundation of power and speed) and explosive power work should be included in the same training block, with the emphasis shifting depending on what you need for your goals.

Below are three power exercises that work well. Pick one or two for a session, do them first, and remember to stop as soon as speed or quality reduces.

If your 1RM pull-up is greater than 160%, you may be able to do this at bodyweight.

Pull as fast as possible, aiming to get your chest as high as possible, almost as if you’re trying to roll into a muscle up. Do four sets of three, resting three minutes between sets. The faster you can complete each rep, the better, so generally use more assistance than you might think.

Always learn how to do this session on a comfortable hold and using your preferred grip type.

Using a hangboard edge (or a load cell, if you have one), pull as hard and as fast as you can for two to three seconds. Do four to eight reps, resting at least three minutes in between. This trains your ability to generate high force quickly, which is exactly what deadpoints need.

These can be done on holds, a hangboard, or a pull-up bar. The critical part is getting the height of the starting position right.

Using your chosen hold, you want to jump from the ground into the middle range of the pull-up motion, using the momentum from your lower body to assist in generating speed and power in the upper part of the pull. You’re jumping into the pull-up with your legs, and your arms and back are finishing off the pull at high speed as you’re already carrying momentum. Do four to eight reps, resting at least three minutes in between.

Train power like this two to three times a week when it’s your focus, and once or twice a week to maintain it the rest of the time. Don’t forget that power fades faster than strength when you stop training it, so it’s worth keeping a small amount in your plan all year round.

So back to Güllich: Is there such a thing as too much power? Probably not. But there’s definitely such a thing as too much fatigue, too much volume, and too little speed and intention when you’re trying to train it. Get strong first, train power fresh in mind and body, keep the quality high, and stop before it drops. I think you’ll be pretty happy with how you feel on the wall after just a couple of months of this.

At 1.8 ounces, this gossamer hoodless jacket is a reliable friend for mountain runners, fastpackers, and anyone who values velocity. Breathability is exceptional, which our tester confirmed after a full day of biking along the Grand Canyon’s South Rim.

First, understand you may have to compromise. While waterproof-breathable membranes are almost ubiquitous, most jackets prioritize waterproofing over breathability, or vice versa. Jackets that can weather a downpour without so much as wetting out may not breathe well, and those that breathe well may be better for scattered showers than the kind of rain that makes you start thinking about building an ark.

Pay attention not just to the breathability of the jacket itself, but to the venting options, too. Even the most breathable fabrics can’t dump heat as well as a set of pit zips or mesh-backed pockets that expose your underlayers to fresh air. Packability is more important than you might think, too: If you’re consistently hot, having a jacket that you can ball up and stick inside your pack without a second thought is a better move than carrying a heavy, bulky one.

Our lead testers for men’s and women’s rain jackets are Drew Zieff and Elizabeth Kwak. Our gear editors pulled these recommendations from their original testing notes and scores to recommend the best rain jackets for hikers who overheat.

#8261. Space Mirrors Promise Daylight in the Dark, But Rescue Teams Aren’t Convinced

A floodlight operated by Reflect Orbital illuminates the night sky. (Photo: Kern County Sheriff’s Office)

In the middle of a dark night on the foothills of Mt. Whitney, onlookers were suddenly flooded by a cone of light 3 miles wide by 10 miles long.

The source was a high-powered floodlight, placed nearby as part of a test exercise by a startup called Reflect Orbital. The Los Angeles-based company’s mission is to “launch the future of sunlight” by placing a swarm of mirrored satellites in low Earth orbit built to redirect sunlight anywhere on Earth on demand. The ground-based floodlight was designed to mimic that effect.

Among a wide range of use cases including agriculture, entertainment, and defense, the company claims rescue as one potential use of its tech in the coming years.

On a country road outside Lone Pine, California, a handful of seasoned rescue volunteers and public safety officials would find out how much — if any — a light field roughly the size of Manhattan and twice as bright as a full moon would improve their chances.

Phillip Cash, operations leader for China Lake Mountain Rescue Group, said his team arrived at the site with optimism.

“My team is largely scientists, engineers, technicians,” he told DarkSky International. “We live for this sort of stuff.”

Group leaders reported to the San Francisco Chronicle and DarkSky International that they envisioned very limited uses for the technology in rescue. They struggled with glare, saw little promise of benefit for helicopter crews, and realized the light could also shut off unexpectedly.

In the test, China Lake MRG and Inyo County SAR rehearsed standard search-and-rescue tasks twice — once in the dark, once under the big light. Crews ran grid searches, stretcher carries, and rope rigging.

Cash first noticed the light made it easier to move around on the ground. His peripheral vision was improved, he told DarkSky, and he didn’t have to worry about stepping in a hole.

But from there, the efficacy mostly faded.

Glare was an issue. While that may or may not be the case with a satellite as the source, Cash noted most rescuers already wear hats at night for this very reason. Limiting any light from the sky or ambient sources preserves night vision.

Another limiting factor of the test was that the organizers placed white pylons in the field as rescue targets, instead of the usual manikins. This created artificial reflectivity that helped Cash’s team find their marks more easily. But, he told DarkSky, his team realized the light could have a problematic effect on actual human subjects — especially anyone lost.

“They’re more likely to go, ‘Oh, look at all this light. Maybe I can find my way back now,’” he said.

Cash was also doubtful it would help SAR helicopter crews locate or navigate at night, noting they already use night vision as standard practice.

His takeaway: For the most part, it’s better to leave the daylight in the daytime.

“It’s not going to make a huge difference to wilderness search and rescue except in a few cases,” Cash told the Chronicle. “We’re pretty good at working at night already.”

Officials’ minds remain open to the technology. A spokesperson for the Kern County Sheriff’s Office told Backpacker that they intend to let SAR groups lead the way on any future implementation. That’s particularly the case with a team like China Lake MRG, a nonprofit that supports its equipment bills mainly through fundraising.

“Given the circumstances, if we needed it, it would definitely be something we would utilize,” said Lori Meza, Kern County Public Information Officer. “But we have no idea what it would cost.”

That price tag could be a real issue. While Reflect Orbital has not officially published any pricing information for its prospective services, Sky & Telescope reported that the company plans to charge around $5,000 per hour for its services, with constellations of multiple satellites — necessary to recreate the kind of bright conditions the team experienced — costing far more. (By comparison, an Airbus H125 helicopter, like the Kern County Sheriff’s Office operates, costs about $2,500 an hour to run, according to charter operator Craft.)

“Most search and rescue teams, at least in California, will not be able to afford it,” Cash told DarkSky. “They won’t even think about affording it. We cannot pay for that sort of thing.”

Emphasizing that any cost was still unknown, Meza said Kern County officials only buy equipment for SAR teams in limited cases. She gave the example of a purchase of vehicles several years ago.

“We do provide certain resources, and there might be an isolated case here or there,” she said. “But a purchase like a contracted service would be a new thing.”

She added that the Sheriff’s Office isn’t taking a position on the technology itself, and that they were grateful to be part of the test.

Other observers are less neutral. DarkSky International has functioned as a sort of public watchdog on Reflect Orbital, lobbying for what it sees as responsible development. Its five principles of outdoor lighting have been widely adopted, and published by the U.S. Department of Energy.

DarkSky sees the same gap in the technology for rescue as China Lake MRG — usefulness, which is also principle one of five.

“The first question is ‘is it needed?’” said Drew Reagan, DarkSky senior marketing and communications manager. “And in this case, the rescue groups found the need was pretty minimal.”

Many of the potential impacts of Reflect’s plan are unknown, because the government has allowed it to move forward with no environmental review.

If its plans become reality, the change in the night environment could be massive. The Federal Communications Commission has given the green light for Reflect to launch its first functional satellite. Its launch plan would place 50,000 in orbit by 2035. Even if they weren’t de facto floodlights, Reagan pointed out, the reflectivity of that many satellites alone would noticeably brighten the night sky everywhere on Earth.

“This represents a fundamentally new technology that will have a direct impact. Not only for the dark sky community or astrotourists, but for migratory birds, for insects,” Reagan said. “It’s not DarkSky’s goal to plunge the world into medieval darkness. We want to be part of these conversations. We just want to make sure we look before we launch.”

#8257. Baby Sign Language 101: Baby’s First Signs

Well before they utter their first words, infants as young as six months can learn to sign. Baby sign language is thought to reduce baby’s frustration levels, boost self-esteem, and bolster language development. And you don’t need to be an expert. Begin with three to five signs, saying the word as you sign it. Encourage other caregivers and siblings to join in. Then repeat, repeat, repeat. Your little one’s motor skills may not allow them to perfectly mimic the sign, so watch for hand gestures that indicate she’s trying, usually within two months of being introduced to it. Here are some great baby sign language starter signs.

Show your little one the sign for a person they know, like mommy, daddy, brother, grandma, or baby. It doesn’t matter if you plan to use mommy, mama, mother, or mom; the sign is the same — using an open palm with fingers spread, tap your thumb on your chin. For “daddy” and its variations, use the same hand position; only tap the forehead. Remember to point to the person as you sign.

Food is a great motivator. Teach your little eater the sign for their favorite food or the ones for eat, milk, or bottle. When Baby’s plate is empty, “more” and “all done” allow them to set the pace for the meal. To sign “more,” press the thumb and fingertips of each hand together, and then tap the fingertips of the two hands together several times. Look for baby to put their fists or palms together as they start to get the hang of this sign.

Animal signs are fun because they often mimic some aspect of the animal. Baby will love learning the signs for her beloved pet or for the animals around the neighborhood. Dog, cat, fish, and bird are all good candidates. You can even have a favorite stuffed animal act out the motions for its sign. The baby sign for “dog” is patting your hand to your hip, as if calling a dog. This is a slight modification from the American Sign Language version, which includes a snap that is too difficult for emerging motor skills.

It’s never too early to introduce your little bundle to being polite. “Please” is a great word to start with. Try this technique when it’s clear your baby desires something specific, like a toy or a drink, and he’s not upset or in any distress. Say that you will get it and ask if they can say “please,” demonstrating the sign as you do so. Then give them the item, regardless of whether they do the sign or not. Eventually the concept will begin to sink in, and they’ll be doing it on his own. With a flat hand and thumb extended, sign “please” by moving the palm of your hand in a circular motion in front of your chest.

Use the repetition of baby’s routine as an opportunity to teach her the signs of daily life. Learn “sleep” for naptime and bedtime. Let baby know it’s playtime by signing “play,” and then show her the sign for whatever you are playing with, be it a ball, blocks, or a book. The sign for “bath” mimics the act of washing. To do this sign, simply move both your fists up and down in front of your chest as if scrubbing it.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8252. 4 Quick Activities to Try If Your Kid Is Wired at Bedtime

As a parent, you probably know that bedtime can go two ways: one, your kid was so busy all day they’re exhausted and can’t wait to get that story and hit the pillow. Or two, they haven’t had a chance to expel the endless amounts of energy they store in their little bodies. The latter is where a normal nighttime routine can get tricky because that second wind is no joke. They’ll be jumping, singing, fidgeting, and doing everything they can to delay the inevitable “lights out” moment, meaning there’s even less time for you to binge a few episodes of your new favorite show.

If you’re dealing with a kid who’s wired at bedtime, there are a few things you can do to make the transition to dreamland easier. Mom and pediatric occupational therapist Courtney English recently shared a few of her favorite sensory activities that help kids calm down before bed, and they’re simple but effective. Her TikTok video shows what parents can do:

Dr. Megan Anna Neff writes for Neurodivergent Insights that “Proprioception plays a role in body awareness, self-regulation, coordination, posture, and the ability to focus.” Playing a short game of tag in their bedroom will allow kids to realize where they are at that very moment in time, helping them to center themselves and be present.

Massage is known to be a great way to receive proprioceptive input, and what English calls a sensory sandwich (putting your child between two pillows and pressing down) is a low-energy activity that’ll give their body what it needs to relax.

Vestibular input is another important factor for kids who are wired at bedtime. As Laura Petrix writes for the OT Butterfly, it’s “a network of parts in your inner ear that contribute to your sense of balance and coordination.” It allows our bodies to know when we’re falling, move in coordinated ways (like riding a bike), and know the right speed to walk around other people. The combination of singing and rocking helps to calm the vestibular system by providing auditory rhythm and linear movement.

This is another great type of massage or touch activity that provides proprioceptive input to the nervous system. Plus, it’s a great chance to get a few snuggles in there before they close their eyes.

These activities are no secret to occupational therapists, who use them often. In fact, English has offered other sensory activities that are appropriate for bedtime, including tossing around a weighted animal and doing the “clock move.” But they’re something we should all have in our back pockets next time we’ve got monkeys jumping on the bed.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8251. The First-Time Experiences Kids Will Never Forget in Citrus County

There’s something magical about watching your child experience something for the very first time. The wide eyes. The nervous excitement. The inevitable “Can we do that again?” And the stories they tell anyone who will listen long after you’ve unpacked the suitcases. In Citrus County, Florida, those moments are practically everywhere.

Welcome to Crystal River, Homosassa, Inverness and Floral City—a refreshingly wild side of the Sunshine State where first-time adventures come naturally. Here, kids can swim alongside gentle manatees, search the Gulf for their own dinner, explore underwater worlds and discover that sometimes the best adventures don’t require a screen, a schedule or even a ticket. It’s outdoorsy without requiring your family to be expert adventurers, educational without feeling like school and relaxed enough that you don’t need a vacation from your vacation.

An easy road trip from many Florida cities and an unexpected nature escape for families traveling from farther away, Citrus County is where your next family vacation can become a collection of unforgettable firsts.

Imagine the look on your child’s face when a 1,000-pound manatee glides through the water nearby. It’s the kind of moment that makes even the too-cool-for-everything tween forget to play it cool.

Crystal River is known as the Manatee Capital of the World, and it’s one of the few places in North America where families can swim with these gentle giants in their natural habitat. Book a certified tour with an outfitter like Explorida, where guides teach families the importance of respectful wildlife viewing, including the all-important “Manatee Manners.” Tours operate year-round, but winter is prime time for seeing larger numbers of manatees as they gather in the area’s warm springs.

Not ready to snorkel? Explorida also offers manatee-viewing eco cruises, so younger kids, grandparents and anyone who prefers staying dry can still experience the magic.

Why they’ll remember it: Because seeing a manatee in a book or aquarium is one thing. Sharing the water with one in the wild? That’s a story they’ll be telling for years.

For little explorers (and grandparents) who aren’t ready to jump into the water, the next best thing might be watching nature unfold right beneath their feet.

At Three Sisters Springs, a boardwalk winds around the crystal-clear spring complex, offering an incredible vantage point for spotting manatees during the winter months. The surrounding wetlands are also home to birds and other wildlife, turning an ordinary walk into an impromptu nature safari.

Give your kids a challenge: How many manatees can they spot? Can they find a mother and calf? What other animals can they discover along the way?

It’s stroller-friendly, wonderfully unhurried and proof that you don’t have to get wet to make a splash.

Why they’ll remember it: The thrill of spotting their first wild manatee all on their own, and the pride of being the one who shouts, “I SEE ONE!”

Forget searching for seashells on the beach. In Citrus County, kids can head underwater on a real-life treasure hunt and bring home something delicious.

During summer scalloping season, families venture into the shallow Gulf waters off Crystal River and Homosassa, armed with snorkels, masks and mesh bags, to search the seagrass for bay scallops. Think Easter egg hunt, except underwater. And instead of chocolate, the reward might end up on your dinner plate.

Never tried scalloping? That’s part of the fun. Guided excursions with operators like Explorida help beginners learn the ropes, with equipment, guidance and plenty of encouragement along the way. And the moment your child spots that first scallop hiding in the grass? Pure victory.

Why they’ll remember it: There’s something incredibly satisfying about finding your own food. Just wait until they proudly announce at dinner, “I caught that!”

Tinybeans tip: Scalloping is seasonal, typically July through September. Check current dates, regulations and tour availability before planning your adventure.

For kids who’ve never tried kayaking and paddleboarding, Citrus County offers a pretty spectacular introduction. Imagine pushing off from shore, dipping a paddle into clear spring water and realizing that, for the first time, you’re helping steer the adventure.

At Hunter Springs Park in Crystal River, families will find a freshwater swimming area, kayak launch, waterfront boardwalk, picnic spots and a playground. The spring water stays around 72°F year-round, and during cooler months, there’s even a chance of spotting a manatee.

Bring your own paddle craft or book with a local outfitter. Younger kids can ride along with an adult, while older children can take a more active role in navigating.

The best part? There’s no rush to get anywhere. Stop to watch a bird, look for fish beneath the surface or simply float and take it all in.

Why they’ll remember it: That first feeling of independence. The realization that they can help navigate a kayak, explore somewhere new and discover what’s around the next bend.

What if your kids could explore an underwater world without ever putting on a swimsuit? At Ellie Schiller Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park, they can. The park’s famous Fish Bowl Underwater Observatory lets visitors descend beneath the surface of the spring to watch fish and, when present, manatees swim past the windows. For kids, it’s a little like stepping inside a nature documentary.

Back above water, shady, stroller-accessible boardwalks lead past native Florida wildlife, including black bears, alligators, red wolves and Florida panthers. Daily manatee programs offer another opportunity to learn about these remarkable animals and why protecting their habitat matters.

It’s an ideal first introduction to Florida’s wild side, especially for families with younger children or anyone who prefers wildlife encounters on dry land.

Why they’ll remember it: Because the first time you see the underwater world from a fish’s point of view, you never look at the water quite the same way again.

Remember the first time you rode your bike somewhere that wasn’t your driveway or neighborhood? The freedom. The excitement. The feeling that you could go anywhere? That’s what makes the Withlacoochee State Trail such a great family adventure.

Stretching approximately 47 paved miles through forests, lakes and charming small towns, the trail is flat, scenic and easy to explore in family-sized sections. No one expects your six-year-old to conquer all 47 miles.

Start in downtown Inverness, where the trail passes through the Depot District, and let your kids help choose how far to ride. Along the way, keep an eye out for birds, turtles and other wildlife. When everyone starts asking about snacks, make The Train Station part of your plan for pizza, pretzels and a well-earned break.

Why they’ll remember it: Their first real biking expedition, complete with the satisfaction of going farther than they thought they could. Bonus points if they proudly tell everyone how many miles they conquered.

You can tell your kids mermaids aren’t real. Or you can take them somewhere that might make them question everything.

At Mertailor’s Mermaid Aquarium Encounter in Lecanto, live mermaids perform underwater alongside fish, rays and other marine life, creating a magical experience that feels straight out of a storybook. But there’s more here than mermaid magic. The indoor aquarium features over 20 exhibits, interactive touch tanks, sharks, stingrays and freshwater animals, giving curious kids plenty to explore.

For children ages nine and up, the separate Discover Mermaid experience takes things a step further, with the chance to put on a mermaid tail and monofin and learn to swim like one. It’s also a great rainy-day adventure or a welcome break from the Florida sunshine.

Why they’ll remember it: Because watching a mermaid swim with sharks is pretty unforgettable. But getting to be a mermaid for the first time? That’s next-level vacation bragging rights.

Not every unforgettable first requires an adrenaline rush. Sometimes it’s the first time your kids experience what it feels like to slow down.

Head to Homosassa for a waterfront meal at Crumps’ Landing, where palm trees, water views and laid-back Florida charm set the scene for a different kind of family dinner. No rushing to make a reservation across town. No squeezing in one more attraction. Just good food, waterfront views and time to talk about everything you’ve done together. Let the kids recap their favorite adventures while you watch the sky change colors over the water.

Why they’ll remember it: It may not be the meal they remember years from now, but they’ll remember the feeling: salty air, sunset skies and everyone together with nowhere else they need to be.

Remember when simply staying in a hotel felt like the most exciting thing in the world? Now imagine staying somewhere that puts you right in the middle of the action.

Paddletail Waterfront Lodge sits on King’s Bay in Crystal River, giving families easy access to the area’s most memorable experiences. With paddlecraft activities, manatee excursions, waterfront dining, a pool and complimentary hot breakfast, the lodge makes it easy to spend less time coordinating logistics and more time having fun. Rooms with refrigerators and microwaves, and select kitchenette options also make traveling with kids a little easier.

Wake up knowing that another adventure is waiting just outside.

Why they’ll remember it: Because when the place you stay is part of the experience, even the moments between activities become vacation memories.

Here’s a first that might surprise you: What if you gave your kids an entire afternoon to decide what the family does? No packed itinerary. No racing from one attraction to another. No pressure to squeeze every last minute out of your vacation.

One of the best things about Citrus County is that it gives families room to explore at their own pace. Maybe your kids want another swim at Hunter Springs. Maybe they want to wander downtown Crystal River, go for another bike ride, find ice cream or sit by the water and watch for wildlife. Let them choose.

Because sometimes the most meaningful first isn’t swimming with a manatee or spotting a scallop. It’s the first time your child discovers that an adventure doesn’t need to be planned to be unforgettable.

Why they’ll remember it: Because they helped create the memory themselves. And those are often the moments that stick.

Someday, your kids might forget what they packed, what they ate for breakfast or how long the drive took. But they’ll remember the first manatee they saw. The first scallop they found. The first time they paddled across a spring or rode their bike farther than ever before. And you’ll remember the look on their faces when they did.

That’s the magic of Citrus County. It’s not just a place to visit. It’s a place to try something new, discover something extraordinary and make the kinds of memories that grow more meaningful with time.

Ready to make some first-time memories? Plan your Crystal River and Citrus County getaway and request a FREE Visitor Guide, or book a certified manatee tour and get ready for an adventure your family won’t soon forget.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8250. The Best Nonprofits That Support Dads and Fatherhood

The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.

Research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better. We celebrate dads on Father’s Day because we should celebrate everything that makes children’s lives — and outcomes — better. When children have close relationships with father figures, they tend to avoid high-risk behaviors; have higher-paying jobs and healthy, stable relationships; and have higher IQ test scores. The benefits go on, but one thing’s for sure: Dads matter in the lives of children, and so we should support and celebrate their presence in their kids’ lives.

Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.

All Pro Dad is a program of Family First that provides tools and resources to dads that allow them to be more present in the lives of their children. Spearheaded by former NFL coach Tony Dungy, NFL player Benjamin Watson, ESPN personality Dan Orlovsky, and many other prominent sports figures, All Pro Dad hosts a yearly interactive get-together for kids and dads at an NFL or NCAA stadium and a monthly school program where dads meet up with their children at school to spend time bonding and relationship building.

The Center for Family Policy and Practice is a nonprofit organization that advocates for fair and equitable laws and policies that affect low-income families and fathers. Focusing on child support, family safety and security, and financial and economic security, the CFPP acts as a think tank to develop solutions to barriers experienced by low-income fathers and fathers of color.

The Child & Family Blog provides research-driven content on the impact of family on social, emotional, and cognitive child development. In addition to covering topics like race, divorce, and inequality, the Child & Family Blog covers research on the importance of fathers and the role they play in both the family dynamic and the development of children.

The Family Equality Council works to ensure that members of the LGBTQ community have the ability to create families and provide support, education, activism and advocacy, and the resources they need to become parents and foster loving, healthy family relationships. The FEP also tracks national and state legislation that affects the ability of LGBTQ couples to become parents and maintain parental rights.

Fathering Together provides anyone who identifies as a father with tools and resources to uplift and support them as they work to create a “more equitable society.” The organization hosts different communities so that dads from every walk of life can reach out to peers for help, support, and advice while working to make the world a better and safer place for their children.

The Fatherhood Project is a Massachusetts-based program that empowers fathers to become more “knowledgeable, active, and emotionally engaged with their children.” Through research-based principles and curricula and programs like Dads Matter, Dads in Recovery, Teen Dads, and Divorcing Dads, the organization aims to help all dads be more present and engaged with their children while focusing on dads in marginalized and underserved communities.

Fathers Incorporated is an Atlanta-based nonprofit that works with federal lawmakers and leaders in the responsible fatherhood movement, faith and business leaders, and family law practitioners to advocate for legislative and community changes that promote fathers’ involvement in the lives of their children. The group focuses on co-parenting, domestic violence, incarceration, child development, child support, and employment and financial stability. Fathers Incorporated provides resources and programs for fathers to engage with their children healthily and raise awareness through programs like the Million Fathers March and Black Dads Count.

Fathers’ Uplift is a one-of-a-kind organization that provides fathers with the tools they need to overcome trauma, addiction, racial barriers, and emotional issues to help them fully engage with their children and families. Fathers’ Uplift provides therapy, coaching, training opportunities, and youth enrichment with the aim of reducing the number of children raised without positive father figures in their lives. It is the only organization in the United States that offers therapy, counseling, and addiction support specifically geared toward fathers and their families with the aim of reuniting families and providing them with the framework to thrive.

The National Fatherhood Initiative is the country’s largest provider of research on the involvement of fathers and the impact fathers have on families. It provides communities with resources and training to increase father engagement with the goal of ensuring that communities and human service organizations have the tools and training they need to be father-inclusive so fathers can be more involved in the lives of their children.

The Native American Fatherhood and Families Association is an Arizona-based nonprofit focusing on nourishing family relationships through its Fatherhood Is Sacred/Motherhood Is Sacred (FIS/MIS), Linking Generations by Strengthening Relationships, and Addressing Family Violence & Abuse programs. Employing culturally sensitive curricula and materials, NAFFA is able to address the specific concerns of the Native American community to reunite families and empower fathers to become family leaders.

The National Partnership for Women and Families understands that families benefit when dads are present and actively engaged. One way the NPWF is creating a more equitable world for women is by spearheading programs, legislation, and calls to action that support fathers by promoting active fatherhood and gender equality.

Established in Brazil in 1997, Promundo has worked globally to engage fathers in the care economy, promote active fatherhood and promote gender equity and justice by engaging men and boys with women and girls. The organization is currently undergoing a rebranding to be more inclusive of all genders. Its new name, Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, “reflects our commitment to fostering gender equity and our roots in social justice. The name change also captures our approach of collaborating with and never overshadowing our diverse partners worldwide.”

An all-inclusive vacation with kids should make family time easier, not leave parents juggling restaurant reservations, activity schedules, and snack requests every few hours. At Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort, Spa & Casino in the Dominican Republic, families can explore a sprawling resort, splash in pools, and enjoy activities for all ages.

The resort is part of the Lopesan Costa Bávaro Resort, Spa & Casino complex in Punta Cana, a destination known for its white-sand beaches and turquoise Caribbean waters. With family accommodations, supervised kids’ activities, and options for teens who prefer to spend time away from their parents, Lopesan Caoba Lagoon offers a setup that makes multigenerational family trips or vacations with school-age kids easier to plan.

Whether your family wants to spend most of the day in the water or mix pool time with games, dining, and evening entertainment, there are plenty of ways to make the vacation your own.

The largest family accommodation configuration combines a Resort Junior Suite Connecting room with a Family Junior Suite Connecting room. Together, the rooms offer 1,179 square feet of space for up to seven guests, with one king bed, two queen beds, a sofa bed, and two bathrooms.

That layout is especially useful for families traveling with several children, grandparents, or another family member. Two bathrooms make getting ready for dinner much less chaotic, while connecting rooms let parents stay close to younger children without everyone sharing the same sleeping space.

#8247. The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era. At one time, men preferred “Sire.” Other times, “Father” was preferable. What we do know is that the most agreed-upon way to refer to dad these days is by calling him, well, ‘dad.’

But why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad? The short answer is that things have gotten a little less formal. But the reason we’ve moved away from formality is that we’ve embraced what’s more linguistically natural for children and parents. ‘Father’ comes from the Proto-Indo-European “pəter” and Old English ‘fæder,’ meaning “he who begets a child,” reflecting the baby-talk sound “pa” as well as a phonetic shift from ‘p’ to ‘f’ in Middle English.

However, ‘dad’ did not evolve from ‘father.’

“It’s from ‘dada,’” says Professor John H. McWhorter, a professor at Columbia University, “a natural sound from children’s mouths as a second stab at consonants after they try the most natural ‘mama.’ Next is often either ‘dada, ‘tata,’ ‘baba’ or … ‘papa.’ Upon which, ‘father’ starts in Proto-Indo-European as “puh-TAIR,” and the ‘puh’ part is this same thing: what started as ‘pa’ in ‘papa.’ The words for Mommy and Daddy are the closest thing to linguistic universals because they are about mouth anatomy in infants rather than thought.”

There are also another key reason why this is reinforced over time. Emie Tittnich, a specialist at the University of Pittsburgh, speaking to Live Science, noted that parents generally refrain from using pronouns like ‘I’ or ‘you’ to avoid confusing their kids with abstract concepts early on. “‘Parents will use [‘mommy’ and ‘daddy’] to help their children learn the role names and also to indicate the relationship, ‘mommy and me,'” says Tittnich. “It usually takes the child awhile to understand that the same person can be called two different names.”

The agreed-upon naturality of these linguistic principles mean that as American society has become more colloquial and secular over time, we move (at least in this instance) away from a term that’s reflective of a status quo based in rigid concepts of class and religion—one of the meanings of ‘fæder’ in Old English is ‘supreme being,’ according to the Online Etymology Dictionary. As a result, we’re generally caught off guard when we hear a child refer to a parent as ‘father.’

However, this is not the case unanimously. We spoke with six dads who prefer — or simply stuck with — ‘father’ instead of ‘dad.’ Some do it as an homage to their own fathers; others do it to sound more authoritative. Others do it because it’s what their kids like. All have their reasons and, maybe, deep inside, some are just big fans of Proto-Indo-European language. Here’s what they say.

I sometimes worry that it sounds a little austere out loud, but it’s just what my father always asked us to call him, and it felt like it was important to me that we carry that on. No one in my family has had a problem with it. I think you can still be a ‘dad’ and be called ‘father,’ if that makes sense. It’s basically semantic, in that way, but it’s also more than semantics. — John, Baltimore, MD

It’s less of a request or a demand or anything, but when we were teaching my oldest what everything is called, we always just said ‘this is your mother’ and ‘this is your father,’ and he liked to say that, too. So we’ve kept it. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t think it was just adorably proper to have our little man coming up to us and saying, “father, mother, may I use the bathroom,” or what have you. But as with everything, I don’t mind anything that seems to feel natural for my kids and makes them happy. — Eric, Austin, Texas

My son didn’t start until he was older. I think he thought it sounded more respectful, or just more professional. We’ve always been a more traditional family, in how we carry ourselves, I guess you would say. So perhaps this was his way of taking that in stride, or contributing to that. My wife teases me about it sometimes. I should clarify, it’s generally him introducing me to other people that way. ‘This is my father, have you met my father?’ etc. — Patrick, Twin Cities, MN

In the past two years, my older daughter, age 21, began calling me ‘father’ and as strange as I found it, I didn’t mine it at all. Now, my four-year-old calls me “father” and I guess I now have a new title. As long as I am not being called ‘Henry,’ I am okay with it. — Henry, Boston, MA

I have eight children—three boys and five girls. I’ve always asked that they call me ‘father’ not to be domineering but because the house could get a little chaotic, as you can imagine, and my wife and I felt that it was a label that was more authoritative and kept things from being too chaotic. ‘Please don’t touch your father’s golf clubs’ just has a better ring to it, I guess. — Elliott, Charlotte, NC

I love that my children call me ‘father,’ because of the sense of responsibility it instills in me. Your ‘dad’ or ‘daddy’ is there to lend you the car, your ‘father’ is there to raise you, and protect you and make sure that you have the tool you need to succeed in life. When my kids call me ‘father,’ it reignites that sense of purpose for me every day, and reminds me it’s up to me to make their world a great place to grow up in. — Sam, Alachua Country, FL

This article was originally published on May 17, 2019

#8246. How Fatherhood Changes Men's Brains And Bodies Forever

Men experience neurobiological and physiological changes to prime them for fatherhood — not unlike how women’s bodies prepare them for motherhood.

We know how women’s bodies adapt to motherhood. Hormonal shifts, neurological flips, and, of course, the obvious post-partum biological changes. But only recently have scientists begun to focus on how men’s bodies adapt to fatherhood. We now know that fathers experience changes in their hormone levels (especially testosterone and oxytocin); their brains respond differently to parent-related stimuli, and even their socioeconomic status tends to change once children arrive.

Here’s the data behind these conclusions:

In 2014, a team of scientists at Emory University recruited 88 heterosexual, biological, married fathers of children between the ages of 1 and 2, for an unprecedented experiment. They tested their hormone levels (among other metrics) and compared these results to a group of 50 non-fathers. One of the most striking results is depicted below. Compared to non-fathers, dads had lower levels of testosterone, a male hormone linked to aggression, and higher levels of oxytocin, a hormone thought to play a role in maternal (and now, perhaps, paternal) attachment. The findings suggest that fathers, not just mothers, experience hormonal changes to help them adapt to their new roles as highly attached and less aggressive caregivers.

After running the hormone analysis, the researchers at Emory took the experiment one step further. They hooked each man up to an fMRI—which measures activation of different brain regions—and show him images of children and adults making happy, sad, and neutral faces. In the middle frontal gyrus, a brain region responsible for face emotion processing, fathers’ brain activities spiked for children’s faces significantly more than for adult faces. As depicted below, non-father brains made no such distinction. The results suggest that fathers’ brains change, too, helping them augment empathy towards children.

Beyond the biological implications of fatherhood, studies have shown that men with children experience psychological and social changes, too. But, unlike women who take pay cuts when they give birth, the financial impact of fatherhood on men is quite positive. The data below comes from City University of New York research, which found that fathers in the city have made more money, on average, than non-fathers since at least 1990. It is unclear whether the sudden burden of diapers and saving for college drives men to earn more, or whether it’s simply wealthier men who choose to start families. But one thing is clear from the preponderance of research: fatherhood changes men. Financially, hormonally, and neurologically.

#8245. What They Don’t Tell You About Paternity Leave

Paternity leave is a time to take in the necessary seismic shift in the way you think about time management, work, and life.

The first month that you have a child is life-changing in ways that are hard to describe. While there is plenty of scientific research to back up the idea that fathers get their brains rewired by having a child, the biggest change that occurs is that your concept of time is forever altered. And that’s why, at the start of your child’s life, you need to take some time off. Taking paternity leave is one of the most important things a dad can do, not just for their partner and their child, but for themselves. This may seem obvious on paper, but the vast majority of men who have access to reasonable paternity leave benefits end up not taking advantage of it.

Don’t become a statistic. Your time will become more precious to you than ever before once you’re a parent. And paternity leave is the only buffer you have to get yourself and your family adjusted to the new normal.

Here’s how dads need to advocate for paternity leave, and what to do with your time once it happens.

Regardless of the job you're in or the pay structure, the conversation with your boss about leave shouldn’t be a question of permission, it should be a conversation about how much time you’re taking off. There may be some legal questions about what your state is technically obligated to offer you, so certainly do your homework first. But, even in the absence of a clear paternity leave policy, you shouldn’t be begging for time, but rather, approaching the conversation as a negotiation for exactly how much time is reasonable for you, versus what makes sense for your job.

If your job already has a paternity leave policy, the amount of time you should take should be the maximum amount offered. “But I don’t need all that time?” you say. Well, you probably do.

You’re going to end up needing other parenting time off, and you’re going to have to negotiate a new relationship with work. This is one of the many things that paternity leave does. From pretty much now until the end of time you will have someone else’s schedule on your mind. This will impact your work schedule — not for better or worse, it just will — and paternity leave is your transition to this new juggling of schedules. In another sense, you’re setting a precedent with your job. Do you want it to be one that is sustainable? If so, take paternity leave.

No matter how you think of your career, having a kid is, without question, a pivot point for it. Before now, work-life balance was more of a theory; a calculus about how many drinks you could have at happy hour versus how hungover you’d be the next day. Having a child makes all of those prior considerations seem quaint. And so, the best way to think about paternity leave is that it’s the transition from one kind of career to the next.

In your previous life, you managed your time and money, perhaps, with a shoulder shrug and a “good enough” mentality. But being a parent isn’t like that. Everything you do, from hitting a deadline to taking out the trash, matters a little bit more. Good enough isn’t really good anymore. Yes, you’re going to make mistakes. That’s what parenting is all about. But it’s also nothing like a job. You’re not clocking in and out. If you think you’re suddenly going to have time off from being a parent, you won’t.

This is what makes time management so crucial — and why you need to take paternity leave to get your new schedule in order. Because you’re not at work, you are able to live in this period of transition. It’s weird. It’s hard. But without paternity leave, you’d barely be able to process it.

Unless you are the primary caregiver who is nursing with the child, the vast majority of the time you’ll have a job that will suddenly be more important than you’ve ever realized — cleaning up. When it comes to bottles, breast pump parts, new baby clothes, and blankets, keeping everything clean in those early months is essential. If your wife was the person who did laundry before, or kept an eye on your dirty dishes, those days are over.

Here’s a hot tip: Do you still have your apron from when you waited tables? Don’t have an apron? Get an apron. Preferably one with pockets. It's great for storing bottles, burp clothes, diapers, and pretty much everything else to keep your household sane.

When you add it all up, parents lose about six years of sleep when they have a child. This will not magically get resolved when your child turns six, by the way. But the strange sleep patterns that you have during those first few weeks are truly hellish. The only way to deal with this is to accept it as soon as possible. Again, this is one of the reasons why paternity leave is so important. Both you and your partner are going to have to come up with an ad hoc sleep schedule in order to literally not lose your minds.

The sooner you understand that feeding and caring for a newborn is like working a double shift that never ends, the better. If you slept on a few chairs pushed together in the delivery room when your kid was born, the first month or two aren’t too different from that. It does get better, but the sooner you get over how horrible it is, the better.

Chances are, your partner will be even more exhausted than you are. And so, amid all the cleaning, helping, and wrestling in your mind with your raging id, you have to remember how special this time is. Yes, take a ton of pictures. No, you’ll never regret taking a million pictures when your child is a newborn. If anything, these photos will become even more incredible to you as the years pass. You’re lucky to live in a time when you have a movie studio in your pocket. Take advantage of it. Pay for the extra phone data. Get those digital photos printed up into albums right away. It’s all worth it.

But when you’re not being the support parent, when you’re not contemplating how the rest of your life is forever different, the best thing you can do is hold your child as much as possible. You’ve probably heard of the “football” grip by now, the thing where you can fit your kid into the crook of your arm. This is one of the coolest things ever, and it may seem like it will never end, but you won’t believe how fast this time goes.

Newborn babies sleep all the time. Yes, statistically, they’re going to do a big chunk of that sleeping with mom. But you’re on paternity leave for one big reason, a reason that is more important than all the other reasons: You need to put that kind on your chest, and in your arms, and make sure this little person knows that they are safe with you, forever.
